en: The Scripture Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin,
Volume One. Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Dispersing Grandee, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, and the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Dharmapāla, et al.
Translated by Imperial Decree. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa together with a great assembly of seventy-two thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats—whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions; whose minds were well-liberated and whose wisdom was well-liberated; who, like great dragon kings, had accomplished all that was to be done; who had laid down their heavy burdens and attained their own welfare; who had exhausted the fetters of existence; whose minds were liberated through right knowledge; who possessed mastery over their minds and had reached the supreme further shore; who had skillfully entered the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and raised the banner of the Dharma; who could renounce all gain and honor; who had rightly and excellently gone forth and were perfectly complete; and who were fulfilled in all aspirations and dwelt in the path of nirvāṇa—with the sole exception of one person still abiding in the stage of training, namely the Venerable Ānanda.

There were eighty-four thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were in their final birth before buddhahood—having attained all dhāraṇīs and realized all-knowledge; they were currently advancing toward all-knowledge, gradually entering into all-knowledge, expanding all-knowledge, and had obtained unimpeded dhāraṇīs and all samādhis.

Furthermore, they are able to dwell securely in the wondrous *samādhi* of the King of Śūraṅgama, possessing great supernormal powers and moving with sovereign ease. Treading the path of lightness and tranquility, they are free from all arising obstacles and burdens. Their great loving-kindness and great compassion pervade all worlds throughout the ten directions; they transcend boundless Buddha-fields and penetrate the practices of emptiness and signlessness, remaining detached from all vows. They diligently initiate supreme practices for the benefit of all sentient beings and skillfully enter the realm of all Buddhas.
Their minds are like space, endowed with boundless wisdom; their minds are like the great ocean, deep and bottomless;
their minds are like Sumeru, the king of mountains, firm and immovable; their minds are like the lotus flower, free from all defilement and attachment; their minds are like...
Their jewels were exquisitely pure, and their minds were as refined, brilliant, and immaculate as the finest gold— namely,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnaketu, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnapāṇi, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnamudrāhasta,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnakuṇḍala, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnaśikhin.
...the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnakūṭa, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnākara, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnaśikhara,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnadhvaja, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Suvarṇagarbha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnagarbha, and Śrī...
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Gocara, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Viśuddhagocara, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vimalaviśuddhagocara,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Tathāgatagarbha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jñānagarbha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sūryagarbha,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samādhigarbha, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Padma...
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Flower Treasury, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Moon of Liberation,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Moon, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Radiance, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal...
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Eye, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Lotus-Eye, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Wide-Eye,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Dignified Conduct, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Adorned Marks,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Universal Precept-Wisdom, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Wisdom.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Dharmamati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vijayamati,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Uttaramati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajramati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Paramamati,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhamati, and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrīḍita.
...the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Great Sound-King, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Lion’s Roar Sound,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Deep and Wondrous Resounding Voice, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Untainted,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Free from All Defilements, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Moonlight, and the Sun...
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prabhāsa, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Jñānaprabha,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Jñānaśrī, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhadraśrī, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Candraśrī,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Padmaśrī, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnaśrī.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta was the foremost among this assembly of bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, there were the sixteen great beings, such as Bhadrapāla, as well as all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, such as Maitreya.
The assembly of devaputras of the Four Great Kings, headed by the Lord of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings;
the assembly of devaputras of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, headed by Śakra, the Lord of Devas; the assembly of devaputras of the Yāma Heaven, headed by Suyāma, the Lord of Devas;
the assembly of devaputras of Tuṣita Heaven, headed by the Lord of Tuṣita Heaven; and the [assembly of devaputras of] Sudarśana...
The devaputras of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, headed by the Lord of Emanation;
the devaputras of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations, headed by the Lord of Controlling Others' Emanations;
the host of the sons of Māra, headed by the leader Sunirmita; the devaputras of the Brahmakāyika Heaven, headed by the Lord Mahābrahmā; and Maheśvara.
The assembly of devaputras from the five Pure Abodes, headed by Śuddha;
the innumerable hundreds of thousands of asuras, including the asura kings Vemacitrin, Mahābala, and Rāhu;
and the great nāga kings Anavatapta and Mānasa.
The great nāga king Sāgara, the great nāga king Ānanda, the great nāga king Vāsuki,
and an assembly of countless hundreds of thousands of nāga kings; the nāga prince Śrītejas and countless hundreds of thousands of sons of nāga kings,
along with various nāga maidens, as well as other countless hundreds of thousands of devas—
A great assembly was gathered, consisting of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.

At that time, within a distance of four *yojanas* in all four directions around Elephant Head Mountain, the great assembly of devas and humans filled the void of space, such that there was not even a space the size of a single hair-tip or a minute atom left empty.

In the midst of such an assembly of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, he spread out for the Buddha a wondrous lion throne upon which he was to sit.

The seat was one yojana in height, with its length and breadth each measuring half a yojana; it was adorned with countless hundreds of thousands of exquisite celestial jewel-garments, and jeweled bells and nets were spread out as canopies, completely covering it from above.
Furthermore, there were countless hundreds of thousands of exquisite celestial silks draped all around, with scattered pearls and various wonderful flowers.

Moreover, the ground surrounding the lion throne was composed entirely of vajra; it was magnificently adorned, as level as the palm of a hand, soft, pure, and fragrant with exquisite scents, with countless hundreds of thousands of exquisite celestial jewel-flowers strewn across its surface.

Furthermore, there were lotuses as large as chariot wheels, with hundreds of thousands of golden petals, stems of lapis lazuli, pericarps of sapphire, and filaments of agate; they possessed exquisite fragrances that were lovely, pleasing, and delightful, and were thus adorned for the enjoyment of the Buddha.

Furthermore, at the four corners of the lion throne, neither too near nor too far, there were four jewel trees that rose up most loftily; they were half a yojana in height and three krośas in circumference, dense and luxuriant.

At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon the lion throne amidst the great assembly; with his supremely pure wisdom, he turned the wondrous Wheel of Dharma, subduing the armies of Māra and remaining untainted by worldly dharmas, letting out a lion’s roar, radiant and fearless.

He is like a great pond, pure and free from impurity; like the great ocean, vast with accumulated wondrous jewels and deep without limit or bottom; like Sumeru, the king of mountains, rising high above all other peaks; like the light of the sun, majestic and brilliantly radiant; like the full moon, beloved and cherished by all people; like the great dragon king, able to rain down the rain of Dharma; and like the Great Brahmā King, supreme within the world.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was together with an assembly of countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of disciples—such as Brahmā kings and world-protectors—who were all infinitely well-disciplined; at that time, this great multitude gazed upon the World-Honored One with single-minded sincerity and truthfulness.

At that time, the World-Honored One first illuminated the great assembly with his ordinary radiance; from within this ordinary radiance, he again emitted a great light from the crown of his head called "Universal Illumination. This light was further accompanied by countless hundreds of thousands of rays of light as its retinue. Having universally shone throughout all worlds in the ten directions, the light circled the Buddha’s presence three times to the right and then re-entered through the World-Honored One’s mouth.

Yet the features of the Buddha, the World-Honored One’s mouth remain entirely without movement or stillness. It is like the light of the sun and moon, which all enters the realm of space, yet the realm of space itself remains without movement or stillness;
when the Buddha’s radiance enters through his mouth, the absence of any sign of movement or stillness is likewise so.
Furthermore, just as when dry sand is piled up and clarified butter or water is poured upon it, there is no movement or stillness whatsoever as they enter;
so too, when the Buddha’s light enters through the opening of the mouth, there is likewise no sign of movement or stillness.

At that time, to the east of this buddha-field, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there was a world named Mahāpadma. In it dwelt a Buddha named Padmanetra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who was proclaiming the essential Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas.

The Dharma he teaches benefits beings solely by means of the One Vehicle; in that Buddha-field, even the names "śrāvaka" and "pratyekabuddha" do not exist, let alone the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, the sentient beings in that world all cultivate the practices of bodhisattvas and attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Moreover, in that world, they do not rely on food and drink for sustenance; those bodhisattvas all take meditative concentration (*samādhi*), dhyāna, and the joy of the Dharma as their nourishment.
Furthermore, that world is not illuminated by the sun, moon, or stars; rather, it is entirely purified by the universal radiance of that Tathāgata’s body.
Moreover, that land is devoid of all grasses, trees, pebbles, gravel, earth, stones, or mountains; its ground is as level as the palm of a hand.

In that place there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin who dwelt alone in a certain spot; if any sentient beings hear this bodhisattva’s name, all their obstructions and karmic burdens will be completely eliminated.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, touched by the radiance of the Buddha’s light, departed from his own abode and proceeded to the place where that Buddha was. Having arrived, he bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

Likewise, the other bodhisattvas, each touched by the radiance of the light, all left their respective abodes and came together to the place where the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Padmanetra, was. Having arrived, they each bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee upon the lotus pedestal, joined his palms in prostration, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"For what reason does this radiance exist—so exceedingly excellent, stainless, pure, and pleasing—that it causes the bodies and minds of all sentient beings who are touched by its light to become harmonious and tranquil?
At that time, the Tathāgata Padmanetra addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin, saying:
"O son of good family!"

To the west, beyond as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River from this Buddha-field, there is a world named Sahā. In it dwells a Buddha, titled Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
If any sentient beings hear the name of that Tathāgata, they shall all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is the light manifested by that Tathāgata.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nīvaranaviskambhin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what cause and by what condition do all sentient beings who hear the name of that Tathāgata all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
The Tathāgata Padmanetra addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin, saying: "Good son!
When that Buddha-Tathāgata was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, he made this vow, saying:”
"I vow that when I have attained perfect enlightenment in the future, all sentient beings who hear my name shall all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin said: "How so,
World-Honored One?"
“Are all sentient beings in that world entirely non-retrogressive? The Buddha said, “No.”
“Good son!
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin asked: “How so?”
“World-Honored One!
If that is so, are there also sentient beings who do not hear the name of that Buddha?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! All have heard it.
Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said:
“If all have heard [the teaching], why is it that there are some who must inevitably regress?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
"What is called 'all those who are non-retrogressive' is also not 'all those who are non-retrogressive.
Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said:
"As the Buddha has taught, 'all those who are non-retrogressive' is also not 'all those who are non-retrogressive.'"
"What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing the name of the Tathāgata, give rise to the seeds of non-retrogression, I say that these sentient beings attain non-retrogression;
it is not the case that all who hear the name of the Tathāgata simultaneously attain the stage of non-retrogression.
“Good son! I shall now further provide an analogy to establish this meaning.

It is like a tree whose seed is first planted; that seed is free from all defects, and subsequently, through various conditions, it produces sprouts and stems, eventually growing until fruits and seeds are formed.
“Good son! For what reason is it said that for those trees there is only the seed?
Bodhisattva Apanīkadharṣaṇa replied:
“World-Honored One!
Because the seed is free from all defects until the fruit is fully realized, it is called a ‘seed.
The Buddha said:

“Good son! It is the same for sentient beings who have attained non-retrogression: as soon as they hear the name of the Tathāgata, the seed of non-retrogression arises in full, and those sentient beings immediately attain non-retrogression regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Tathāgata Padmanetra, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to go to the Sahā world to behold the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, to pay homage, attend upon, draw near to, revere, and make offerings to him.”
Thereupon, the Tathāgata Padmanetra addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, saying:
"Son of good family!
You should go; now is precisely the right time."
The other bodhisattvas together addressed the Tathāgata Padmanetra, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We, too, wish to go to the Sahā world to behold the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, to pay homage, serve, attend upon, revere, and make offerings to him.”
Then that World-Honored One addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Sons of good family!
You may go; now is precisely the right time."
Nevertheless, as you go to that world, do not give rise to negligence. Why is this?

Because the sentient beings in that world are extremely prone to greed, hatred, and delusion; they lack the perception of śramaṇas, brahmins, or their parents; they engage in unrighteous desires; they are violent, cruel, and coarse; they utter evil words; they are haughty and contemptuous; they are stained by attachment and indolence; they break the precepts and commit evil deeds; and their stinginess and envy are rampant—such are the many kinds of afflictions and secondary afflictions [that prevail there].
"That Buddha, the World-Honored One, preaches the Dharma among such evil sentient beings.
Those bodhisattvas addressed their Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"That Buddha-Tathāgata was able to perform what is difficult to do; he was able to preach the Dharma for such evil sentient beings.
The Buddha said, "O sons of good family!
So it is, so it is. That Buddha-Tathāgata was able to perform what is difficult to perform, preaching the Dharma among sentient beings who are wicked.
Furthermore, son of good family!

Those sentient beings are likewise in this regard; they are able to perform what is difficult to perform, for it is extremely difficult for anyone within that world of defilement to give rise to even a single virtuous thought.
Why is this? In a pure world, for pure sentient beings to give rise to a virtuous mind—how could that be considered rare?

It is extremely rare within a defiled world to be able to perform virtuous deeds; to be able to give rise to pure faith for even the duration of a finger-snap, to take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha Jewels for the duration of a finger-snap, to practice pure precepts for the duration of a finger-snap, to abandon a mind of greedy attachment for the duration of a finger-snap, and to give rise to a mind of compassion and resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the duration of a finger-snap—this is truly most rare.
The bodhisattvas said:
"How marvelous is this world!
How marvelous is the Sugata!"
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, headed by the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, all exclaimed in praise: "Excellent!
In the presence of that Buddha, they have acted according to the manner of his conduct, heard what the Buddha spoke, and followed the Buddha’s instructions."
Having each bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet in prostration, they departed from the assembly and simultaneously proceeded to the Sahā world.

There, before the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Buddha, they performed acts of offering; some manifested various jewel trees, their branches and trunks smooth and rounded, their colors and forms flourishing and lush, fully endowed with flowers and fruit.

Some manifested beryl trees, some manifested crystal trees, some manifested kalpa-trees, some manifested trees of pure gold, some manifested various flowering trees, and some manifested various fruit-bearing trees; others manifested clouds of exquisite jewel garments, clouds of ornaments, clouds of ointment-scented incense, clouds of precious garlands, clouds of exquisite parasols, clouds of powdered incense, or clouds of drums and music. Having each manifested these according to what was appropriate, they all gathered together to lead the assembly of bodhisattvas, headed by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, as they came to the Sahā world.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"O noble ones!

The suffering of the sentient beings in that Sahā world is profound and heavy; you should, according to your respective spiritual powers, go there to skillfully transform them, so that those sentient beings may attain supreme and wondrous bliss."
When the bodhisattvas had heard these words, they practiced according to the instructions.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, manifesting various transformations through his own supernormal powers in accordance with their respective forms, emitted from within his body a great radiance—exquisite, stainless, pure, and refreshing—which caused the bodies and minds of all sentient beings who were touched by its light to become harmonious and tranquil.

This light shines universally and extensively throughout this trichiliocosm; all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm who belong to the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and so forth, being touched by the light, are all freed from suffering and their hearts of malice and harm are stilled, such that they all conceive of one another as parents.

Furthermore, within this trichiliocosm, in those places that are secluded, hidden, and shrouded in darkness where the light of the sun and moon does not reach, this radiance shines universally. All the suns and moons, which possess great supernormal power and great majestic virtue to shine with sovereign brilliance, are eclipsed and rendered invisible by this light; they are entirely deprived of their function of blazing and radiant illumination.
Furthermore, this trichiliocosm was universally illuminated by light, such that all sentient beings born therein were able to see one another.

Moreover, throughout this trichiliocosm—including the Cakravāḍa mountains, Mahācakravāḍa mountains, Mucilinda mountains, Mahāmucilinda mountains, jewel mountains, black mountains, and all other mountain ranges—the light shone everywhere, reaching upward to the Brahma world and downward to the Avīci Great Hell; in every direction between them, there was no place not reached by its radiance.

At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas, according to those physical forms and as was appropriate for each, likewise performed various acts of transformation through their supernormal powers, so that all sentient beings obtained food if they needed food, drink if they needed drink, clothing if they needed clothing, carriages if they needed carriages, and wealth if they needed wealth; the blind were able to see, the deaf were able to hear, the naked were provided with coverings, those who were confused regained right mindfulness, the suffering obtained happiness, and all pregnant women gave birth without difficulty.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Apanīkadharanirghoṣa and the assembly of all bodhisattvas came to this Mount Gajaśīrṣa, not far from the mountain.
Those great beings simultaneously manifested exquisite jeweled nets that completely covered the trichiliocosm.

Furthermore, they rained down from the sky a multitude of celestial flowers, as well as clouds of celestial fruits, clouds of celestial jewel garlands, clouds of celestial ointments, clouds of celestial garments, clouds of celestial powdered incense, and clouds of celestial robes, jeweled parasols, banners, and pennants—all various articles of offering.
Once these vast manifestations had appeared according to their respective displays, all sentient beings were able to behold them and attained the most supreme happiness.

At that moment, all the groves of trees on Mount Gajaśīrṣa spontaneously vanished from those locations, and in their place appeared various kinds of exquisite jewel-trees, kalpa-trees, flower-trees, fruit-trees, sandalwood trees, and aloeswood trees—all of which were transformations produced by supernatural power.
Furthermore, from the midst of the sky, the wondrous sound of a celestial drum spontaneously emerged.
Within the sound of that drum, a verse was spoken:
"Born most excellently in the Lumbinī Garden, He cannot be compared to those of the nature of afflictions."
I bow my head to the peerless one, who is like space; therefore I have come to this most excellent mountain.
Seated beneath the supreme tree of the Way, you attained Bodhi;
Awakening and subduing the army of Māra’s power, I bow my head to the one who holds supreme, stainless light; therefore I have come to this most excellent mountain.

Like a phantom, like a mirage, like the moon reflected in water—having fully realized all such principles of reality, I bow my head to the supreme tree of great merit; therefore, I have come to this most excellent mountain.

Realizing that worldly phenomena are like a theatrical play, Skillfully manifesting all dharmas like a rainbow, I bow my head to the Immovable One, the supreme treasury of merit; Therefore, I have come to this most excellent mountain.

Having passed through many hundreds of eons over a vast duration, for the sake of fulfilling the heart of compassion, I bow my head to the Honored One with the stainless moon-like face; therefore, I have come to this most excellent mountain.

Accompanied by many hundreds of koṭis of bodhisattvas, and likewise honored by all the devas, I have bowed my head to those who have departed from the darkness of delusion; therefore, I have come to this most excellent mountain.
Having attained the supreme treasury of the noble Dharma, you have cast aside worldly wealth for the sake of compassion;
I bow my head to you, the peerless one who brings great benefit, and thus I have come to this most excellent mountain.
Abiding in a tranquil mind with constant compassion, like a lotus in water free from all defilement—homage to you, the supreme holder of merit;
therefore, I have come to this most excellent mountain.
A pure body with exquisite features like blooming flowers, Endowed with the marks and signs that sustain the world— I bow my head to the jewel-tree with its boundless branches;
Come here to receive this offering, and I pray you, accept me.

When the drum had finished reciting these verses, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what reason has this auspicious sign appeared at this time?
It is something never before heard and never before seen.
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"To the east of this buddha-field, passing through worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there is a world named Mahāpadma.
Therein dwells the Buddha, the World-Honored One, named Padmanetra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently resides, teaching the Dharma and benefiting sentient beings."

In that buddha-field there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, who, together with countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattva mahāsattvas, has come to this Sahā world; because that assembly is about to arrive, these omens have first appeared.

Having spoken these words, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas, each employing their vast power of great supernormal faculties, came to where the Buddha was. Upon arrival, they each bowed their heads at the feet of the Buddha in prostration.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin spoke these verses:
“Possessor of great renown and supreme wisdom, Attainer of great fearlessness, Great Muni,
Having already crossed the perilous straits of birth and death, I bow my head to you who have transcended the shore of afflictions.”
You are the pervasive, blazing light; you are the all-pervading great torch.
You have attained all doors of liberation; I bow my head and take refuge in the Peerless One.
Firm and immovable like the king of mountains, Deep, vast, and bottomless like the great ocean,
Unable to be shattered by any heterodox or external paths— I bow my head and praise the Great Dharma King.
Phenomena are originally quiescent and unborn; their self-nature is thus eternally extinguished.
You, the Noble Sage of my Dharma, have skillfully elucidated this; I bow my head to the one who turns the Great Wheel of Dharma.
Some proclaim the various right paths; some speak of entering into the true principle;
some speak of the sublime gateway to nirvāṇa; and some speak of bestowing the prophecy of attaining the fruit of enlightenment.
You know the mental dispositions of all sentient beings; therein is not the slightest thing you do not know.
Sentient beings observe that your practice of the Dharma is perfected; therefore, they follow and revere your instructions.

All the three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as all other various defilements, were entirely incinerated by the great fire of wisdom when you sat beneath the Bodhi tree and attained perfect enlightenment, O Honored One.
Having attained liberation yourself, you deliver sentient beings; having attained liberation yourself, you benefit the world.
Having well sought what is virtuous within the world, you have forever shattered the perils of birth and death.
Lacking wisdom, beings have long lain in deep slumber, wandering through the cycle of birth and death;
O Holy One, you skillfully awaken them, and I bow my head to you who regard all equally as your own kin.
Behold this assembly of great beings, all of whom dwell securely on the path to enlightenment;
they all desire to hear the sublime gateway of the Dharma—may the World-Honored One please teach it accordingly.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin had spoken these verses in praise of the Buddha, the Buddha commanded him to sit on a lotus pedestal to one side;
the Buddha likewise commanded the rest of the great assembly of bodhisattvas to each sit on a lotus pedestal to one side, as was appropriate for them.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee upon the lotus pedestal, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I now wish to question the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; if the Buddha, the World-Honored One, would deign to grant me his attention, I shall pose my questions, and I pray that you will explain them for me.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin, saying: “Great Being!
It is but natural that you ask whatever you wish; all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas likewise grant permission for whatever doubts you may have, and the Tathāgata shall explain each point to you.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, receiving the Buddha’s holy command, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice so as to attain the perfection of giving?”
Furthermore, how does one attain the perfection of ethical discipline?
How does one attain the perfection of patience?
How does one attain the perfection of diligence?
How does one attain the perfection of meditative concentration?
How does one attain the perfection of wisdom?
How does one attain the perfection of skillful means?
How does one attain the fulfillment of vows?
How does one attain the fulfillment of power?
How does one attain the fulfillment of wisdom?
How does one attain the bodhisattva who is like the earth?
How does one attain [the bodhisattva] who is like water?
How does one attain [the bodhisattva] who is like fire?
How does one attain likeness to the wind?
How does one attain likeness to space?
How does one attain likeness to the moon?
How does one become like the sun?
How does one become like a lion?
How does one achieve self-mastery?
How does one come to understand?
How does one become like a lotus flower?
How does one attain a vast mind?
How does one attain a pure mind?
How does one attain a mind free from doubt?
How does one attain wisdom as vast as the ocean?
How does one attain subtle and wondrous wisdom?
How does one attain the eloquence of wisdom?
How does one attain the eloquence of liberation?
How does one attain pure eloquence?
How does one attain eloquence that brings joy to all sentient beings?
How does one attain speech that inspires faith and compliance?
How does one attain the speech of the True Dharma?
How does one attain practice in accordance with the Dharma?
How does one skillfully enter the Dharma-realm?
How does one dwell in the realm of emptiness?
How does one attain the practice of signlessness?
How does one attain the state where all vows are free from attachment?
How does one attain the body of loving-kindness?
How does one attain the body of compassion?
How does one attain the practice of sympathetic joy?
How does one attain the practice of equanimity?
How does one attain the playful mastery of supernormal powers?
How does one become free from the eight difficulties?
How does one attain the non-forgetfulness of the bodhicitta?
How does one attain the knowledge of past lives?
How does one attain the non-abandonment of spiritual friends?
How can one always remain far removed from evil associates?
How can one obtain the Dharma-nature body of the Tathāgata?
How can one obtain the adamantine, true reality body?
How does one become a great guide?
How does one become well-versed in all paths?
How does one skillfully expound the non-perverted path?
How does one attain constant abiding in the sublime state of meditative equipoise?
How does one wear rag-robes?
How does one maintain the three robes?
What is meant by always sitting and never lying down?
What is meant by always begging for food?
What is meant by eating in a single sitting?
What is meant by not drinking liquids after a meal?
What is meant by undertaking the dharma of the araṇya?
What is meant by sitting at the foot of a tree?
What is sitting in an open space?
What is dwelling among corpses?
What is moderation in eating?
How does one follow the arrangement of seats?
How does one attain the practice of correspondence?
How does one uphold the sūtras?
What is meant by upholding the Vinaya?
What is meant by upholding the Abhidharma?
And how does one become fully endowed with the rules of conduct, the practices, and the path of dignified demeanor?
How can one become free from the two dharmas of stinginess and envy?
How can one give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings?
And how can one properly perform offerings and service to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas?
How can one subdue all forms of pride?
How can one broaden and increase pure faith?
How can one skillfully understand worldly conventions?
How does one thoroughly understand the ultimate truth?
How does one thoroughly know all dependently originated phenomena?
How does one know oneself?
How does one know others?
How can one be born in a pure buddha-field?
How can one be born free from the defilements of the womb?
How can one abandon home and go forth into homelessness?
How can one obtain a pure livelihood to sustain oneself?
How can one attain a mind free from weariness and indolence?
How does one receive the instructions and commands of all Buddhas?
How does one obtain a joyful countenance?
How does one become free from the expression of frowning?
How does one become one who has heard much?
How does one come to be embraced by the True Dharma?
How does one become a prince of the Dharma?
How can one surpass the Brahma kings, Śakra, and the world-protecting devas?
How can one know the mentalities of sentient beings?
How can one know the various methods for maturing sentient beings?
How can one become a wise person?
How can one attain a state of constant and sublime bliss?
How can one skillfully understand the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*)?
How does one attain the perfection of the excellent marks?
How does one become a refuge for others?
How does one become like a great and wondrous medicinal tree?
How can one diligently cultivate meritorious deeds?
How can one skillfully understand all matters of transformation?
And how can one swiftly realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good son! Your question is most excellent.

Out of compassion for the world, you are able to cause the great assembly of devas and humans to obtain wholesome benefit and happiness by inquiring of the Tathāgata regarding such meanings as these. Listen attentively now and apply your mind well; I shall explain it for you."
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: “Good son!
If a bodhisattva practices ten kinds of giving, they will attain the perfection of generosity.
What are these ten?
First, the gift of the Dharma;
Second, the gift of fearlessness;
third, the gift of material wealth;
fourth, the gift that does not seek a fruit of benefit in return.
Fifth, giving out of compassion;
sixth, giving without contempt;
seventh, giving with reverence.
Eighth, the gift of honoring and serving;
ninth, the gift of non-attachment;
tenth, the pure gift.
“Good son! What is the gift of Dharma?

It means that if a bodhisattva, with no mind for material gain, teaches others the Dharma he has received himself as appropriate, not for the sake of desiring profit, offerings, or honor; not out of a desire to be known by others; not for the sake of reputation; and not for the sake of any other matter.”
One should simply reflect:
"Which sentient beings are undergoing various sufferings and afflictions?
I shall eliminate them for their sake."
"By means of this very Dharma, he likewise harbors no heart of seeking; he proclaims it for others with non-dual equanimity.
Whether he proclaims it for kings and their ministers, or for caṇḍālas and the sons of caṇḍālas, his teaching of the Dharma is likewise."
How much more so for other multitudes of people?
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices this gift of Dharma, they do not give rise to a sense of superiority. Good son!
This is called the bodhisattva’s gift of Dharma.
What is the gift of fearlessness?
It refers to when a bodhisattva personally discards weapons such as swords and staves, and likewise instructs others to discard them as well.
Toward all those sentient beings, one should conceive of them as one's father, as one's mother, as one's child, as one's kinsman, and as other beloved relatives and friends.
Why is this? The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"As the Buddha has taught, throughout all successive births everything undergoes transformation; within the assembly of sentient beings, there has never been anyone who was not one's father, mother, child, or other beloved kinsman and friend. Even toward those with the most subtle life-force, one should give rise to benefit for them, even to the extent of giving one's own flesh."
"How much more so for other great classes of sentient beings?
"Noble son, this is called the bodhisattva’s gift of fearlessness."
"What is the gift of material wealth?
It refers to when a bodhisattva, upon seeing sentient beings who have committed extremely unwholesome deeds, immediately gathers those sentient beings through the gift of material wealth."
Having gathered them through material gifts, he causes them to completely abandon unwholesome actions and establishes them in all wholesome actions.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"As the Buddha has taught, giving is the bodhi of a Bodhisattva."
The practice of giving performed by a bodhisattva eliminates three kinds of unwholesome dharmas:
first, envy; second, stinginess; and third, greed;
for this reason, I have received the dharma of giving from the Tathāgata.
"In that which he gives as alms, he harbors no sense of superiority.
Son of good family!
This is what is called the bodhisattva’s gift of material wealth."
"What is giving that does not seek a beneficial result?

It refers to the practice of giving by a bodhisattva which is not caused by desire, not caused by wealth and profit, not caused by a circle of followers, and not caused by worldly affairs; such is the natural way in which a bodhisattva cultivates and maintains the dharma of giving."
The practice of giving performed by means of those causes and conditions is devoid of all beneficial karmic rewards.
Son of good family!
This is called the bodhisattva’s gift that does not seek beneficial rewards.
"What is the gift of compassion?

It is when a bodhisattva sees sentient beings undergoing various sufferings—whether they are hungry or thirsty, naked, defiled or maimed, or those who are without a master, without rescue, without refuge, without support, or lacking merit—and having seen them, gives rise to a heart of compassion, thinking:

'For the sake of these sentient beings, I have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Considering how these classes of sentient beings, without masters, without rescue, and without refuge, wander through birth and death, by what skillful means shall I now act as their master, their rescuer, and provide for them a refuge and support?'"
When he formed this thought, the Bodhisattva, impelled by this heart of compassion, immediately employed skillful means to accept and guide them accordingly.
As the Bodhisattva accepted those sentient beings, he cultivated roots of goodness together with them, yet remained free from any sense of superiority.
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva’s gift of compassion.
What is the gift that is free from contempt?”

That is to say, when a bodhisattva practices giving, he does not give with discrimination based on lightness or heaviness; he does not give out of an arrogant mind; he does not give out of malice or slander; nor does he give by causing others to labor; he does not give out of prideful indulgence in his wealth and status; he does not give in hope of a reputation; and he does not give out of haughty pride in his great learning.
When a bodhisattva practices giving, their mind must be respectful and reverent, making offerings with focused attention and personally presenting the gifts.
Son of good family!
This is called the bodhisattva’s gift free from contempt.
"What is the gift of reverence?

It means that when a bodhisattva encounters preceptors, teachers, and others who are worthy of respect, as well as those practicing the holy life, they are physically extremely deferential and mentally deeply respectful. Because of this deference and respect, they speak words of consolation, join their palms, prostrate themselves, and welcome those beings with their heads bowed; they then extend to them various matters consistent with virtue."
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva’s gift of respectful reverence.
What is the gift of worshipful service?
That is to say, if a bodhisattva performs the work of a Buddha, or the work of the Dharma and the Sangha;

or if, at the site of a Tathāgata’s stūpa or image, they sweep away dust and filth, or adorn and purify it, or make offerings with exquisite incense, flowers, and unguents, or repair the old and ruined stūpas and temples of the Tathāgata—this is called the work of a Buddha.
What is called "Dharma-activity"?

It refers to whatever Dharma-gate one hears, immediately receiving and upholding it, copying it, reciting it, contemplating it, practicing it, and explaining it to others; or training in accordance with it without error—this is Dharma-activity.
What is meant by performing the affairs of the Saṃgha?

It refers to offering robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicinal requisites for the sick to the community of monks; even providing a mere small amount of clear, cool water as an offering constitutes an affair of the Saṃgha.
“Good son!
This is called the bodhisattva’s gift of honoring and serving.
What is the gift of non-attachment?
That is to say, when a bodhisattva practices giving, they give rise to this thought:
"The gift I now bestow seeks no reward from the heavens, nor anything else from the heavens; it seeks no reward from kings, nor anything else from kings."
“Good son! This is called the bodhisattva’s gift of non-attachment.
What is the pure gift?

That is to say, when a bodhisattva, in accordance with the Dharma of giving as it has been taught, gives rise to investigation; at the time he gives rise to such various investigations, does he, through investigating the Dharma of giving, find it to be free from fault, free from defilement, and free from obstacles?
“Good son! This is called the pure giving of a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva can cultivate these ten dharmas, they will attain the perfection of generosity.”
"Furthermore, noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of precepts, he shall attain the perfection of ethical discipline.
What are these ten?
First, the practice of the prātimokṣa precepts;
second, the bodhisattva’s practice of the vows of restraint (saṃvara-śīla);
third, the practice of the precepts that are free from the burning afflictions (kleśa).
Fourth, the practice of ethical discipline that is free from lack of profound and firm attention;
fifth, the practice of ethical discipline that fears karma;
sixth, the practice of ethical discipline that fears transgressions.
Seventh, the practice of precepts that fears what is not to be grasped;
eighth, the practice of precepts with firm resolve;
ninth, the practice of precepts free from dependence or attachment.
Tenth is the practice of the precepts with the three wheels purified.
"Good son, what is the practice of the prātimokṣa precepts?

That is to say, when a bodhisattva, regarding all the sūtras, the vinaya, and other points of training proclaimed by the Tathāgatas, practices each and every dharma according to reason—just as one who applies correct attention respects what the Great Teacher has spoken—without attachment to lineage, without attachment to views, and without attachment to assemblies; being free from the faults of a self or a person, they develop reverence for those points of training.
"Noble son!
This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the prātimokṣa precepts.
What is the practice of the restraint of moral discipline (saṃvara-śīla)?"
That is to say, if a bodhisattva reflects in this way:
"Within the prātimokṣa precepts, I cannot realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

That is to say, regarding whatever bodhisattva practices and bodhisattva training rules the Tathāgata proclaims in each individual sūtra, I shall practice and train therein according to the principle.
"What is the conduct of a bodhisattva?

It is that for a bodhisattva there is no non-place, no non-direction, and no non-time; their actions are never untimely, their speech is never without knowledge of the proper time, they are never without knowledge of the direction, and they are never without knowledge of the measure."

Why is this? Because there may be sentient beings who have conceived a lack of faith toward the Tathāgata; in order to cause them to give rise to faith and understanding, and for the sake of gathering and protecting those beings, the Bodhisattva is able to personally fulfill the supreme practices of enlightenment, being well-endowed with dignified deportment, gentle and composed, unadulterated by worldly clamor, and tending toward the gate of tranquility and the gate of ultimate purity—this is the conduct of a Bodhisattva.
“What are the training precepts of a bodhisattva?
They are the teachings for the training of a bodhisattva that the Tathāgata proclaims in each and every sūtra.
When a bodhisattva gives rise to faith and compliance toward these, and does not create obstacles or difficulties, this is the training precept of a bodhisattva.”
"Good son! This is called the bodhisattva’s practice of the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*).
From the *Buddhabhāṣita-sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Fascicle Two."
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin,
Scroll Three. Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Rank of Chao San Da Fu, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
the Great Master of Fan, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Fahu, and others.
Translated by Imperial Decree: "Furthermore, noble son, what is the practice of precepts that is free from the burning of all afflictions?

It refers to when a bodhisattva is not burned by the fire of greed, nor burned by the fire of hatred, nor burned by the fire of delusion, nor burned by the fires of other afflictions, nor burned by the fires of other harms caused by the appropriation of enjoyments."
If one wishes not to be consumed by burning, one should give rise to the antidote to craving and should distance oneself from the conditions that give rise to craving.
What is meant by the antidote to craving?
The contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is the antidote to craving.

Regarding this contemplation of impurity: it refers to all the impure things within one's own body—hair, body hair, nails, teeth, saliva, tears, mucus, spittle, phlegm, dirt, sweat, urine, feces, skin, flesh, blood, bones, marrow, fat, grease, brain, membranes, sinews, veins, spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, intestines, stomach, bladder, and abdomen.

A bodhisattva should cultivate the perception of these various impure things and reflect as follows: "Even those in the world who are foolish, ignorant, and unwholesome, once they have come to know such impure things as these, do not dwell in a state of craving."
"How much more so for the wise?
This constitutes the Bodhisattva’s various contemplations on impurity as an antidote to craving.
"What are the conditions from which craving arises?"
This refers to being attached to various sensual desires; or, upon seeing a woman’s beautiful and exquisite form, giving rise to a mind of fondness and conceiving a desire to grasp her.
At that time, having seen her, one should perform this contemplation:
"As the Buddha has taught, the objects of a dream have no reality."
"Why would a wise person give rise to a mind of craving toward this dream-like realm?
This is called the bodhisattva’s distancing from the conditions that give rise to craving.
"What is meant by the bodhisattva’s antidote to anger and the distancing from the conditions that give rise to that anger?

It is said that a bodhisattva frequently gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward all sentient beings; through this mind of loving-kindness and its causal conditions, he is able to subdue the minds of those sentient beings who are agitated, angry, or wrathful, and all conditions for anger are completely distanced. This is called the bodhisattva’s antidote to anger and the distancing from the conditions that give rise to that anger."

When one observes in this manner, one immediately becomes free from the dharma of delusion; because of being free from delusion, those various desires and enjoyments are not incinerated by the fire of affliction. These constitute the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline of being free from the burning of all afflictions.
"What is the ethical conduct of being free from unfirm mental attention?
It means that when a bodhisattva dwells alone in a quiet place, he does not give rise to this thought:

'My practice is not distracted; I dwell in tranquility; I am further able to practice the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata. As for other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, their practices are all distracted and full of worldly bustle, and they have completely fallen away from the Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata.'"
"If one is able not to give rise to such thoughts, this constitutes the bodhisattva’s ethical conduct of being free from unfirm mental attention.
What is the bodhisattva’s ethical conduct of gathering virtuous dharmas?"
That is to say, if a bodhisattva reflects in this way:
"As the Buddha has taught, all bhikṣus should revere the cultivation of merit, revere the protection of the precepts, and revere the cultivation of wisdom."
Why is this? Because one who honors merit finds that merit is the present experience of desirable, radiant, and pleasing karmic results.
One who has such faith is able to distance themselves from all unwholesome karma; this constitutes the bodhisattva’s practice of the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas.
"What is the practice of precepts characterized by dread of transgressions?

It means that if a bodhisattva perceives even a transgression as small as a mote of dust, they feel total dread toward it and refrain from committing it; they do not regard even the slightest transgression with indifference, but reflect:

'As the Buddha has taught, just as a person who ingests a small amount of poison will meet their end, so too one who ingests a large amount will meet their end; likewise, those who possess transgressions—whether few or many—all fall into the evil destinies.'"
"When a Bodhisattva, while conducting such an investigation, gives rise to a sense of dread toward transgressions, this is called the Bodhisattva’s ethical conduct of fearing transgressions.
What is the ethical conduct of fearing what is not to be grasped?"

This means that if there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or other persons who possess faith, and because they have faith in the bodhisattva, they entrust and deposit gold, silver, mani-jewels, pearls, coral, lapis lazuli, conch shells, precious treasures, wealth, and other articles of enjoyment with the bodhisattva; even if the bodhisattva is alone, he does not give rise to a mind of greedy attachment nor suddenly conceive a desire to take them for himself.

Furthermore, regarding the property of various stupas and temples, as well as the property of the Saṃgha, even if someone were to urge him to take charge of it, the Bodhisattva would not seek to take it for his own sustenance.

He reflects thus: "As the Buddha has taught, a Bodhisattva would rather cut the flesh from his own body and eat it than ever harbor a desire to take what another has not given or permitted, whether it be drink, food, or other things."
This is the bodhisattva’s practice of the precepts regarding fear of what is not to be grasped.
What is the practice of the precepts with firm resolve?

It refers to when a bodhisattva is being harassed and disturbed by the King of Māras, various hosts of Māras, or other devas—whether they manifest in female forms or through other means—to perform demonic deeds and seek to destroy them; yet the bodhisattva remains unmoved, unshaken, and suffers no loss. This is the bodhisattva’s practice of the precepts with firm resolve.
"What is the practice of precepts free from dependence and attachment?
It means that when a bodhisattva practices the precepts, they do not give rise to such thoughts as:
'The precepts I uphold are for the sake of seeking the reward of rebirth as a deva or other celestial realms; or for the sake of seeking the reward of kingship or other worldly status.'"
This is the bodhisattva’s precept practice of non-attachment and non-reliance.
What is the precept practice of the purity of the three spheres?
It refers to when a bodhisattva’s physical action is pure, verbal action is pure, and mental action is pure.
Purity of bodily action means being far removed from the three unwholesome bodily actions:
first, killing; second, stealing; and third, sexual misconduct. These are what are called unwholesome bodily actions.
Purity of verbal action refers to being far removed from the four unwholesome verbal karmas:
first, false speech; second, divisive speech; third, harsh speech; and fourth, frivolous speech. These are called the unwholesome verbal karmas.
Purity of mental action refers to being far removed from the three unwholesome mental actions:
first, greed; second, hatred; and third, wrong view; these are called unwholesome mental actions.

Because one is able to distance oneself from all unwholesome karmas, one thereby attains the purity of the three wheels; this is the bodhisattva’s ethical conduct of the purity of the three wheels. Good son!
If a bodhisattva practices these ten dharmas, they will attain the perfection of ethical conduct. "Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the perfection of patience."
What are the ten?
First, the patience of enduring suffering;
second, external patience; [and so forth].
Third, the patience of discerning phenomena;
fourth, the patience approved by the Buddhas;
fifth, the patience that is not fixed in direction;
Sixth, the patience of non-differentiation;
seventh, the patience that is not based on external causes or conditions;
eighth, the patience in enduring enmity and harm.
Ninth is the patience of compassion;
tenth is the patience of rescuing through the power of vows. "Good son!
What is the patience of enduring suffering?

It means that when a bodhisattva experiences sorrow, lamentation, pain, or affliction within his own mind, as soon as they arise, the bodhisattva remains composed and is able to endure them all without giving rise to a mind of anger; this is the bodhisattva’s patience of enduring suffering.
"What is external patience?

It refers to when a bodhisattva personally hears harsh words uttered by another, or hears them through hearsay, because that person has slandered their parents, teachers, elders, relatives, or spiritual friends, or has used abusive language to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha."

When a bodhisattva hears these things, they do not give rise to anger or resentment; remaining tranquil therein, they are able to endure them all. This is called the bodhisattva’s external patience (*bāhya-kṣānti*).
What is the patience of the thorough investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-kṣānti*)?

That is to say, when a bodhisattva hears within the most profoundly deep sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata that there is a dharma capable of severing the seeds of saṃsāra, liberating one from all fetters, and destroying the continuity [of existence]—namely, that all dharmas are originally quiescent and that all dharmas are by nature in nirvāṇa.
Having heard such a teaching as this, the bodhisattva does not give rise to fear or alarm, but reflects thus:
"If one does not understand this Dharma, nor attain this Dharma, how could one possibly realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
"For this reason, one should, within such profound dharmas, uphold, contemplate, cultivate, investigate, and give rise to resolute conviction.
This is called the bodhisattva’s patience through discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya-kṣānti*).
"What is the patience approved by the Buddha?
It means that if a bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of anger, resentment, or malice, they should immediately investigate:
'From where does this mind of resentment and malice arise, and in what place does it cease? "
"By what cause does it arise, and once arisen, where does it abide?

When one contemplates in this way, one perceives no dharma of anger or harm—neither its arising nor its ceasing—that can be apprehended as two distinct phenomena. It ceases immediately upon arising; neither its causes nor its conditions can be apprehended. For this reason, the Bodhisattva remains serenely patient within it and no longer gives rise to such thoughts. This is what the Buddha permits; this is called the Bodhisattva’s "Buddha-permitted patience."
"What is patience that is not restricted to specific circumstances?

It means that a bodhisattva is not able to practice patience during the day but cannot do so at night; or is able to practice patience at night but cannot do so during the day; or is able to practice patience in his own country but cannot do so in another country; or is able to practice patience in another country but cannot do so in his own country; or is able to practice patience toward those with whom he is familiar but cannot do so toward those with whom he is unfamiliar."

The bodhisattva is not like this; he is able to endure in all lands, in all places, at all times, and in all ways. This is called the bodhisattva’s patience that is not restricted to a fixed direction.
"What is non-discriminatory patience?
It refers to when a bodhisattva is able to practice patience toward his own parents, teachers, elders, relatives, friends, and acquaintances, yet is unable to do so toward other people."

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva is able to endure all forms of injury and affliction, even when coming from the families of caṇḍālas and others; this is called the bodhisattva’s impartial patience.
"What is patience that is not for the sake of worldly causes?

It means that when a bodhisattva practices patience, they do not do so for the sake of profit, nor out of fear, nor for the sake of sustenance, nor for the sake of mundane affairs, nor for the sake of concealing shame or modesty."
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva constantly practices the mind of patience; thus, it is said that a bodhisattva does not practice patience for the sake of external circumstances.
What is the patience of enduring enmity and harm?
That is to say, if a bodhisattva is not met with external conditions that inflict harm upon him, he has nothing at that time to endure.

Yet, if at some point an adversary should approach with a raised blade or staff, or with a clenched fist, intending to strike him out of a mind of anger and malice, or if they should threaten him and revile him with harsh words—when the bodhisattva sees such adversaries approaching to strike or abuse him, he fortifies his mind and deeply subdues himself through patience, reflecting as follows:

"These adversaries are all brought about by my own karma; having reached maturity, this karma now oppresses and afflicts me. Truly, they were not created by parents, kinsmen, or friends, but are entirely the result of the maturation of my own karmic actions. Furthermore, they are not produced by the external elements of earth, water, fire, or wind, nor are they produced by the internal four great elements."

When the Bodhisattva reflects in this way, by virtue of these causes and conditions, he is able to maintain an even mind toward both those who cause harm and those who do not, and to endure them all; this is called the Bodhisattva’s patience in enduring harm.
"What is the patience of compassion?

It means that even if a bodhisattva should attain the rank of king, or serve as a minister, or possess great wealth, sovereignty, and exceptional majesty, when he sees sentient beings who are beset by much suffering and affliction, and those sentient beings give rise to a mind of anger toward him as king, coming to revile, abuse, and harass him."
At that time, the king gave rise to no anger; he did not rely on his noble status to act with oppression, but reflected thus:

"These sentient beings are those whom I must convert; I ought to provide them with protection. Therefore, I shall now not rely on the majestic power of a king, but shall instead serve as their guardian so that they are not destroyed."
"Because of these causes and conditions, he endures with composure due to the arising of a compassionate heart; this is the bodhisattva’s patience of compassion.
What is the patience of rescue through the power of aspiration?"
That is to say, if a bodhisattva reflects thus:
"In the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, I utter this lion’s roar and make this vow:
'May I, having attained the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, universally rescue and deliver all sentient beings from the ocean of birth and death.'"

"I diligently practice to rescue and deliver all sentient beings without grasping at their signs; I do so only to bring all sentient beings to complete liberation and to cause their minds to be tamed and abide in śamatha."
At that time, if the Bodhisattva feels anger arise in his own mind and is unable to endure it, it is as the Buddha has said:
"Good son! It is like a person skilled in treating eye diseases, who can remove the patient's cataracts, obscurations, and dark veils."
At that time, the ophthalmic physician thought to himself,
"I wish to universally cause all patients to be rid of their cataracts and obscurations.
Suddenly, the physician lost his own eyesight.
"Good son! What do you think?
Is that physician able to cure the eye?"
He replied, “No. The Buddha said:
“Good son! It is the same for a bodhisattva:

wishing to use the eye of wisdom to guide all sentient beings in the world who are shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, if the bodhisattva themselves is covered by that very darkness of ignorance, they will be unable to remove the darkness from all sentient beings.”

Therefore, when a bodhisattva encounters various harms and afflictions, they do not give rise to anger but accept them with composure; this is called the bodhisattva’s patience of rescue through the power of aspiration. Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the perfection of patience.
Furthermore, son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the perfection of diligence.
What are the ten?
First, the diligence of donning the armor;
second, the invincible diligence;
Third, diligence that avoids the two extremes;
fourth, diligence for the benefit and happiness [of others];
fifth, diligence of application.
Sixth, continuous diligence;
seventh, pure diligence;
eighth, uncommon diligence.
Ninth, diligence that does not follow the instructions of others;
tenth, diligence free from arrogance. "Good son!
What is armor-like diligence?

It refers to when a bodhisattva arouses great diligence for the sake of all sentient beings universally: to cause those who have not attained nirvāṇa to attain it; to cause all those who have not been delivered to be delivered; to cause all those who are not liberated to be liberated; to cause those who are not at peace to find peace; and to cause those who have not realized perfect enlightenment to realize it.
When a bodhisattva exerts such diligence, some māras may come, wishing to sever and destroy the bodhisattva’s superior practice and to cause him affliction.
The māra speaks thus:
"O son of good family!..."
"You should now cease this exertion. Why is that?

I too once gave rise to such exertion, universally for the sake of all sentient beings: to cause those who had not attained nirvāṇa to attain it; to cause all who had not crossed over to cross over; to cause all who were not liberated to be universally liberated; to cause those who were not at peace to find peace; and to cause those who had not attained perfect awakening to attain perfect awakening."
All of these are unreal, false, and erroneous teachings—the words of fools’ disputations.
Son of good family!

I have never seen anyone who, by exerting such diligence, could cause even a single sentient being to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; I know only that they lead countless *koṭis* of sentient beings toward the realization of the *nirvāṇa* of the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
"Good son!
For these reasons, you ought to turn back from the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If you do not, the diligence you exert will only increase your afflictions and cause your efforts to be wasted in vain."
After Māra had spoken these words, the Bodhisattva reflected to himself:
"These evil Māras are seeking an opportunity to come and disturb me.
Having understood this matter, the Bodhisattva then addressed Māra, saying:
"You should not now distress me; you need have no concern for the world.
As the Buddha has taught, everything in the world grows from the seeds of one's own karma; whatever various karmas one has created oneself are the destination to which one goes."
Now you are likewise; because you have grown from the seeds of your own karma, it is your own created karma to which you must return.

You should now quickly return to your original place by the path from which you came and no longer harass me. Because you have disturbed me, you shall for a long night be tormented by suffering among sentient beings and bring them no benefit.
At that time, the evil Māra, cowering and disheartened, immediately vanished from that place and remained hidden.

When these hosts of evil Māras, or the Māra-devas and others, come to harass and disturb him, the Bodhisattva’s mind is neither startled nor terrified, nor does it become weak; this is called the armor-like diligence of a Bodhisattva.
"What is invincible diligence?

It refers to when a bodhisattva initiates diligence according to its various characteristics, such that at the very moment it arises, it is supreme. Even if all other bodhisattvas who have long practiced the path were compared to this bodhisattva’s superior practice of diligence, they would not equal even a fraction, a calculation, or even an *upaniṣad* part of it; how much less so could śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas?"

Why is this? Because as soon as a bodhisattva gives rise to a single thought of diligence, they possess all supreme powers and are thus able to universally encompass all Buddha-dharmas and sever all unwholesome dharmas; this is called the bodhisattva’s invincible diligence.
“What is diligence that is free from the two extremes?
It means that the diligence initiated by a bodhisattva should neither be excessive nor should it sink into despondency. Why is this?

If the mind becomes haughty when [exertion] intensifies, or if agitation arises when it sinks low, then to remain free from these two extremes is called the bodhisattva’s superior practice of diligence; this is the bodhisattva’s diligence that avoids the two extremes.
"What is the diligence of benefit and happiness?

It is when a bodhisattva arouses this diligence, making the vow: 'May this body of mine become equal to the body of a Buddha; may I obtain the Buddha’s mark of the invisible crown of the head (*anavalokitamūrdhatā*), as well as the Buddha’s circular halo and the full array of marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*); and may I attain the Buddha’s unsurpassed and boundless supreme wisdom, his great majestic virtue, and his supreme sovereignty.'"
The bodhisattva initiates diligence for the sake of these beings; this is called the bodhisattva’s diligence for the benefit and happiness [of others].
What is diligence of application (*prayoga-vīrya*)?

This application is, for example, like a person who takes a mani jewel or pure gold and polishes, refines, and smelts it to remove all flaws and impurities, so that the jewel becomes bright, pure, pristine, and its luster resplendent.
At that time, the mani-jewel and the true gold are seen to shine with a distinct brilliance.
It is the same for the bodhisattva: by applying effort and cultivation among all forms of diligence, they cause the removal of defilements and thereby depart from faults.

The defilements of diligence (*vīrya*) are as follows: laziness is a defilement of diligence; mental depression is a defilement of diligence; lack of moderation in food and drink is a defilement of diligence; false attachment to a self as a master is a defilement of diligence; not relying on the true Dharma is a defilement of diligence; and a lack of profound and firm attention (*manasikāra*) is a defilement of diligence. When such defilements exist within various forms of diligence, they are termed faults.
Therefore, if a bodhisattva is free from these [faults], they will attain a pure and stainless nature that is luminous; this is called the bodhisattva’s diligence of application (*prayoga-vīrya*).
What is the diligence of continuity (*prabandha-vīrya*)?

This refers to the diligence that a bodhisattva arouses within all modes of conduct; whenever it arises, whether in body or mind, it is characterized by an absence of weariness and proceeds in an uninterrupted succession. This is called the bodhisattva’s continuous diligence.
"What is pure diligence?

It means that when a bodhisattva is engaged in that very continuous practice of diligence, they should constantly eliminate and sever all unwholesome karma, as well as those factors that obstruct the path to enlightenment and lack beneficial purpose."

If there are any wholesome dharmas—namely, those that accord with nirvāṇa, conform to the practice of the right path, and lead toward bodhi and the factors of enlightenment—he causes all these wholesome dharmas to become vast and further increase. He does not give rise to even the most subtle unwholesome dharma for even a single moment, let alone grosser faults and afflictions.
This is the pure diligence of a bodhisattva.
What is uncommon diligence?
It is when a bodhisattva reflects as follows:

"Suppose that throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, great masses of fire were to emerge from the Avīci Great Hell and fill all these worlds, forming a single conflagration; and suppose that beyond these worlds, there were a single sentient being undergoing extreme suffering, without a master, without a savior, and without refuge. I would rather endure such suffering myself, traverse those worlds, and cross over that mass of fire to reach that sentient being and deliver them—how much less could I fail to endure a minor suffering?"
The diligence thus exerted by a bodhisattva is not shared with any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or those of heterodox and external paths; this is called the uncommon diligence of a bodhisattva.
"What is diligence that does not follow the instructions of others?
It means that a bodhisattva does not give rise to such a thought as a śrāvaka might:
'In the stage of an ordinary person, it is extremely difficult to seek the bodhi of a Buddha; the diligence I have aroused is very slight, and I am indolent and weak.'"

If I were to seek enlightenment, even if I were to carry a torch upon my head for many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, practicing with such diligence, I could not achieve it; therefore, I cannot endure such suffering, nor can I bear this heavy burden.
A bodhisattva should give rise to this thought:

"All the Buddhas of the past who have already attained perfect enlightenment, all the Buddhas of the present who are currently attaining perfect enlightenment, and all the Buddhas of the future who shall attain perfect enlightenment—all these Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, diligently practiced with vigor for the sake of seeking Bodhi."
Thus they cultivate these various sublime practices; yet the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not seek to attain perfect enlightenment for their own sake alone.
I am likewise now: I practice with diligent effort to accomplish these sublime deeds, not merely for my own sake, but so that all roots of virtue may be shared universally with all sentient beings.

For the sake of sentient beings, I arouse diligence; the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment that I seek to attain is for the universal benefit and happiness of all sentient beings. I shall not realize nirvana for my own sake alone; rather, for the sake of sentient beings, it would be far superior even if I were to dwell eternally within the great hells.
This is called the bodhisattva’s diligence that does not follow the instructions of others.
What is diligence without an arrogant mind?
It means that when a bodhisattva exerts diligence, they do not develop attachment to it within that state; they do not disparage others nor do they praise themselves.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"If one does not diligently attend to one's own task while exhorting others, how can one be called wise?
Therefore, the superior practices undertaken by the Bodhisattva do not give rise to arrogance.
This is the bodhisattva’s diligence free from pride.
Son of good family!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the perfection of diligence.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll Three.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master, Court Scattered Grandee and Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Imperial Preceptor Guǎngfàn, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject Wéijìng,
et al., by imperial decree: "Furthermore, son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyāna)."
What are the ten?
First, extensively accumulating merit;
second, frequently giving rise to wearying detachment.
Third, the arousal of diligence;
fourth, being endowed with extensive learning;
fifth, practicing and cultivating without inverted instruction.
Sixth, practicing in accordance with the true Dharma;
seventh, having faculties and natures that are clear and sharp;
eighth, possessing a purely virtuous mind.
Ninth, they skillfully master śamatha and vipaśyanā;
tenth, they do not cling to the signs of dhyāna.
What is meant by "extensively gathering merit"?

That is to say, if a bodhisattva has long accumulated roots of goodness within the Mahāyāna teachings, has skillfully cultivated ethical conduct throughout various lifetimes, and is sustained by spiritual friends, then wherever they are born, they will always be born into a great Brahmin family, or a great Kṣatriya family, or a great householder family, all of whom possess right faith.
In those births, by means of those causes and conditions, they further expand and increase their roots of goodness, never being separated from spiritual friends. Who are these spiritual friends?
Regarding the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—being able to increase their roots of goodness from previous lives through the power of habitual practice—they reflect thus:

"The world is great suffering; the world is afflicted by calamities; there is no moment of rest in the world, as it has long been entangled and shrouded by the darkness of ignorance. All of this is caused by and conditioned by craving."
"Having understood these causes and conditions, this constitutes the Bodhisattva’s extensive accumulation of merit.
What is meant by 'generating much weariness and aversion'?
It refers to when a Bodhisattva, for this reason, gives rise to the following reflection:"
"I should not now, amidst these worldly phenomena of conjunction, become stained by attachment or draw near to the objects of desire; for all such desires are false conceptual constructions."
