Why is this? Because these devas, humans, asuras, and others know that before long this bodhisattva shall sit at the site of enlightenment and realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; thus, they do not treat this person, the bodhisattva, with contempt.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will become like fire.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will become like the wind.
What are these ten?
First, because their conduct is unimpeded like the wind;...
Second, because the spheres of their activity are boundless;
third, because they shatter, disperse, and cause to fall the mountains of pride in sentient beings, like the wind;
fourth, because they blow forth and spread the rain from the vast clouds of the Dharma.
Fifth, because it extinguishes and removes the blazing heat of all worldly afflictions;
sixth, because it provides sustenance and nourishment for the wholesome dharmas of all sentient beings so that they remain unshakable;
seventh, because it contains the moisture of immeasurable dharma-clouds and sustains the great rain of Dharma.
Eighth, because it is beautifully adorned with various pavilions and galleries of the Great Dharma;
ninth, because the kalpa-trees adorning all assemblies constantly produce the rain of flowers of the definitive, sublime, and wondrous Dharma-sound that gladdens the mind;

tenth, because it is the cause of liberation through the mandala of the wind of wisdom that turns according to circumstances, being well-established in the unsurpassed, formless refuge, and adorned by the maturation and discipline of all sentient beings, as well as the arrays of the Mount Sumeru, the light of the sun and moon, the groves of Dharma-teachings, excellent palaces, and the Cakravāḍa mountains, which have been established and accumulated through oceans of samādhis, liberations, and dhāraṇī-doors within pure assemblies of noble ones over incalculable aeons.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll Six.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
The Great Master of Sanskrit Transmission, the Imperially Ennobled Purple-Robed Śramaṇa,
Subject Dharmarakṣa, and others, respectfully translated by imperial decree: "Furthermore, noble son,
how does a bodhisattva move without obstruction like the wind?"
"Good son!

Just as the wind in the world has no dependence and no attachment in any place, and possesses no form or appearance, yet is able to perform all its functions within those palaces, towers, pavilions, Mount Sumeru, the great oceans, and so forth."

The wind of a bodhisattva’s wisdom is likewise: while remaining unattached in all places, it is able to establish all those phenomena, such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

The aggregates are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. The elements are the eye element, form element, and eye-consciousness element; the ear element, sound element, and ear-consciousness element; the nose element, odor element, and nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, taste element, and tongue-consciousness element; the body element, tactile element, and body-consciousness element; and the mind element, mental-object element, and mind-consciousness element.
The bases are the eye base, form base, ear base, sound base, nose base, odor base, tongue base, taste base, body base, tactile base, mind base, and mental-object base.

Even regarding mundane and supramundane dharmas, as well as devas, wheel-turning sage kings (*cakravartin*), Brahmā kings, Śakra, the world-protecting devas (*lokapāla*), Maheśvara, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, the stages of all bodhisattvas, and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*)—though there is that which is performed, in all cases there is no dwelling or attachment.

Because they abide in non-attachment toward all things, whether they be of an existent nature or a non-existent nature, a singular nature or a diverse nature, or the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) and so forth—despite the countless mental states—they possess no differentiation of seeds, no volitional construction, and no objective referent; all are the unobstructed realm of liberation.

Therefore, the Brahma Kings, Śakra, the World-Protecting Devas, and others act in accordance with the Dharma; throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions, they cause all sentient beings and their affairs to obtain fulfillment. Having accomplished this in all places, they remain hidden and do not appear even until the final limit of the kalpa. Yet the Dharmakāya cannot be conceptualized as either distinct or non-distinct. This is what is meant by the Bodhisattva proceeding without obstruction like the wind.
"What is the boundless sphere of activity of a bodhisattva?

Just as the wind of the world can, throughout the ten directions, bring forth and perfect all seeds within immeasurable worlds, so too is the wind of a bodhisattva’s wisdom: it extensively manifests, awakens, and arranges all phenomena—both conventional and ultimate—within the universal and boundless realm; it widely proclaims the assemblies of Tathāgatas, the assemblies of bodhisattvas, and all worldly assemblies; and following thought and action, with an unimpeded mind, it penetrates all places in every direction without limit. This is the boundless sphere of activity of a bodhisattva."
"How does this bodhisattva, like the wind, shatter, disperse, and cause to fall the mountain peaks of the pride of sentient beings?"

Just as the winds of the world can blow against, strike, shatter, scatter, cause to fall, or obscure all mountains, stones, forests, and palaces, so too is the wind of a bodhisattva’s wisdom. There are sentient beings who, out of pride and delusion, cling to the view of a self and are haughty; they rely on their physical appearance, youth, nobility, wealth, physical strength, long life, health, and ease, as well as their skills, extensive learning, intelligence, retinue, riches, and eloquence. Relying on such things, they become intoxicated with arrogance. Because of these conditions, these sentient beings give rise to the notion of a self and turn away from the right path. The bodhisattva is able to proclaim the supreme Dharma for them to shatter that pride, enabling them to skillfully attain freedom from defilement and purity. This is how a bodhisattva is like the wind that shatters, scatters, and causes to fall the mountain peaks of sentient beings’ high arrogance.
"What is meant by the Bodhisattva blowing forth and spreading the great cloud of Dharma?

It is like the wind of the world blowing forth great clouds that arise from the four directions; these multicolored cloud-wheels produce thunderous, profound, soft, and beautiful sounds, as well as the sound of ocean tides and various kinds of chanting—resonant, uninterrupted, pure, subtle, and pleasing to the mind. Adorned with garlands of lightning, they universally cover hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of worlds. They are able to blow forth everything in all worlds that is lovely and delightful, such as crops, seeds, and all forest trees, while constantly pouring down rains of various jewels."

The wind of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom is likewise: it manifests clouds of various sublime physical forms, whose radiance shines universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions; it is a source of delight for all sentient beings, adorned with the most excellent marks and the lightning-garlands of light, and it issues forth the sound of the Dharma as it truly is, along with sixty thousand kinds of supreme and wondrous voices.

The wind of the Bodhisattva’s great compassion universally pervades the entire Dharma-realm and encompasses all worlds; it broadly covers all realms and rescues all sentient beings from the difficult places of the evil destinies. It manifests the wheel of light of all marks and signs, illuminating with the empowerment of pure radiance, causing all sentient beings to fully accomplish right conduct and destroy wrong conduct. It rains down the great rain of Dharma and adorns all with various ornaments, establishing the supreme joy of all worlds and placing all devas and humans in a state of unsurpassed bliss. It plants all seeds of mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas, as well as medicinal herbs and groves, and bestows the empowerment of the Dharma at all auspicious times. This is the Bodhisattva blowing forth and spreading the great cloud-rain of Dharma.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva extinguishing all the blazing fires of worldly afflictions?"

Just as the winds of the world blow upon and stir up excellent, pure, and cool water, universally quenching the suffering of heat experienced by sentient beings and causing them all to feel refreshing and joyful, so too is it with the wind of a Bodhisattva’s wisdom. It is able to extinguish all these blazing fires: the greed, hatred, and delusion of all sentient beings; the evil destinies, wrong views, misdeeds, and perverse conduct; extreme poverty and attachment to sensory objects; the suffering of encountering the hated and the suffering of being separated from the beloved; the afflictions of various diseases and even the craving for dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*). By pouring down the water of the Dharma, they attain supreme coolness. Through the power of their non-empty vows, whether seen or awakened to, there is no obstruction whatsoever. This is how a Bodhisattva extinguishes all the blazing fires of worldly afflictions and establishes all sentient beings in the stage of sorrowlessness (*araṇābhūmi*).
"What is meant by a bodhisattva sustaining and nourishing life without disturbing any wholesome dharmas of sentient beings?

Just as people of the world sustain their lives through the power of the winds of inhalation and exhalation, so too does the bodhisattva: by means of the wind of wisdom, they accomplish all wholesome dharmas for sentient beings, causing all sentient beings to become fully endowed with them and to give rise to joy."
"Furthermore, noble son!

Just as the winds of the world are able to establish all worlds—adorned with various kinds of exquisite and lovely features, namely the Diamond Rim, the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, and the four great continents; the great oceans and various jewels supported by the Golden Wheel; Mount Sumeru, Mahāsumeru, and other jewel mountains, up to the Snowy Mountains, Mount Gandhamādana, and so forth."
The various palaces and towers, Jambudvīpa and the four great continents, the small thousand-world system, the intermediate thousand-world system, and the great trichiliocosm.

The wind of a bodhisattva’s wisdom is likewise: it is able to initiate and accomplish the vast accumulations of merit for all sentient beings, arranging them in succession like the formation of the Snowy Mountains (Himavat). One should view it in this way: it is precisely the accumulation of worldly merit that has been accomplished.
Just as the formation of the four great continents and Mount Sumeru should be understood as the śrāvakas who are formed;
so too, the formation of a small thousandfold world system should be understood as the pratyekabuddhas who are formed.
Just as the formation of a medium chiliocosm should be understood as the sign of the vast accomplishment of a bodhisattva,

so too should the formation of a trichiliocosm be understood as the sign of the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s body endowed with the hundred merits— a body that rises high above all worlds, pervades all worlds throughout the entirety of space, is supremely wondrous, pure, and most highly praised, and which arrays all the objects and signs for the most excellent offerings.
When all these have been thus manifested, one abides eternally in samāhita.
Just as it was formed into a great ocean, it should be understood that this is the ocean of samādhi that has been accomplished.

Just as the great continents, intermediate islands, and other mountains, rocks, and the four great continents are formed, one should know that these are the various dhāraṇīs for the purpose of transforming and delivering sentient beings and the assembly of practitioners.
Just as the formation of palaces, towers, and various groves should be understood as the meritorious adornments of a pure buddha-field;

so too, the manifestation of various transformations from the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) should be understood as the ten stages (bhūmi), the ten perfections (pāramitā), the thirteen meditative absorptions (samādhi), the various dhāraṇīs, the light of the six supernormal knowledges (abhijñā), the three types of clear knowledge (vidyā), the various wisdoms, the ten masteries (vaśitā), and so forth—the supreme, sovereign, and vast qualities such as the powers (bala), fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), unique attributes (āveṇika-dharma), and great compassion (mahākaruṇā) of bodhisattvas and buddhas.
"Good son! Among these, what are the marks of the hundred merits of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones? Good son!"

Suppose that for the duration of one eon, worlds were accumulated throughout the ten directions, with each direction containing as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River times an incalculable number (*asaṃkhyeya*). If every sentient being within all those worlds were to possess the same mass of merit as a minor universal monarch (*kṣudra-cakravartin*) ruling over a trichiliocosm, and if the total aggregate of the merit of all such beings—each possessing the merit of a minor universal monarch—were calculated and combined, it would equal the mass of merit of a single great universal monarch (*mahā-cakravartin*).

Furthermore, beyond all worlds in the eastern direction, every sentient being within those worlds possesses a mass of merit equal to that of a single great universal monarch (*cakravartin*), as previously described; and so on, until all sentient beings throughout every world in the entirety of space across the ten directions each possess the mass of merit belonging to a great universal monarch. When these numbers are calculated, the mass of merit of such sentient beings is equal to the mass of merit of a single Śakra.

"Furthermore, suppose that in each of the ten directions there are worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and that every sentient being in each of those worlds were endowed with a mass of merit equal to that of Śakra."

All these Śakras, taken together and consolidated as one Śakra, [would possess such merit]; by this same calculation, all sentient beings throughout every world in the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm would each possess a mass of merit equal to that of the aforementioned Śakra.
By calculating according to these numbers, the mass of merit of such sentient beings is equal to the mass of merit of a single Great Brahmā King.

Furthermore, if in each of the ten directions there were worlds as numerous as the sands of an incalculable number of Gaṅgā rivers, and every sentient being in each of those worlds possessed a mass of merit equal to that of a Great Brahmā King;

If all these Great Brahmā Kings were gathered together as one single Great Brahmā King, and if, by that same calculation, every sentient being in all worlds throughout space and the entire Dharma-realm were endowed with a mass of merit equal to that of such a Great Brahmā King.

By calculating according to these numbers, the mass of merit of such sentient beings is equal to the merit of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who have attained the great earth, the great clouds of light, the bestowal of the dharma-empowerment, and the ten masteries.

“Good son! By means of this very matter, all sentient beings throughout the boundless worlds of the ten directions, as far as the limits of space, accumulate the entire mass of merit belonging to the three periods of time.

Taking that mass of merit from the three periods of time, equal in measure to all the atoms within every world throughout the entirety of space, and multiplying it a hundredfold, one constitutes each and every pore of the Tathāgata.
The mass of merit contained within each of those pores, multiplied by a factor of ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands, constitutes the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) of the Tathāgata.
The entire mass of merit contained within each of those secondary marks, multiplied by a factor of ten unspeakable numbers, constitutes the thirty primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Tathāgata.

Each of those individual marks, when multiplied ten times by an ineffable number, constitutes the mark of the Tathāgata’s supreme white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa), which is perfectly round, stainless as a lunar disc, and more exquisite and sublime than a thousand other lights located between his eyebrows.

Taking these very marks and multiplying them by ten unspeakably unspeakable thousands of koṭis, one thus accomplishes the Tathāgata’s mark of the uṣṇīṣa, which is preeminent throughout all worlds and invisible to sight.

When these very characteristics are multiplied by a factor of ten times unspeakably unspeakable *koṭī-nayuta-śata-sahasra*, they constitute the sixty thousand kinds of infinite sounds of the Tathāgata’s objects of focus; these flow forth as exquisite and unconditioned, causing all sentient beings to give rise to great joy and revealing the pure speech and the great eloquence of the Buddha throughout all worlds.

“Good son! This is called the mark of the hundred merits of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones. The Tathāgata universally adorns himself with these inexhaustible practices of merit and wisdom, extensively nourishing and sustaining the lives of all sentient beings.”

“Good son! Suppose that throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of space and pervading the entire Dharma-realm, all sentient beings in every world were to dwell for the duration of one eon in the rank of a Bodhisattva on the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā), possessing all superior marks—namely, those adorned by body, speech, and mind—and endowed with all dhāraṇīs and the ten masteries.”

These bodhisattvas, using vessels made of Jambūnada gold equal in measure to the expanse of space and as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, each filled with various kinds of jewels, come and go moment by moment throughout that duration until the final limit of the *pariniṣpanna-kalpa*, each entering into a single pore of the Tathāgata; yet, within a single pore of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the mass of merit neither increases nor decreases.
"Good son! These are the marks of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable hundredfold merits.
Furthermore, what are the twelve stages?

These are the so-called Ground of the Unarisen Bodhicitta, the Ground of Joy, the Ground of Purity, the Ground of Radiant Light, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground Difficult to Conquer, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Going, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Excellent Intelligence, the Ground of the Dharma Cloud, and the Ground of Universal Radiance of the Buddha—these constitute the twelve grounds.
"What herein is the stage of the bodhisattva who has not yet set forth the mind for enlightenment?

It refers to this bodhisattva who transcends all the erroneous practices of foolish worldlings, as well as all the Brahmā kings, Śakras, World-Protectors, gods, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas of the three periods of time; who is most supreme, surpassing all worlds; whose every mode of conduct is auspicious and who adorns his body, speech, and mental actions; who universally illuminates the boundless worlds of the ten directions with a great wheel of light; who attains the *dhāraṇī* of unimpeded power of action; and who, within each and every mark throughout incalculable worlds, exercises mastery without restriction."

“In the world-system of the four great continents, there appears a vast adornment of a pervasive network of fragrant light. Standing upon lotuses that serve as footstools, he sits upon a wondrously adorned throne the size of the limits of a great trichiliocosm. Having attained perfect mastery over all phenomena, he skillfully observes and accomplishes the characteristics of objects of focus that are unimpeded and pleasing. He manifests ten kinds of great signs and incalculable signs, demonstrating the dharma of non-retrogression.”

"In all boundless directions and locations, as they travel, they emit inconceivable great nets of light; manifesting bodily images within the various adornments of immeasurable lands, they act as sovereigns of unspeakably many worlds, exhorting them to receive empowerment and supreme sustaining grace. Throughout all mundane and supramundane realms, they constantly rain down the great rain of immeasurable Dharma-jewels; through the gateways of wondrous radiance, they remain entirely unobstructed, universally and extensively performing the most supreme acts of giving and merit."
He accords with all worlds and is universally able to fulfill the non-empty aspirations of all sentient beings.

Those who behold him all give rise to wholesome, wondrous, lovely, and pure minds. He causes all worlds to tremble and rescues all infinite sentient beings in the evil destinies and elsewhere according to their thoughts. He is universally able to embrace the dharma-gates for making offerings to infinite Buddhas, and he sports in all incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) samādhis, dhāraṇīs, liberations, supernormal powers, and clear insights. He delights in the gardens of infinite, supreme, and wondrous dharmas without attachment, attaining the light of joyful conduct that is free from conceptualization and doubt throughout infinite *koṭi* kalpas.

“Throughout countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, he has brought to perfection his cultivation within the stages of the pure Mahāyāna; he has accomplished various deeds for the benefit of others, and his hundreds of thousands of types of superior practices of merit and wisdom have reached ultimate fulfillment through vast prior conduct.”

If one were to possess the practice of the dharma through the most supreme faith and understanding, one would attain the first stage; however, according to the sequential stages of development, this bodhisattva has not yet generated the mind of enlightenment.

“Good son! For example, although a wheel-turning sage king has already transcended the physical appearance of humans, he has not yet attained the physical appearance of a deva; likewise, this bodhisattva has also transcended all the stages of the world’s śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, yet has not yet attained the supreme bodhisattva stage.”

"Furthermore, the Buddha-ground of Universal Radiance is without center and without periphery, entirely pure without exception; it possesses mastery over all phenomena and is able to skillfully contemplate infinite varieties of signs, universally causing all sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness."
“What are the ten kinds of samādhis practiced by bodhisattvas?
They are: first, Ratnoccaya;
second, Supratiṣṭhita;”
Third, immovability;
fourth, non-retrogression;
fifth, the Jewel Accumulation;
Sixth, Sunlight Flame;
seventh, Accomplisher of All Aims;
eighth, Wisdom Radiance;
Ninth, abiding before the Buddhas of the present;
tenth, the Śūraṅgama and other such boundless samādhis practiced by bodhisattvas.
"Furthermore, there are twelve kinds of dhāraṇīs.
What are the twelve? They are:
first, the consecration (abhiṣeka);..."
Second, great wisdom;
third, pure vocal resonance;
fourth, the inexhaustible treasury;
Fifth, the Boundless Revolution;
sixth, the Ocean Seal;
seventh, the Lotus Array;
Eighth, entering the gate of non-obstruction;
ninth, definitively giving rise to the various analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*);
tenth, abiding in the adornments of a Buddha.
Eleventh, the mark of boundless color;
twelfth, the fulfillment and perfection of the Buddha’s bodily marks—these are the twelve kinds of dhāraṇīs.
"Furthermore, there are the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). What are the six?
First, the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*);..."
Second is the supernormal power of the divine ear;
third is the supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds;
fourth is the supernormal power of knowledge of recollecting past lives.
Fifth is the supernormal power of the knowledge of psychic transformations;
sixth is the supernormal power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows—these are the six supernormal powers.
Furthermore, there are ten kinds of mastery belonging to the bodhisattvas.
What are the ten?
First, because one possesses the power of longevity throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, there is mastery over life;
second, because one continuously enters into unspeakably unspeakable gateways of *samādhi* through supreme correspondence, there is mastery over the mind.
Third, the mastery of enjoyment (*bhoga-vaśitā*), which is the manifestation corresponding to the empowerment of adorning all worlds with countless ornaments;
fourth, the mastery of karma (*karma-vaśitā*), because one manifests all the power of karmic retributions according to their respective times;
fifth, the mastery of birth (*upapatti-vaśitā*), because one manifests taking birth in all worlds.
Sixth, because of seeing the Buddha’s perfect manifestation in all worlds, there is mastery over faith and understanding;
seventh, because of manifesting the attainment of enlightenment within various lands whenever one so desires, there is mastery over vows;
eighth, because of manifesting boundless miraculous powers in all worlds, there is mastery over supernormal powers.
Ninth, because the light of the dharma-gate that is boundless and centerless is constantly manifested, this is mastery over phenomena (*dharmavaśitā*);

tenth, regarding the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four analytical knowledges, eighteen unique qualities, thirty-two marks, and eighty minor characteristics, as well as the manifest realization of supreme enlightenment—filling all Buddha-fields throughout the three times, numbering as many as atoms in an *asaṃkhyeya*—one understands that a single mark possesses all excellent marks, and even manifests and displays the realization of all-knowledge;
this is mastery over wisdom (*jñānavaśitā*). These are the ten kinds of mastery of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, what are the ten powers of a bodhisattva?
They are: first, the power of intention;
second, the power of profound firmness;"
Third, the power of skillful means;
fourth, the power of wisdom;
fifth, the power of aspiration;
Sixth, the power of practice;
seventh, the power of the vehicle;
eighth, the power of spiritual transformations;
Ninth is the power of awakening;
tenth is the power of turning the wheel of Dharma.
These are the ten powers of a bodhisattva.
"What are the four fearlessnesses of a bodhisattva?
They are as follows: first, the fearlessness of proclaiming the principles of meaning upon receiving them as they are heard through various dhāraṇīs;

second, the fearlessness of accomplishing vast protection through the purity of the three karmas, having realized the dharma of non-self without disturbing others, and having accumulated the fundamental practices and dignified conduct of signlessness without deficiency; [and so forth]."

Third, they constantly uphold the True Dharma without forgetting it, ultimately abiding in wisdom and skillful means; with a mind free from negligence, they rescue and deliver sentient beings, revealing the wholesome dharmas so that they may attain fearlessness in being free from obstacles and difficulties.

Fourth, they do not forget the mind of omniscience, and they also achieve perfect mastery over the various paths of renunciation in other vehicles; thus they attain fearlessness in the accomplishment of all aspects and all matters. These are the four fearlessnesses of a bodhisattva.
"What are the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) of a bodhisattva?
They are: first, the bodhisattva’s unattached generosity;
second, unattached ethical discipline;"
Third, unattached patience;
fourth, unattached diligence;
fifth, unattached meditative concentration;
Sixth, unattached wisdom;
seventh, gathering all sentient beings through the four means of attraction;
eighth, skillfully understanding all methods of dedication.
Ninth, skillfully employing expedient means to bring about the superior practice of all sentient beings;
tenth, revealing the path of transcendence of the Supreme Vehicle;
eleventh, never regressing from the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Twelfth, it indicates the gates of birth-and-death and nirvana;
thirteenth, it does not diminish the phrasing of any scriptural texts;
fourteenth, in all actions performed, wisdom serves as the precursor.
Fifteenth, he is free from all faults among all classes of beings;
sixteenth, he is endowed with the ten virtuous actions of body, speech, and mind;
seventeenth, he is able to endure all sufferings without abandoning any sentient beings.

Eighteenth: He manifests all that is beloved and delightful to all the world, pervading all the world’s foolish commoners as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; he skillfully adorns [the world] with various jewels and kalpavṛkṣa trees; he makes the mind of omniscience firm and never forgets it; he attains the empowerment of all dharmas according to the Dharma;
and he constantly seeks with joy to behold the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. These are the eighteen unique qualities of a bodhisattva.
"What are the ten powers of the Tathāgata? They are:
first, the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible;
second, the power of knowing the ripening of the causes and effects of karma in the past, future, and present;"
Third, the power of knowledge regarding various inclinations and understandings;
fourth, the power of knowledge regarding various elements;
fifth, the power of knowledge regarding the discernment of the faculties of oneself and others;
Sixth, the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading to all destinations;
seventh, the power of knowledge regarding the arousal of all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis, as well as their defilement and purification;
eighth, the power of knowledge regarding the recollection of past abodes.
Ninth, the power of knowledge regarding birth and death;
tenth, the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows;
these are the ten powers of a Tathāgata.
"What are the four fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata? They are:
first, the fearlessness of the wisdom that has realized all phenomena;
second, the fearlessness of the wisdom that all outflows have been exhausted;"
Third, the fearlessness of definitively proclaiming the obstacles to the path;
fourth, the fearlessness of proclaiming the path that leads to the exhaustion of suffering.
These are the four fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll Seven;
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Imperial Preceptor for Transmitting the Sanskrit, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject Dharmarakṣa, and others, by imperial decree:
"Furthermore, what are the eighteen unique qualities of a Tathāgata?"
The first is that the Tathāgata’s body is free from weariness;
the second is that his speech is free from abruptness;
the third is that he is free from loss of mindfulness.
Fourth, there is no unconcentrated mind;
fifth, there is no perception of diversity;
sixth, there is no lack of awareness regarding equanimity.
Seventh, his desire does not diminish;
eighth, his diligence does not diminish;
ninth, his mindfulness does not diminish.
Tenth, there is no decrease in meditative concentration;
eleventh, there is no decrease in wisdom;
twelfth, there is no decrease in liberation or the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Thirteenth, he possesses unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision that operate with respect to the past;
fourteenth, he possesses unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision that operate with respect to the future;
fifteenth, he possesses unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision that operate with respect to the present.
Sixteenth, all bodily actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom;
seventeenth, all verbal actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom;
eighteenth, all mental actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom.
These are the eighteen unique qualities of a Tathāgata.
"What, son of good family, is the great compassion of a Tathāgata? [The Buddha said:
"Son of good family!"

By diligently practicing the thirty-two marks, one gives rise to the Tathāgata’s mind of great compassion; throughout the boundless worlds of the ten directions, one extensively manifests inconceivable signs, all of which proceed from the Tathāgata’s mind of great compassion.
What are the thirty-two marks? They are as follows:

First, all phenomena are without self, yet sentient beings are unable to believe in or understand this principle of selflessness; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion for the sake of these sentient beings.
Second, all phenomena are without sentient beings, yet sentient beings cling to them as if they existed; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
Third, all phenomena are devoid of a life-principle (*jīva*), yet sentient beings cling to them as if they existed; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
Fourth, all phenomena are devoid of a person (*pudgala*), yet sentient beings give rise to grasping and attachment toward them; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
Fifth, all phenomena are without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet sentient beings give rise to the view that they possess intrinsic nature; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
Sixth, all phenomena are without obstruction, yet sentient beings cling to that which is obstructive; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
Seventh, all phenomena have no storehouse, yet sentient beings give rise to attachment toward them; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
Eighth, all phenomena have no sovereign master, yet sentient beings cling to the mark of a self; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
Ninth, all phenomena are without possession, yet sentient beings give rise to grasping; therefore, the Tathāgata arouses great compassion.
Tenth, all phenomena are without substantial form, yet sentient beings are attached to objective things; therefore, the Tathāgata arouses great compassion.
Eleventh, all phenomena are without lineage, yet sentient beings produce grasping and attachment; therefore, the Tathāgata arouses great compassion.
Twelfth, all phenomena are without arising and without cessation, yet sentient beings are attached to arising and cessation; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
Thirteenth, all phenomena are without defilement, yet sentient beings produce defilement for themselves; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
Fourteenth, all phenomena are free from craving, yet sentient beings give rise to craving and attachment; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
Fifteenth, all dharmas are free from hatred, yet sentient beings give rise to hatred; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
Sixteenth, all dharmas are free from delusion, yet sentient beings give rise to folly; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
Seventeenth, all dharmas have no coming, yet sentient beings cling to the various realms of existence; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
Eighteenth, all dharmas are without going, yet sentient beings are attached to birth; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
Nineteenth, all dharmas are without activity, yet sentient beings act within the sphere of conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*); therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.

Twentieth, all dharmas are without conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), yet sentient beings delight in and are attached to conceptual proliferation; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
Twenty-first: All phenomena are empty, yet sentient beings give rise to the view of existence; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion. Twenty-second:
All phenomena are signless, yet sentient beings cling to the signs of objective realms; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion. Twenty-third:
All phenomena are wishless, yet sentient beings engage in various aspirations; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.

Twenty-fourth: When sentient beings of the world gather together and engage in mutual disputes and litigation, giving rise to all such faults as greed and hatred, the Tathāgata, having observed this, teaches them the essentials of the Dharma so that they may sever those faults of greed, hatred, and the like; for this reason, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.

Twenty-fifth: When sentient beings of the world gather together and diligently practice perversions, treading dangerous and evil paths and dwelling in heterodox and deviant places, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion in order to lead them into the path of reality.

Twenty-sixth: When sentient beings of the world gather together, their stinginess and greed increase such that they seize the wealth of others without ever being satisfied; in order to cause them to possess the noble treasures of ethical discipline, learning, relinquishment, and wisdom, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.

Twenty-seventh: Because sentient beings of the world give birth to craving and attachment for houses, wealth, wives, and children, they treat their own bodies as lowly as servants, perceiving what is unreal as real; for their sake, the Buddha proclaims the essential Dharma to make them know the law of ultimate impermanence, and thus the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.

Twenty-eighth: Because sentient beings in the world deceive one another in their pursuit of a livelihood through hardship, the Buddha proclaims the essential Dharma for them, causing all sentient beings to sustain themselves through pure livelihood; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion. Twenty-ninth:

Because sentient beings in the world firmly pursue fame and gain without ever feeling weary or satisfied, [the Buddha] acts so that they may understand reality as it is and develop weariness with such pursuits, ultimately ceasing suffering and attaining the bliss of Nirvāṇa; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.

Thirtieth: Sentient beings in the world constantly give rise to craving and attachment; dwelling within the vessel of suffering, they are consistently defiled. For their sake, the Buddha proclaims the essential points of the Dharma, enabling them to transcend and go beyond the triple world;

therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion. Thirty-first: Because all phenomena are devoid of [independent] causes and conditions, sentient beings in the world give rise to a mind of indolence, thereby creating obstacles within the gateway of liberation of the noble Dharma. For their sake, the Buddha proclaims the true Dharma of liberation, causing all sentient beings to practice with diligence; therefore, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.

Thirty-second: Worldly sentient beings abandon the supreme, unattached, wondrous wisdom of the sublime nirvana and instead delight in seeking the inferior vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. To cause them to take joy in the vast [path] and seek after the Buddha-wisdom, the Tathāgata gives rise to great compassion.
“Good son! Because he diligently practices these thirty-two kinds of marks, the Tathāgata gives rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Regarding this practice of the Tathāgata’s great compassion that has been thus described, if there is a bodhisattva who diligently practices these thirty-two kinds of marks and gives rise to the mind of great compassion, then this bodhisattva-mahāsattva, within the realm of meritorious qualities, will be able to fulfill vast and majestic radiance, and will attain non-retrogression in activities corresponding to the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.”

Therefore, you should know that regarding the various states of such immeasurable and innumerable sovereign dharmas, even if all Tathāgatas or Bodhisattvas were to proclaim them extensively throughout the final eons, they would be unable to reach their limit.

What has been explained here is but a very small portion; it is intended solely to inspire the highest pure faith and joy in all sentient beings, and serves as the Bodhisattva’s immovable sustenance and nourishment for the wholesome dharmas of all sentient beings.
“Good son! What is the Bodhisattva’s immeasurable cloud of Dharma that contains moisture and sustains the vast rain of Dharma?
It is like the wind of the world, which has no boundaries, yet its wind-wheel is vast, stable, and all-pervading.”
It sustains all worlds, whether in their period of formation or their period of destruction,
as well as the waters and clouds, together with the great oceans, the four great continents, Mount Sumeru, Mount Mucilinda,
Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Snowy Mountains, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, and Mount Gandhamādana.
Just as mountains, forests, palaces, and various towers support all things, so too is the wind-circle of the boundless *dhāraṇī* of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva;
it is able to sustain the clouds of all the Truly Perfect Buddhas and cause them to pour down the vast and unobstructed rain of Dharma, thereby accomplishing the work of the Buddha in all worlds.

The dharmas of merit consist of the various worldly characteristics as they have been described, such as Mount Sumeru and so forth; these are the marks of supreme excellence resulting from a hundred merits,
the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the thirteen meditative concentrations (*samādhi*),
the twelve dharanis, the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the ten masteries (*vaśitā*), the ten powers (*bala*), and the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
He is fully capable of upholding and perfecting all the qualities of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, including the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*),
the eighteen unique dharmas (*āveṇika-dharma*), and the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Furthermore, they constantly maintain all hundreds of thousands of mundane and supramundane aggregates of Dharma and achieve them in their entirety; this is the Bodhisattva’s immeasurable cloud of Dharma, which contains moisture and sustains the vast rain of Dharma.
“Good son! What is the Bodhisattva’s magnificent pavilion, adorned with various great dharmas?

It is like the wind in the world, which is able to universally blow upon and spread through all pavilions of adornment—arranging them in various ways that are exquisite and lovely—as well as all forest trees, their branches, leaves, sprouts, stems, flowers, fruits, and filaments, and all the various states of the bodies of sentient beings; all of these are constantly blown upon and spread by the power of the wind.”

The wind of the bodhisattva is likewise: through the power of wisdom consisting of boundless, unimpeded, and non-attached understanding and eloquence, they are able to establish all manner of mundane and supramundane dharma-gates;
being fully arrayed and complete, they illuminate and reveal various most excellent and sublime dharmas, namely that "this characteristic is..."
"This is a phenomenon produced by the miserable realms; this is a phenomenon produced by the happy realms;
this is a phenomenon produced by predominance; this is hell; this is the realm of hungry ghosts;
this is the animal realm; this is the human realm; this is the celestial realm; this is a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin); this is Śakra."
The Brahma Kings and the world-protecting devas—this is their physical appearance, retinue, intelligence, and power of merit;
this is their clear wisdom and skillful calculation; this is their artistic talent; this is their proficiency in understanding various scriptural canons;
this is the vehicle of the Śrāvakas by which the fruit of a Śrāvaka is attained; and this is the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas by which [the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha] is attained.
The fruit of the Pratyekabuddha—this is the Dharma of the Mahāyāna, endowed with all supreme characteristics;
it perfects the activities of benefiting oneself and others, accomplishes all the supreme wisdom of Samantabhadra, and extends even to these:
the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the thirteen meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), the twelve dhāraṇīs, and the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The three knowledges, the ten masteries, the eight liberations, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses,
the four analytical knowledges, and the eighteen unique qualities.

“Good son! A bodhisattva is skillfully able to establish such immeasurable varieties of dharmas as the *padmavyūha* and other dharanī-doors. These serve as a sublime and ingenious arrangement for the adornment of the Dharma; this constitutes the exquisite decoration of the bodhisattva’s great dharma pavilion of manifold adornments.”

“Good son! What is this bodhisattva’s adornment of all assemblies by kalpa-trees, which invariably and constantly produces the rain of flowers that gladdens the mind through the sounds of the truly sublime Dharma?”

Just as when a grove of kalpavṛkṣa trees is stirred by the wind, it constantly rains down various kinds of fragrant flowers, exquisite jewels, garments, musical instruments, and other articles of adornment, all of which are fully provided.

These various ornaments flow forth in continuous succession, causing all devas and humans to give rise to the most supreme satisfaction, joy, and freedom from sorrow; they constantly possess beautiful forms for play and amusement, with their power, vigor, and delight never diminishing.
The wind of a bodhisattva’s wisdom is likewise: within the great Dharma assemblies in the pure worlds of the Tathāgatas,
the bodhisattva constantly proclaims for the sake of all sentient beings the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas,
nidānas, avadānas, itivṛttakas, jātaka-s, vaipulya-s, and so forth.
The Dharma of the Vinaya and the twelvefold division of the teachings constantly rain down such precious flowers of the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
Within the habitual circumstances of both favorable and adverse conditions, they sequentially proclaim instructions and guidance,
as well as all worldly objects of focus, thereby inducing and demonstrating selflessness and nirvāṇa.
The pure *dharmatā* reveals and elucidates the universal gateways of all phenomena; it comprehensively subsumes the nature of reality and guides beings into the inconceivable,
illusion-like state of phenomena, manifesting the great wisdom of the illusion-like gateway of Dharma.

Furthermore, they cause sentient beings to increase their playful engagement with the joy of all phenomena; in all questions and answers—whether regarding the non-existent or the infinite—they are able to skillfully inspire them so that all may rejoice. They constantly cause them, within the garden of the True Dharma, to find delight through play and sport by means of faultless actions of body, speech, and mind, never giving rise to indolence or retreat. They cause the gods and humans to be fully provided with all necessities, ensuring that wholesome qualities do not diminish and that the light of wisdom shines forth, so that they may dwell eternally within the most supreme and pure Dharma.
This constitutes the kalpa-tree adornment of all the assemblies of Bodhisattvas, which invariably and constantly produces the rain of the sublime and wondrous Dharma-sound that gladdens the mind.
"O Son of Good Family!

How is it that these bodhisattvas, throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), have purified the assembly of the noble ones and established and accumulated an ocean of gateways to samādhi, liberation, and dhāraṇī; how have they spread the groves of Dharma teachings, the light of the sun and moon, the excellent palaces, and the Cakravāla mountains of Mount Sumeru; and for what reason do they serve as the cause of liberation within the maṇḍala of the wind of wisdom, which proceeds in accordance with the supreme, formless reliance, and the maturation and discipline of all sentient beings?

For example, when the world is being destroyed by the kalpa-wind, that wind is unimpeded; its power and momentum are so swift and fierce that it blows everywhere across the trichiliocosm, shattering and grinding to dust without remainder the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Iron Ring Mountains, Mount Sumerus, great oceans, and so forth, until they are identical to empty space.

The wind of the Bodhisattva is likewise: throughout many hundreds of thousands of kalpas, having accumulated various adornments of merit and wisdom, the Bodhisattva, by means of vast power and majesty, can manifest various supernatural transformations, skillfully turn the unimpeded and pure wheel of Dharma, and produce sublime sounds that universally subdue all assemblies.

Because of this, from the wind-circle of wisdom (*jñāna-vāyu-maṇḍala*), there emerge the aggregates of all phenomena (*dharma-skandha*). Those who are to be disciplined observe the supreme light of the sublime Dharma and its unattached activities; possessing superior power, they cultivate profound and firm mental attention (*manasikāra*) and dwell correctly within their own minds, thereby achieving *samādhi*. They cause the conceptual aggregates, the bases (*āyatana*), the elements (*dhātu*), and all conditioned activities of the three realms of existence to be utterly dispersed. Realizing that all bodily activities are merely false conceptualizations (*vikalpa*), they transcend all worlds. Thereafter, they manifest inconceivable, signless, supramundane, and perfect merit; relying upon and following this, they attain supreme purity and abide at the ultimate limit, free from all sorrow and affliction.

This constitutes the bodhisattva’s assembly of pure sages throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; it is the establishment and accumulation of an ocean of gates of samādhi, liberation, and dhāraṇī; it is the arraying of the forest of Dharma teachings and the radiance of the sun and moon upon Mount Sumeru, as well as the arraying of exquisite palaces, the Cakravāḍa mountains, and so forth; it is the adornment for the maturation and subduing of all sentient beings; and it is the cause of liberation through the maṇḍala of the winds of wisdom that turn in accordance with reality, being well-established in the unsurpassed, formless refuge.
“Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain [a state] like the wind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Rare, World-Honored One! Rare, Sugata!
You have well expounded such a vast Dharma, complete with all supreme characteristics, which is able to cause all the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas to give rise to joy.”
"Bhagavān!

If gods and humans are able to have faith, understanding, and practice such a Dharma as this, then, as the Buddha has taught, these persons shall obtain all things in abundance and experience supreme, wondrous bliss, with joy and mastery, becoming equal to Brahmā, Śakra, and the World-Protecting Devas."
"Whatever supreme practices for benefiting others that achieve all perfections throughout this life and future lives have been attained, they shall not be discussed here.
The Buddha said,
"O son of noble family!"

So it is, so it is. Just as you have said, those sentient beings transcend all worlds and are universally gazed upon by many people; having severed all unwholesome dharmas and being endowed with all wholesome dharmas, they are the refuge for the entire world.

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who are able to practice within this Dharma, yet others instead give rise to contempt and slander, I declare that such people are deluded; they shall fall into the Great Hell of Darkness to undergo various sufferings, and they will be objects of shared compassion for the world, including devas, humans, and asuras.”
"Furthermore, noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they are like space.
What are these ten?
That is to say: first, stainlessness;
second, non-obstruction;
third, tranquility.
Fourth, signlessness;
fifth, boundless wisdom;
sixth, impartially and accordingly knowing all phenomena.
Seventh, the liberation through realizing that all phenomena have the nature of empty space;
eighth, non-abiding;
ninth, transcending all characteristics of objective realms.
Tenth, they transcend applied and sustained thought.
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they are like space. "Good son!
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas; if a bodhisattva cultivates them, they are like space.
What are these ten?
They are as follows: first, neither craving nor loathing toward any forms, whether agreeable or disagreeable;
Second, they feel neither attachment nor aversion toward any sounds, whether agreeable or disagreeable;
third, they feel neither attachment nor aversion toward any odors, whether agreeable or disagreeable;
fourth, they feel neither attachment nor aversion toward any tastes, whether agreeable or disagreeable.
Fifth, one neither loves nor hates any contact, whether agreeable or disagreeable;
sixth, one neither loves nor hates any phenomena, whether agreeable or disagreeable;
seventh, one neither loves nor hates the conditions of gain or loss.
Eighth, one neither loves nor hates the phenomena of pleasure and pain;
ninth, one neither loves nor hates the phenomena of praise and blame;
tenth, one neither loves nor hates the phenomena of fame and infamy.
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they are like space.
Furthermore, son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they attain likeness to the moon.
What are these ten? They are:
first, causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy;
second, being a sight that all delight in beholding.
Third, wholesome dharmas increase;
fourth, unwholesome dharmas diminish;
fifth, all offer praise.
Sixth, the purity of physical form;
seventh, mounting the supreme vehicle;
eighth, constant self-adornment.
Ninth, they sport in the joy of the Dharma;
tenth, they possess great supernormal powers and majestic virtue. "Good son!
How does a bodhisattva cause all sentient beings to give rise to joy?

Just as when the new moon first appears, all sentient beings attain coolness and, because it is pleasing to the mind, they all experience joy; so too is the moon of the bodhisattva. When it first appears, all sentient beings are able to distance themselves from the scorching heat of afflictions and give rise to blissful joy. This is how a bodhisattva causes all sentient beings to give rise to joy.
"What is meant by 'the assembly of bodhisattvas who delight in beholding'?

It is like the new moon first appearing, which all sentient beings joyfully gaze upon; that is to say, because it is excellent, wondrous, and pure, causing the hearts of all sentient beings to give rise to joy."

The moon of the bodhisattva is likewise: when it first rises, all sentient beings find it delightful and pleasing; that is to say, its faculties are pure, its seeds are immaculate, and it is fully endowed with proper conduct and deportment—this is why the bodhisattva is a joy for all to behold.
"What is the increase of a bodhisattva’s wholesome dharmas?
It is like the moon of the waxing fortnight: from its first appearance, it increases day by day until the fifteenth day, when the moon is full and all its characteristics are perfectly complete."

The moon of the bodhisattva is likewise: from the first generation of the mind of awakening until sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*) increase gradually day by day; once seated at the site of enlightenment, all supreme characteristics are fully perfected. This is called the increase of the bodhisattva’s wholesome qualities.
"What is the diminution of a bodhisattva’s unwholesome dharmas?
It is like when the moon reaches the dark fortnight; the radiance of its lunar orb gradually diminishes, and as it diminishes, by the end of the month, nothing at all remains visible."

The moon of the bodhisattva is likewise: when it reaches the stage of possessing supramundane wisdom, unwholesome dharmas gradually diminish; as they diminish, until finally sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they are entirely extinguished without remainder. This is called the bodhisattva’s diminution of unwholesome dharmas.
"What is meant by 'the Bodhisattva being universally praised'?

Just as when the moon first rises, all Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, men and women, great and small, and all the people offer praise, so too is it with the moon that is the Bodhisattva; when it first appears, all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others—all offer praise. This is what is meant by the Bodhisattva being universally praised."
"What is meant by the purity of the Bodhisattva’s physical form?

Just as the physical form of the Moon Deity is pure, white, and unstained—being produced by the ripening of superior karma—the physical form of the Bodhisattva is likewise so: it is originally unstained, formed of purity, and born through transformation (*upapāduka*). It is not produced from the impurities of the parents’ *kalala* and so forth; this is called the purity of the Bodhisattva’s physical form."
"What is the Bodhisattva Vehicle, the Supreme Vehicle?

Just as the Moon Deity, riding upon a pure vehicle, illuminates the four continents, so too is the Bodhisattva-moon: riding upon the supreme Bodhisattva vehicle, it extensively illuminates all boundless worlds. This is the Bodhisattva Vehicle, the Supreme Vehicle."
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s constant self-adornment?

Just as the Moon Deity is naturally adorned with his original, pure marks, not because he is adorned by bathing, so too is the moon that is the bodhisattva: he is constantly adorned by all supreme merits. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva’s constant self-adornment."
"What is the bodhisattva’s sporting in the joy of the Dharma?

Just as the Moon Deva-son constantly experiences celestial bliss, so too is the Bodhisattva-moon: he constantly sports in the sublime and wondrous joy of the Dharma, remaining unstained by the realms of worldly desires; this is the bodhisattva’s sporting in the joy of the Dharma."
"What is meant by a bodhisattva possessing great supernormal powers and majestic virtue?

Just as the Moon Deva possesses great supernormal powers and great majestic virtue that shine broadly upon all, so too is the moon of the bodhisattva; because it possesses the supreme merit of great fortune and wisdom, this is what is meant by a bodhisattva possessing great supernormal powers and majestic virtue."
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will become like the moon.
*The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin*, Scroll Eight.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin,
Scroll Nine. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Appointed Court Dispersing Grandee,
Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of the Transmission of the Sanskrit Canon, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject.
Translated by Imperial Decree: "Furthermore, noble son, if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will become like the sun.
What are these ten?"
First, it shatters the darkness of ignorance;
second, it causes all things to bloom;
third, it pervades the ten directions so that all may attain warmth.
Fourth, the arising of all wholesome dharmas;
fifth, the cessation and disappearance of outflows;
sixth, the production of illuminating light.
Seventh, to restrain all that is heterodox and deviant;
eighth, to reveal and clarify both the high and the low;
ninth, to accomplish all undertakings.
Tenth is the aspiration of virtuous persons. "Good son!
How does a bodhisattva shatter the darkness of ignorance?

Just as when the sun first rises, it is able to dispel all darkness and gloom, so too is the sun of the Bodhisattva; when it first rises, it can shatter all the darkness of ignorance. This is what is meant by the Bodhisattva’s destruction of the obscurity of ignorance.
"What is meant by 'the Bodhisattva causes all to blossom'?

Just as when the sun rises, it is able to cause all flowers and plants, such as the pure lotus, to blossom, so too is the sun of the Bodhisattva; it awakens all sentient beings who are ready to be transformed. This is what is meant by the Bodhisattva causing all to blossom."
"What is meant by 'the Bodhisattva causes all directions throughout the ten quarters to attain warmth'?
Just as when the sun rises, all directions throughout the ten quarters attain warmth;

so too is it with the sun that is the Bodhisattva. When it first rises, the light of wisdom shines universally upon all things in the ten quarters, causing them all to become warm, yet without afflicting the sentient beings of the world. This is what is meant by 'the Bodhisattva causes all directions throughout the ten quarters to attain warmth.'"
"What is meant by a bodhisattva giving rise to all wholesome dharmas?

Just as when the sun is about to rise, the first sign of light appears within Jambudvīpa and one knows that the sun is coming, so too is it with the sun of the bodhisattva; when it is about to arise, it first manifests the signs of the radiance of wisdom, and sentient beings know that the bodhisattva is appearing. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva giving rise to all wholesome dharmas."
"What is meant by the bodhisattva’s extinction and disappearance of outflows?

Just as when the sunlight in Jambudvīpa fades away, one knows that the sun has set, so too it is with the bodhisattva: when all defiled afflictions fade and do not appear, one knows that the bodhisattva’s outflows have been exhausted; this is called the bodhisattva’s extinction and disappearance of outflows."
"What is meant by the Bodhisattva producing the illumination of light?

Just as when the sun first rises, all sentient beings within Jambudvīpa are universally illumined by its light, so too is it with the sun that is the Bodhisattva: when it first rises, the light of wisdom universally illumines all sentient beings, removing all the darkness and obscurations of ignorance. This is what is meant by the Bodhisattva producing the illumination of light."
"What is meant by a bodhisattva subduing all heterodox and deviant views?
It is like the manifestation of the sun's light which eclipses all lesser lights, yet the sun does not form this thought:
'I am able to eclipse those various minor lights.'"
Why is this? Because it is the natural law that when the sun rises, such is its nature.

It is the same with the sun that is the Bodhisattva: when the light of wisdom emerges, all the minor lights of heterodox and external paths are completely eclipsed; yet this Bodhisattva does not form such a thought:
"I am able to obscure all other minor lights that are heterodox or inferior. Why is this?
Because it is the natural law of such minor lights that they do not appear when eclipsed.
This is how a bodhisattva restrains all that is erroneous and heterodox.
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s “revealing the high and the low”? It is like when the sun rises:

within Jambudvīpa, all elevations and depressions, as well as all level ground, can be clearly seen by all people. The sun of the bodhisattva is likewise; its light of wisdom shines universally, causing all sentient beings to clearly perceive all elevations and depressions—whereby "level ground" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path and "elevations and depressions" refers to the eightfold wrong path. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva’s “revealing the high and the low.”
"What is meant by a bodhisattva accomplishing all activities?

Just as when the sun first rises, all the agricultural activities of plowing and sowing are undertaken, so too is it with the rising of the Bodhisattva-sun: all the activities of the wholesome dharmas of sentient beings are fully accomplished. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva accomplishing all activities."
"What is meant by 'the Bodhisattva being desired by virtuous people'?

Just as when the sun first rises, virtuous people rejoice while wicked people loathe it, so too is it with the rising of the Bodhisattva-sun: those possessed of wisdom all give rise to joy and affection, whereas those who follow deviant paths, the deceitful and evil, the ignorant and witless who delight in attachment to birth-and-death and turn their backs on Nirvāṇa, all feel loathing. This is what is meant by the Bodhisattva being desired by virtuous people."
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will become like the sun.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they are like a lion.
What are these ten?
First, they are themselves free from fear.
Second, they do not fear others;
third, they advance directly without turning back;
fourth, they are able to roar the lion's roar.
Fifth, fearless observation;
sixth, constantly dwelling in forest groves;
seventh, delighting in residing among mountain crags.
Eighth, being free from all fetters;
ninth, possessing personal valor and strength to crush the armies of others;
tenth, being skillful in providing protection.
“Good son! How is it that this bodhisattva is himself free from fear?
It is like a lion, who walks with a composed gait, neither startled nor terrified.”
Why is this? Because they do not perceive anyone who can equal themselves.
The Bodhisattva is likewise; as he travels everywhere in all directions, he is without alarm and without fear.
Why is this? Because they do not perceive anyone who is their equal.
This is what it means for a bodhisattva to be personally free from fear.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva not fearing others?

Just as a lion does not fear the various evil cries of others, so too is it with the bodhisattva: when engaging in debate with all other schools and non-Buddhists, their mind is neither timid nor inferior. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva not fearing others."
"What is meant by the bodhisattva’s direct advancement without turning back?

Just as that lion advances straight ahead without retreating, so too is the bodhisattva: by their very nature they advance directly, never again retreating to the teachings of heterodox schools; furthermore, the bodhisattva’s eloquence is inexhaustible—this is called the bodhisattva’s direct advancement without turning back."
"What is meant by a bodhisattva being able to roar the lion’s roar?

For example, when a lion roars, all the deer, wild animals, and jackals are utterly terrified and flee in the ten directions. The bodhisattva is also like this: when he utters the lion’s roar of non-self, all those who cling to the grasping of a self—including heterodox outsiders—are utterly terrified and flee in the ten directions. Yet the bodhisattva does not afflict them; rather, it is solely for the purpose of shattering those with views that cling to a self that he utters this thundering lion’s roar of non-self. Furthermore, it is also for the sake of taming other sentient beings. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva being able to roar the lion’s roar."
"What is the fearless observation of a bodhisattva?

Just as that lion displays a fearless demeanor while surveying all around, so too does the bodhisattva, with pure conduct and resolve, display a fearless demeanor while observing universally; this is called the fearless observation of a bodhisattva."
"What is meant by a bodhisattva constantly dwelling in the forest?

Just as the lion, by its very nature, delights in roaming through forests and wilds, so too does the bodhisattva; being naturally tranquil and far removed from clamor, they delight in dwelling in the forest. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva constantly dwelling in the forest."
"What is meant by a bodhisattva delighting in dwelling among mountain crags?

Just as that lion delights in dwelling among mountain crags, so too does the bodhisattva delight in dwelling among the mountain crags of wisdom and meditative concentration; this is what is meant by a bodhisattva delighting in dwelling among mountain crags."
"What is meant by 'the bodhisattva is without fetters'?

Just as that lion is without fetters, so too is the bodhisattva; having removed the heavy burden of all afflictions and being free from all fetters, this is what is meant by 'the bodhisattva is without fetters.'"
"What is meant by a bodhisattva possessing the power to personally subdue the armies of others?

Just as a lion, being solitary and without companion, can subdue other creatures, so too is the bodhisattva: when sitting alone and without companion at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he subdues the army of Māra through his own power. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva possessing the power to personally subdue the armies of others."
"What is meant by a bodhisattva providing excellent protection?

Just as when a lion dwells near a village, the deer and other such creatures do not damage the crops, so too is it with the bodhisattva: in whatever kingdom, town, or region they go, all those heterodox outsiders—who are like deer—do not damage the seeds of the wholesome dharmas of sentient beings; this is what is meant by a bodhisattva providing excellent protection."
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they are like a lion.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to subdue [the mind].
What are these ten?
First, firmness in the bodhicitta.
Second, cultivating and purifying bodhisattva conduct;
third, guarding the sense faculties;
fourth, proceeding toward the right path.
Fifth, being able to bear heavy burdens;
sixth, not giving rise to weariness or retreat for the sake of sentient beings;
seventh, sustaining oneself through right livelihood.
Eighth, being free from all flattery and crookedness;
ninth, not giving rise to deception or delusion;
tenth, having a straightforward body and mind—these are the ten dharmas.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to subdue [the mind].
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to skillfully mount [the vehicle].
What are these ten?
First, although they cultivate the practice of meditative concentration, they constantly contemplate emptiness;
Second, although they have exhausted all hindrances, they constantly cultivate wholesome conduct;
third, although they are free from all conditioned activities, they skillfully accord with the Buddha’s teachings without contradiction;
fourth, they impartially comprehend all phenomena and understand the principle of the dharma-realm.
Fifth, one is able to humble oneself in the world like a *caṇḍāla* and keep one's mind modest;
sixth, one remains far removed from arrogance and always regards others as wise;
seventh, through the wisdom of direct perception (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*), one understands the Buddha-dharma and is free from all doubt.
Eighth, although knowing the distinctions among all phenomena, they attain the mark of certainty;
ninth, they personally take up the right path and do not follow the teachings of others;
tenth, they skillfully accord with the world and serve as a field of merit for the world.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, he will be able to skillfully mount [the vehicle].
Furthermore, good son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they are like a lotus flower.
What are these ten?
First, being free from all defilements.
Second, not associating with even the slightest evil;
third, being suffused with the fragrance of precepts;
fourth, having a fundamentally pure essence.
Fifth, his facial features are serene and joyful;
sixth, they are supple and not coarse;
seventh, all who behold him find auspiciousness.
Eighth, the perfection of full blossoming;
ninth, the purity of maturation;
tenth, the perception that [the fruit] has already arisen.
“Good son! What is meant by a bodhisattva being free from all defilements?
It is like a lotus flower that emerges from the water yet remains unstained by it.”
Why is this? Because such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
It is likewise with the bodhisattva: although dwelling within the stream of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they remain unstained and unattached.
Why is this? Because such is the nature of wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*).

By means of his skillful means, the bodhisattva dwells within birth and death (*saṃsāra*) without being defiled by the faults of birth and death; for he is sustained by the integration of skillful means and wisdom. This is what it means for a bodhisattva to be free from all defilements.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva not being accompanied by even the slightest evil?

Just as a lotus flower does not retain even a single drop of water, so too is the bodhisattva: they are not accompanied by even the slightest evil. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva not being accompanied by even the slightest evil."
"What is meant by 'the fragrance of a bodhisattva’s precepts pervading everywhere'?

Just as when a lotus flower blooms, its exquisite fragrance spreads far and wide according to its location, so too is it with the bodhisattva: wherever they go—be it a kingdom, a city, or any other place—the fragrance of their precepts wafts forth and pervades all. This is what is meant by 'the fragrance of a bodhisattva’s precepts pervading everywhere.'"
"What is meant by the bodhisattva’s essential nature being pure?

It is like the lotus flower, which at the moment of its birth is naturally white and pure; wherever it arises, it is praised by brahmins, kṣatriyas, and all people alike. The bodhisattva is also like this: in whatever region or town he is born, his nature is white and pure."
Why is this? Because their precepts are pure.

All devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans alike praise them together; they are sustained by all buddhas and bodhisattvas—this constitutes the purity of the bodhisattva’s essential nature.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s countenance being serene and joyful?

Just as when a lotus flower is about to bloom, it causes those who see it to feel a sense of ease and give rise to delight in their minds, so too is it with the bodhisattva: his countenance is serene and joyful, free from all frowning, his faculties are pure, and those who see him rejoice; this is what is meant by a bodhisattva’s countenance being serene and joyful."
"What is meant by a bodhisattva being supple and not harsh?
Just as the nature of a lotus flower is supple, so too is the bodhisattva; his own body is pure, supple, and exquisitely subtle. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva being supple and not harsh."
"What is it that makes a bodhisattva auspicious for all who see him?
It is like a lotus flower; even to see one for a mere moment within a dream is virtuous and auspicious. Why is this?"

Because all aims are accomplished, it is likewise with the Bodhisattva: if those who see him in any state whatsoever obtain the most supreme auspiciousness, this is what is meant by "the Bodhisattva being auspicious for all who behold him."
"What is meant by the bodhisattva’s full blossoming?

Just as a lotus flower is said to be 'fully developed' once it has blossomed, so too is it with the bodhisattva: when the flower of wisdom-awakening blossoms, they are said to be 'fully developed. This is what is called the bodhisattva’s full blossoming."
"What is meant by 'maturation and purity'?

For example, when a lotus flower has reached maturity, the faculty of the eye is purified when it is beheld by the eye; the faculty of the nose is purified when it is smelled by the nose; the faculty of the body is purified when its touch is sensed by the body; and the faculty of the mind is purified when the heart rejoices."

The Bodhisattva is likewise in this regard: at the time when the fruit reaches maturity, there is the characteristic of the light of wisdom. When all sentient beings see him with their eyes, their eye-faculties become purified; when they hear him with their ears, their ear-faculties become purified; when they smell the fragrance of the Bodhisattva’s merit of precepts with their noses, their nose-faculties become purified; when they make offerings to his body, their body-faculties become purified; and when they contemplate and praise the Bodhisattva’s supreme merits, their mind-faculties become purified. This is called the purification through the Bodhisattva’s maturation.
"What is meant by 'the Bodhisattva’s perception of having been born'?

For example, when a lotus flower comes into being, whether humans or non-humans perceive that it has been born; so too is it with the Bodhisattva. At the moment of his initial birth, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protecting Deities (Lokapālas), all joyfully protect and sustain him, perceiving that he has been born. This is what is meant by the Bodhisattva’s perception of having been born."
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they are like a lotus flower.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain a vast mind.
What are these ten?
First, they give rise to a vast mind in order to cause sentient beings to fulfill all the pāramitās.
Second, to bring all Buddha-dharmas to full completion;
third, to transform and deliver all sentient beings;
fourth, to sit upon the site of enlightenment and achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Fifth, having attained perfect enlightenment, he turns the sublime wheel of Dharma for all the world—including śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, humans, māras, and brahmās;
sixth, in order to bring about the welfare and happiness of sentient beings, he travels throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds to establish transformative practices;
seventh, by means of the boat of wisdom, he ferries sentient beings across to the far shore beyond birth and death.
