Eighth, because he acts as a support, a refuge, a kinsman, and a relative for all those in the world who are without support, without rescue, without a haven, without a destination, and without kin;

ninth, because he intends to manifest the Buddha—the Great Bull King—and his wondrous lion’s roar, sporting in the dharma-gates of the supernatural powers of all Buddhas, and like a great dragon king gazing with discernment, universally observing the śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, humans, Māras, and Brahmās throughout the entire world, so that all may equally attain the merits of a Buddha;

tenth, because he generates the vast mind in order to transform and deliver sentient beings, being endowed with the majestic power of a Buddha and free from coarse or harsh conduct, free from difficult practices, free from inferior or weak conduct, and free from base or lowly conduct.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain a vast and expansive mind.
Furthermore, good son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain a pure mind.
What are these ten?
First, the fulfillment of the profound mind; the profound mind being unshakable, the profound mind being securely established, and the profound mind being upright and sincere.

Second, one is free from insincere mental attention (*amanasikāra*). Insincere mental attention refers to initiating the practice of the *śrāvaka*, the practice of the *pratyekabuddha*, and giving rise to various minor conditions.
Third, being free from all defilements; "defilements" refers here to the stains of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Fourth, being free from physical faults; "physical faults" refers to being free from artificial modes of deportment.
Fifth, he is free from faults of speech; "faults of speech" refers to failing to correctly reveal the true meaning.

Sixth, he is free from faults of mind; "faults of mind" refers to further abstentions regarding body, speech, and mind: because he knows his body is not in disharmony, because he constantly utters words of few desires and contentment, and because his mind is free from seeking.
Seventh, they recognize kindness and remember to repay it; having received even a small favor, they do not forget it, let alone one that is vast and manifold.

Eighth, they bestow kindness upon others without displaying their own virtues or disparaging the shortcomings of others; even for the smallest act of kindness, they do not expect a reward, but instead joyfully instruct and praise the virtues of those who have helped them.

Ninth, as it is said, they are able to act accordingly: while a bodhisattva does not utter gentle words outwardly while harboring thoughts of anger and malice within; nor does a bodhisattva utter words of praise outwardly while contemplating means to cause harm within; nor does a bodhisattva utter loving speech outwardly while firmly maintaining resentment within; nor does a bodhisattva manifest a virtuous appearance outwardly while giving rise to evil intentions within; nor does a bodhisattva manifest an air of reverence outwardly while conceiving a mind of contempt within.

The Bodhisattva is entirely without that which is not true and without falsehood; furthermore, he is free from stinginess and envy, as well as guile and deception; he does not incite strife nor break apart those in harmony. Why is this?
At all times, the bodhisattva manifests reverence through the body, proclaims the true meaning through speech, and brings to fulfillment all wholesome dharmas through the mind.
Tenth, regarding the teaching of the Tathāgata, they remain free from slander; for the bodhisattva ultimately never gives rise to slander toward the teaching of the Tathāgata.
For what reason do bodhisattvas not disparage the teaching of the Tathāgata?

It is because, having resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, these bodhisattvas shave their hair and beards, don the saffron robes, and go forth into the pure monastic life within the teaching of the Tathāgata.

One does not go forth from home into homelessness because of the hardships of kingship, nor because of the hardships of bandits, nor because of being oppressed by debt, nor out of fear for one's livelihood; rather, one does so solely out of right faith.

Having sought to go forth from the household life, they seek the wholesome Dharma, drawing near to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and serving them with reverence. From those spiritual friends, they listen to and receive the true Dharma; having heard it, they practice it. They do not give rise to pride or arrogance; because they are free from pride, they eliminate inverted attachments. Because they are free from inversion, they attain realization of the Right Path. Because they realize the Right Path, they enter the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). Because they enter the Dharma-nature, they will certainly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. For this reason, a bodhisattva does not give rise to slander within the teachings of the Tathāgata.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain a pure mind.
Furthermore, good son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain deep faith and a mind free from doubt.
What are these ten?
First, they believe in the secret of the Tathāgata’s body.
Second, faith in the Tathāgata’s secrecy of speech;
third, faith in the Tathāgata’s secrecy of mind;
fourth, faith in the practices undertaken by all bodhisattvas.
Fifth, faith in the emergence of the Tathāgata;
sixth, faith in the dharma of bodhi;
seventh, faith that the Tathāgata teaches only the One Vehicle (ekayāna).
Eighth, they have faith in the various teachings spoken by the Tathāgata;
ninth, they have faith in the profound and far-reaching voice of the Tathāgata;
tenth, they have faith in the Tathāgata’s skillful means in delivering sentient beings according to their individual needs.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s faith in the Tathāgata’s secret body?
It is when a bodhisattva gives rise to this thought:”

"I have heard that the Tathāgata’s body is the Dharma-body, the tranquil body, the peerless body, the body equal to the unequaled, the immeasurable body, the unique body, and the vajra-body; such is the reality, free from falsehood, and in this I have faith without doubt."
This is the bodhisattva’s faith in the Tathāgata’s secret of body.
What is the bodhisattva’s faith in the Tathāgata’s secret of speech?
The bodhisattva forms this thought:

"I have heard that the Tathāgata’s speech is secret: he grants predictions to sentient beings either openly before them or secretly. I know that the Tathāgata’s body is free from error and his speech is free from abruptness."
For this reason, the fault of false speech has no source from which it comes. Why is this?

Because the Tathāgata has already severed all faults; he is free from all defilements and far removed from all dust; he has extinguished all burning fevers and is detached from all afflictions; he is pure white, sovereign, immaculate, and unstained.

If it were said that the Tathāgata’s body has faults or his speech has such defects as abruptness and violence, this would be impossible; such a truth is without falsehood, and regarding this matter, I have faith and no doubt.
This is the bodhisattva’s faith in the Tathāgata’s secret of speech.
What is the bodhisattva’s faith in the Tathāgata’s secret of mind?
The bodhisattva forms this thought:

"I have heard that regarding the Tathāgata’s secret of mind, all the Tathāgata’s intentions are entirely conjoined with his wisdom-mind; because they rely upon that mind, they cannot be known by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or other sentient beings, except for those empowered by the Tathāgata’s spiritual authority."

Why is this? The wisdom of the Tathāgata is profoundly deep and bottomless, beyond investigation; it transcends the sphere of all discursive thought and deliberation, being immeasurable, vast, and equal to the realm of empty space. It further surpasses the sphere of all worldly measurements. Such is the truth, free from falsehood; regarding this, I have faith and no doubt.
This is the bodhisattva’s faith in the Tathāgata’s secret intention.
What is the bodhisattva’s faith in the conduct of all bodhisattvas?
The bodhisattva forms this thought:

"I have heard that for the sake of sentient beings, all bodhisattvas manifest and perform various beneficial deeds, giving rise to neither weariness nor fear; they shoulder the heavy burden with steadfast resolve and firm diligence, fulfilling all the pāramitās and gradually accomplishing all the Buddha-dharmas."

With unimpeded wisdom, boundless wisdom, peerless wisdom, and unique wisdom, he has donned the firm armor of steadfast diligence, steadfast vows, immovable vows, and unique vows—namely, the causes of enlightenment, the characteristics of enlightenment, and the conditions for enlightenment. Thus, in this sequence, he has perfected the vast activities of great supernormal power; such is the truth, free from all falsehood, and regarding this I have faith and no doubt.
This is how a bodhisattva has faith in the practices of all bodhisattvas.
What is the bodhisattva’s faith in the emergence of the Tathāgata?
The bodhisattva forms this thought:

"I have heard that after the Bodhisattvas have sat upon the site of enlightenment, they attain the supernormal knowledge of the divine eye—unattached, unimpeded, and free from obscuration—the supernormal knowledge of the divine ear, the supernormal knowledge of others' minds, the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives, the supernormal knowledge of the range of psychic powers, and the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. Having attained such wisdom as these—which is unattached, unimpeded, free from all objects of perception, and the equal wisdom of the single characteristic common to the three times—they are able to contemplate the realm of sentient beings as it truly is: 'This class of sentient beings has performed various evil deeds of body, speech, and mind; they have reviled the noble ones, given rise to false views, and possessed the karma of false views. Due to these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, they fall into the evil destinies and undergo the retribution of the hells.'"

Furthermore, he sees another class of sentient beings who perform various wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind; they do not revile the noble ones, give rise to right view, and possess the karma of right view. By reason of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in a happy destination and receive the superior retribution of the devas.
"In this way, the Bodhisattva observes the realm of sentient beings as it truly is and is able to know, as it truly is, their wholesome and unwholesome karma.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva reflects:
'Just as I, when practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, made great vows, so too, having personally awakened to these practices, I shall cause all sentient beings to fully awaken to them.'"
In this way, my aspiration shall be fulfilled; my hope is also satisfied. This is true and without falsehood; regarding this matter, I have faith and no doubt.
This is the bodhisattva’s faith in the emergence of the Tathāgata.
What is the bodhisattva’s faith in the dharma of enlightenment?
It is when a bodhisattva is able to realize the enlightenment of the Buddha.
"By means of my own power of wisdom, I have attained the fruit of perfect enlightenment; in this regard, I have faith and no doubt.
This is what it means for a bodhisattva to have faith in the Dharma of Bodhi.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s faith that the Tathāgata teaches only the Dharma of the Single Vehicle?"
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"I have heard that the Dharma of the One Vehicle is the Tathāgata-vehicle; it is such that it is true and without falsehood, sincere, without variation, the ultimate truth, and not unreal."

Why is this? It is because all vehicles are produced from the vehicle of the Tathāgata. Just as all the various small islands within Jambudvīpa are subsumed under Jambudvīpa and entirely depend upon Jambudvīpa, they are therefore counted as being of the same name, "Jambudvīpa."

The vehicle of the Tathāgata is likewise so: all vehicles are subsumed within the vehicle of the Tathāgata, they are born from the vehicle of the Tathāgata, and they all rely upon the vehicle of the Tathāgata. Therefore, the One Vehicle is precisely the vehicle of the Tathāgata; regarding this point, I have faith and am without doubt.
"This is how a bodhisattva has faith that the Tathāgata teaches only the Dharma of the Single Vehicle (ekayāna).
What is the bodhisattva’s faith that the Tathāgata teaches various teachings?
The bodhisattva reflects thus:"
"I have heard that the Tathāgata has taught various instructions and various sūtras, which are thus true and without falsehood.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata observes those sentient beings who are to be delivered and teaches the essentials of the Dharma according to their respective inclinations and understandings; regarding this, I have faith and no doubt."
This is how a bodhisattva has faith in the various teachings spoken by the Tathāgata.
What is the bodhisattva’s faith that the Tathāgata possesses a profound and far-reaching voice?
The bodhisattva forms this thought:
"I have heard that the Tathāgata is endowed with a profound, far-reaching, and pure voice; this is true and without falsehood. Why is this?

For even those sons of gods, by the power of cultivating but a small portion of roots of goodness, have already attained such pure, profound, and wondrous voices—how much more so for the Tathāgata, who has accumulated and cultivated supreme practices throughout immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of kalpas?"
"In this regard, I have faith and am free from doubt.
This is how a bodhisattva has faith in the profound and distant voice of the Tathāgata.
"What is it for a bodhisattva to have faith in the Tathāgata’s ability to deliver sentient beings according to their respective needs?"
The Bodhisattva reflects thus: "I have heard that the Tathāgata accords with the minds of sentient beings;

according to how each being should believe and understand, he brings them to transformation and deliverance through various skillful means. With a single voice, the Buddha cuts through all doubts and delusions. Those sentient beings whose faculties and natures are matured and ready for deliverance each perceive the Tathāgata as preaching the Dharma specifically for them, and each understands it accordingly. Yet the Buddha-Tathāgata has no discrimination, nor is he without discrimination. This is truly so and without falsehood; I have faith in this matter and harbor no doubt."
"This is how a bodhisattva has faith that the Tathāgata transforms and delivers sentient beings according to what is appropriate for them.
Son of good family!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain a mind free from doubt."
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll Nine.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, Chao San Da Fu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Imperial Preceptor Guāngfàn, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject Wéijìng,
et al., by imperial decree: "Furthermore, son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, he is like the great ocean."
What are these ten?
First, it is a great accumulation of jewels;
second, it is deep and difficult to fathom its bottom.
Third, it is vast and immeasurable;
fourth, it becomes progressively deeper;
fifth, it does not harbor corpses overnight.
Sixth, they are all of one single flavor;
seventh, they receive and contain all streams;
eighth, their tides do not miss their appointed time.
Ninth, it is that upon which aquatic creatures rely;
tenth, it has no boundaries. "Good son!
How is it that a bodhisattva is a great treasury of jewels?

It is like the great ocean, which extensively accumulates all manner of jewels; all the people within Jambudvīpa may take these jewels from it without end. In the same way, the bodhisattva extensively accumulates the jewels of the merit of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and all sentient beings may take these jewels from them without end. This is what it means for a bodhisattva to be a great treasury of jewels.
"Furthermore, noble son!
Just as the great ocean is so deep that its bottom is difficult to fathom, so too it is with the Bodhisattva; all sentient beings cannot measure the limits of the Bodhisattva's Dharma."
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as the great ocean is vast and immeasurable, so too is the Bodhisattva; his merit and wisdom are likewise vast and immeasurable."
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as the great ocean becomes progressively deeper, so too it is with the Bodhisattva: the depth of all-knowledge, the gradual deepening of all-knowledge, and the ultimate depth of all-knowledge."
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like the great ocean, which does not harbor a corpse. Why is this?
Because it is the natural law of the great ocean to be thus, so too is it with the bodhisattva: they do not dwell together with afflictions, fetters, outflows, or unwholesome associates.
Why is this? Because it is the natural law of Bodhisattvas to be thus.
Furthermore, good son!

Just as when the great ocean receives the many rivers that flow into it, they all become of one single taste—namely, the taste of salt—so too it is with the Bodhisattva: having accumulated all wholesome dharmas, they all become of one single taste—namely, the taste of omniscience.
"Furthermore, noble son!

Just as the great ocean receives all flowing streams yet its waters neither increase nor decrease, so too it is with the bodhisattva: they receive the immeasurable waters of all dharmas, yet their wisdom neither increases nor decreases."
"Furthermore, noble son!
Just as the great ocean tide does not miss its appointed time, so too it is with the bodhisattva: they do not let the time pass for those sentient beings who ought to be matured and delivered."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Just as the great ocean serves as the dwelling place and refuge for all aquatic creatures, so too does the bodhisattva serve as the basis and support for all wholesome dharmas of all sentient beings."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Just as all sentient beings may take water from the great ocean yet it remains without limit, so too is it with the Bodhisattva: he extensively proclaims the essentials of the Dharma for all sentient beings, and this too is without limit."
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, he is like the great ocean.
Furthermore, good son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain subtle and wondrous wisdom. What are these ten?
First, skillfully seeking liberation;
Second, they skillfully know all dharmas of renunciation;
third, they skillfully know the equality of all dharmas;
fourth, they skillfully know that all dharmas are like illusions.
Fifth, they skillfully know the characteristics of all phenomena;
sixth, they skillfully understand the profound and unfathomable dharma of dependent origination;
seventh, they skillfully know the inconceivability of karma.
Eighth, skillfully knowing the meaning of all that is taught;
ninth, skillfully comprehending the meaning as it truly is;
tenth, skillfully contemplating the wisdom of reality.
“Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s skillful seeking of renunciation, up to and including the skillful contemplation of true knowledge?
It is when a bodhisattva reflects as follows:”
"I should observe the characteristics of all worlds.

Upon observing that the world is ablaze with the fire of greed, thick with the smoke of hatred, and shrouded in the darkness of delusion—blind and without refuge—the Bodhisattva then gives rise to this thought:
"How can these sentient beings achieve liberation?"
The Bodhisattva then diligently seeks liberation and the dharma of liberation; by attaining the dharma of liberation, he is able to know the equality of all phenomena accordingly.
Because one knows the equality of all phenomena, one is able to know all phenomena as they truly are—like illusions.
Because one knows all phenomena are like illusions, one knows the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are.
By virtue of knowing the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one is able to contemplate and investigate the profound and unfathomable law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
By virtue of being able to contemplate and investigate the law of dependent origination, one is able to understand that karma is inconceivable (*acintya*).

Therefore, although a bodhisattva knows that all phenomena in the world lack substantial reality, they nevertheless manifest various karmic retributions. By means of this, they attain subtle and wondrous wisdom, enabling them to fully comprehend the meanings taught by all Buddhas and bodhisattvas; through such comprehension, they are able to open up and understand the meaning of reality as it truly is.

Because one understands the meaning as it truly is, one is able to contemplate true reality through wisdom; because one sees true reality, one is able to deliver sentient beings from birth and death. Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain subtle and wondrous wisdom.
Furthermore, son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain responsive eloquence.
What are these ten?
First, revealing that all phenomena are without self;
second, that there are no sentient beings;
Third, there is no life-span;
fourth, there is no nourishment;
fifth, there is no person (pudgala).
Sixth, there is no agent;
seventh, there is no experiencer;
eighth, there is no knower.
Ninth, there is no seer;

tenth, it is revealed that all phenomena are empty and entirely devoid of a sovereign, being all merely false and unreal conceptualizations, for all dharmas exist only because they arise from conditions.

“Good son! If one attains the correspondence with the selflessness of all phenomena, one then accords with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). For this reason, regarding all phenomena as being without a sentient being, without a life-span, without a nourisher, without a person (pudgala), without an agent, without an experiencer, without a knower, and without a viewer—one who thus corresponds to reality is able to accord with the nature of phenomena.”

For this reason, one thoroughly understands that all phenomena are empty and entirely devoid of a sovereign; they are all false and unreal conceptualizations. All phenomena exist merely because they arise from conditions; thus, through correspondence with reality, one is able to accord with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

“Good son! If one accords with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), one does not contradict that nature of phenomena; because one does not contradict it, one is able to correctly expound all phenomena; because one correctly expounds phenomena, one skillfully enters the nature of phenomena; because one enters the nature of phenomena, one is able to reveal and teach all those phenomena; and because one reveals and teaches phenomena, that eloquence is called ‘responsive.’”
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain responsive eloquence.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna*). What are these ten?
First, unimpeded eloquence;
Second, inexhaustibility;
third, continuity;
fourth, fearlessness before the great assembly.
Fifth, not being base;
sixth, being without fear;
seventh, not being common.
Eighth, non-contempt;
ninth, boundlessness;
tenth, unimpeded understanding.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the eloquence of joyful speech.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain pure eloquence.
What are these ten?
First, being free from stammering;
Second, their speech is free from confusion;
third, they remain far removed from what is base and inferior;
fourth, their speech is neither arrogant nor harsh.
Fifth, the meaning is without loss or diminution;
sixth, the phrasing is without omission or defect;
seventh, the voice is without deficiency or interruption.
Eighth, there is nothing he does not know the proper time for;
ninth, his speech is never coarse or harsh;
tenth, there is nothing he does not explain with clarity.
“Good son! All bodhisattvas possess eloquence that is free from stammering. Why is this?
Because a bodhisattva is without timidity amidst the great assembly.
Furthermore, whatever eloquence a bodhisattva possesses is free from confusion. Why is this?
The wisdom of a bodhisattva is serene and fearless.
Furthermore, the eloquence possessed by a bodhisattva is never inferior. Why is this?
When a bodhisattva dwells amidst the great assembly, he is like a lion, free from all fear.
Furthermore, the eloquence of a bodhisattva is such that his speech is neither arrogant nor perverse.
Why is this? Because they have already abandoned the afflictions (*kleśa*).
If one possesses afflictions, speech will be haughty and perverse; if one lacks them, it is not so.
"Furthermore, for a bodhisattva, all eloquence is never diminished in meaning.
Why is this? Because they have already attained the Dharma."
If one does not grasp the Dharma, there will be a deficiency in its meaning; if one grasps it, this is not so.
Furthermore, the eloquence possessed by a bodhisattva is flawless in its phrasing.
Why is this? Because it provides an extensive explanation of various treatises.
If the explanation of the treatises were meager, there would be omissions in the text; however, this is not the case with an extensive explanation.
"Furthermore, the eloquence of a bodhisattva possesses no deficiency in its sound.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva has a sublime understanding of all sounds."
If one does not understand, there will be deficiencies and omissions regarding sounds;
if one understands, it is not so. Furthermore, for a bodhisattva, there is no eloquence that is not timely: what should be said first is not said last, and what should be said last is not said first.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva skillfully knows all temporal divisions.
Furthermore, whatever eloquence the bodhisattva possesses is free from coarseness, free from anything unpleasant, and free from anything that is not a joy to hear.
Why is this? Because one has already been able to distance oneself from faults of speech.
If there were faults of speech, one's words would be coarse and harsh; in their absence, this is not the case.
"Furthermore, whatever eloquence a bodhisattva possesses is entirely lucid. Why is this?
Because the bodhisattva’s faculties and nature are sharp."
If one of dull faculties does not understand clearly, one of sharp faculties will not be thus.
Son of good family!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain pure eloquence.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the eloquence that delights all sentient beings.
What are these ten?
First, pleasant speech;
second, a cheerful countenance free from frowning;
third, speech that accords with the truth.
Fourth, speaking in accordance with the Dharma;
fifth, speaking with impartiality;
sixth, not exalting oneself;
Seventh, not disparaging others;
eighth, being free from attachment;
ninth, being free from provocation or vexation.
Tenth, they possess various forms of eloquence.
Good son! A bodhisattva is able to cause all sentient beings to give rise to joy through words of affection.
"Furthermore, a bodhisattva always manifests a serene and joyful countenance, remaining free from frowning, so as to cause all sentient beings to give rise to joy.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva always utters speech that is meaningful and exquisite, so as to cause all sentient beings to give rise to joy."
"Furthermore, a bodhisattva constantly utters words of Dharma and words of benefit, causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva constantly teaches the Dharma equally to sentient beings, causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy."
"Furthermore, a bodhisattva does not exalt himself; he remains far removed from the fault of arrogance and haughtiness, causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva does not disparage others; he always teaches the Dharma with reverence for sentient beings, causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy."
"Furthermore, a bodhisattva is free from all defiled attachments and possesses pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva is free from all provocation and possesses great power of patience (*kṣānti*), causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy."
"Furthermore, a bodhisattva possesses various forms of eloquence and constantly utters pleasing speech, causing all sentient beings to give rise to joy. Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will immediately attain the eloquence that delights all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain faith and compliance in the teaching of the Dharma.
What are these ten?
First, the bodhisattva does not teach the Dharma to sentient beings who are not vessels for the Dharma.
Second, one does not preach the Dharma to those who possess obstructions;
third, one does not preach the Dharma to those who hold views of attainment;
fourth, one does not preach the Dharma to heterodox outsiders.
Fifth, one does not preach the Dharma to those who have not given rise to a mind of aspiration;
sixth, one does not preach the Dharma to those who have not developed a pure mind;
seventh, one does not preach the Dharma to those with a crooked and deceitful mind.
Eighth, one does not preach the Dharma to those who seek only a livelihood;
ninth, one does not preach the Dharma to those who are greedily attached to gain and offerings and are entangled by stinginess and envy;
tenth, one does not preach the Dharma to those who are blind, deaf, or mute.
"Why is this? Son of good family!

A bodhisattva does not practice stinginess regarding the Dharma nor keep the Dharma secret; he has compassion for all sentient beings without exception and does not abandon them for the sake of benefiting them."
Why is this? If there are sentient beings who are not vessels for the Dharma, the Bodhisattva gives rise to this thought:
"These sentient beings have developed an attitude of indifference toward the discipline and teachings of the Tathāgata."
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If that is so, for what kind of sentient beings should the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! For sentient beings who possess faith, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas shall preach the Dharma for them."

Furthermore, for those sentient beings whose roots of goodness have already matured, who are vessels of the Dharma, who have planted the foundations of various virtues under previous Buddhas, who are free from flattery and deception, who do not falsely manifest dignified conduct, who do not crave gain and offerings, who are endowed with a profound resolve, who are sustained by spiritual friends, who possess auspicious marks that others delight to behold, whose faculties are sharp and clear such that they understand the meaning of the teachings they hear, who practice with diligent effort according to the Dharma they have received, and who are able to practice as taught by the Buddhas—for these beings, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma.
“Good son! If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, he will attain faith and compliance regarding the teaching of the Dharma.
Furthermore, good son!”
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they become a teacher of the Dharma. What are these ten?

First, they teach the Dharma for the sake of cultivating and gathering the Buddha-dharmas, yet they do not perceive any Buddha-dharmas to be attained, nor do they perceive anything that is being cultivated or gathered.

Second, he preaches the Dharma because he has cultivated and accumulated the *pāramitās*, yet he does not perceive that the *pāramitās* can be apprehended, nor does he perceive anything that has been cultivated and accumulated;

third, he preaches the Dharma because he has cultivated and accumulated the bodhisattva-dharmas, yet he does not perceive that the bodhisattva-dharmas can be apprehended, nor does he perceive anything that has been cultivated and accumulated;
fourth, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of severing afflictions (*kleśa*), yet he does not perceive that afflictions can be apprehended, nor does he perceive their severance.

Fifth, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of weariness with the world, detachment, and the cessation of craving, yet he does not perceive that there is any weariness, detachment, or cessation to be attained;

sixth, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of attaining the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning, yet he does not perceive that there are any stream-enterers, once-returners, or non-returners to be attained, nor does he perceive those fruits;
seventh, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of attaining the fruit of arhatship, yet he does not perceive that there is any arhat to be attained, nor does he perceive that fruit.
Eighth, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of attaining the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, yet he perceives no pratyekabuddha to be attained, nor does he perceive the fruit;
ninth, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of severing the grasping of self-clinging, yet he perceives no self to be attained, nor does he perceive the clinging;
tenth, he preaches the Dharma to manifest the retribution of karma, yet he perceives no karma to be attained, nor does he perceive the retribution.
"Why is this? All such dharmas lack any substantial reality; they are merely proclaimed by way of provisional names, and even those names do not exist. Why is that?"
Letters have no intrinsic nature, for phenomena are free from letters; yet, by means of conventional and provisional designations within the nameless, the names of all phenomena are established.
Because those names are empty and fundamentally false, there are no false names within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Since there are no false names, there are no deceptive phenomena within the ultimate truth.
Those dharmas of falsehood are for the purpose of deceiving and deluding foolish people. Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, he is then a teacher of the Dharma.
"Furthermore, noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to contemplate the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) in accordance with it.
What are these ten?

First, although the bodhisattva contemplates the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) accordingly, he does not destroy the characteristics of form; although he contemplates the nature of phenomena accordingly, he does not destroy the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
Second, although he contemplates the nature of phenomena accordingly, he does not destroy the characteristics of the desire realm.
Third, although he contemplates the nature of phenomena accordingly, he does not destroy the characteristics of the form realm.
Fourth, although he contemplates the nature of phenomena in accordance with reality, he does not destroy the characteristics of the formless realm;
fifth, although he contemplates the nature of phenomena in accordance with reality, he does not destroy the characteristics of all phenomena;
sixth, although he contemplates the nature of phenomena in accordance with reality, he does not perceive any characteristic of conformity within all phenomena.
Seventh, although he contemplates the nature of phenomena accordingly, he does not perceive the marks of sentient beings;
eighth, although he contemplates the nature of phenomena accordingly, he does not fall into the view of nihilism;
ninth, although he contemplates the nature of phenomena accordingly, he does not lose the right path.
Tenth, although one contemplates the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) in accordance with reality, one does not depart from wisdom and skillful means.
Son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to contemplate the nature of phenomena in accordance with reality.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will skillfully understand the principle of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
What are these ten?
First, possessing wisdom;
second, being sustained by spiritual friends;
third, initiating diligence.
Fourth, being free from all obstructive defilements;
fifth, skillfully cultivating pure conduct;
sixth, honoring and praising the Dharma.
Seventh, skillfully cultivating the contemplation of emptiness;
eighth, being free from views that grasp at attainment;
ninth, tending toward the right path.
Tenth, seeing the true Dharma.
Son of good family!
Because the bodhisattva is endowed with wisdom, he is able to diligently seek out spiritual friends.
Having seen the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), one gives rise to joy in the heart and regards them as a teacher and a venerable one, drawing near to and relying upon them.

Because one is able to rely upon the spiritual friend, one immediately initiates diligence to sever all unwholesome dharmas and to perfect all pure wholesome dharmas. One exerts oneself in distancing oneself from all obstructive defilements; by being free from obstructive defilements, one attains pliancy (praśrabdhi) and skillfully cultivates pure conduct, becoming free from all faults of body, speech, and mind.

Because of this purity, one respects and praises the Dharma that has been attained; because of this respect for the Dharma, one frequently practices the contemplation of emptiness; because of practicing the contemplation of emptiness, the view of attaining anything does not arise; because of being free from the view of attaining anything, one proceeds in accordance with the right path; and because of entering the right path, one is able to contemplate reality as it truly is.
The Bodhisattva Nivaranaviskambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is called ‘reality’?”
The Buddha said,
"Good son! The meaning of reality as it truly is is what is called 'the real.'"
The Bodhisattva Nivaranaviskambhin addressed the Buddha, saying,
“What is meant by ‘reality as it is’ (yathābhūta)?
The Buddha said:
"Because it is not false, it is called 'as-it-is' (yathābhūta).
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by 'not false'?"
The Buddha said,
“That which is called suchness is nothing that is not suchness, and there is no suchness other than suchness.
Bodhisattva Apahāritāvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is called 'True Suchness'?
The Buddha said,
"Good son!..."
This Dharma is realized only within; it cannot be expressed by means of written characters or spoken language.

Why is this? Because this Dharma transcends all written characters, is free from all verbal discourse, and surpasses the realm of all speech. It lies beyond the path of words, is devoid of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and is free from both action and non-action. It is neither moving nor still, transcends all discursive thought (*vitarka* and *vicāra*), and is an inconceivable realm.

Neither signless nor non-signless, it is utterly remote from and emerges beyond all realms of signs; it transcends all mundane realms, exceeds the conduct of ordinary beings, passes beyond all demonic realms, and surmounts every sphere of affliction.

Transcending the objects of all consciousnesses, one dwells securely in the supreme, tranquil realm of noble wisdom that is non-abiding; therefore, this Dharma is realized only within. It is stainless, undefiled, pure, and pristine; it is the most supreme, the most excellent, the foremost, and peerless. It is a dharma that is eternally abiding, firm, ultimate, and indestructible; whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, this Dharma remains eternally present.

“Good son! For the sake of seeking this Dharma, a bodhisattva undergoes hundreds of thousands of kinds of difficult practices and ascetic austerities; having attained this Dharma, they cause all sentient beings to abide entirely within it.”

“Good son! Therefore, this Dharma is called True Suchness (tathatā), it is called the Reality Limit (bhūtakoṭi), it is called All-Knowledge (sarvajñā), it is called the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvākārajñā), it is called the Inconceivable Realm, and it is called the Non-dual Realm.”
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll Ten.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll Eleven.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Court, the Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, the Great Dharma Master of Radiant Sanskrit, the Imperially Ennobled Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, the Subject Weijing and others, by imperial decree. At that time, the Bodhisattva Apannaka (Remover of Obstructions) addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"How can this Dharma be realized?
How can it be understood?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! It is through supramundane wisdom that one can realize and enter into internal, self-luminous understanding.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin said:
“Is it not the case that wisdom-realization is precisely the internal understanding and entry into one’s own mind?
The Buddha said, “No.”
Good son! Why is this?
Because wisdom is able to contemplate all phenomena exactly as they are, and because it is realized through bodily witness.
The Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin said:
"O sons of noble family!
Is it not the case that when one realizes the Dharma through those wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one is immediately able to attain internal realization and entry?"
The Buddha said:
“No, son of good family!”
It is not that upon merely hearing it, one can immediately understand and enter [this state] through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation within oneself.
I shall now briefly clarify this meaning by means of a simile. "Good son!

For example, in the midst of a vast wilderness during the height of summer, there might be one person traveling from east to west and another from west to east, both oppressed by the scorching heat and parched with thirst. At that time, the person coming from the west says to the one coming from the east:
"I am now extremely hot and tormented by thirst; you have come along a well-trodden path—where might there be flowing springs, ponds, or pools of cool, clear water?"
"I pray that you will speak for me, so that I may drink it and be relieved of this thirst and distress.
The one coming from the east, who thoroughly knew all the roads in the eastern region and likewise knew exactly where there was water—its sweet flavor, its depth, and so forth—immediately told him:
"Go forward now; you will see a place where two roads diverge. You should not take the one leading out from the left; you should instead proceed along the one on the right."
"There is a grove there, lush and verdant, with a pond within it, its clear, sweet, and delicious waters overflowing and filling it to the brim.
"Noble son, what do you think?"

When that thirsty person merely hears it described that there is a wondrous pond, and gives rise to the thought of it, can they thereby eliminate the affliction of thirst and immediately attain inner coolness?
The Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin said: "No,
World-Honored One!"

Yet if a person scorched by heat and thirst were to go in person to that place where water is found, and having drunk the water from that pool, that person would then be able to eliminate their burning thirst and become internally cool and refreshed.
The Buddha said,

“Good son, it is likewise with the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation: one cannot immediately enter into and understand the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) from within simply by having heard them.”
You should now know that the great wilderness is the realm of birth and death;
those who suffer from heat and thirst during the height of summer are all sentient beings;
and the extreme, blazing heat is the realm of the six sense objects and the afflictions of craving.
Those who know the road well are the bodhisattvas who are skillfully able to know the path to all-knowledge;

those who drink the water are those who have inwardly realized and attained understanding, obtaining the supreme flavor of the Dharma—light, pure, sweet, and delicious—the true nature of all phenomena as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
“Good son! Listen now, and I shall further provide a parable.

Suppose the Tathāgata were to remain for the duration of an eon and, before all people in Jambudvīpa, were to praise the celestial *sūda*—its wondrous color, its exquisite fragrance, and its most supreme, pure, and refined flavor—and how those who drink it obtain a touch of sublime bliss.”
“Good son!
When the people of Jambudvīpa hear such an explanation, do they internally understand [the nature of] form, fragrance, and so forth?
Bodhisattva Apahāritāvara replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:

“Good son! For this reason, you should know that the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation do not enable one to internally understand and enter the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) merely upon hearing them.

Listen further: it is as if there were a person who, among various fruits, knows the name of one fruit; having eaten it himself first, he describes its taste, color, fragrance, and so forth to someone who has not yet eaten it.”
"Good son! What do you think?
Can that person who has not yet eaten know the taste of its fruit?"
The Bodhisattva Nīvaranaviskambhin said: “No,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:

“Good son! For this reason, you should know that the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation do not enable one to internally understand and enter the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) at the very moment of hearing.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Well spoken, World-Honored One!
Well spoken, Sugata!"

Regarding this principle of the Dharma realized within, if there is a son of good family who can hear it even once, you should know that such a person is immediately able to fulfill the practices of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.
"Why is this? Because these people have already fulfilled the causes for non-perversion, they have attained this Dharma.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is. Noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain a thorough understanding of the principle of the dharma-realm."
"Furthermore, noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will thoroughly understand the realm of emptiness.
What are these ten?
First, knowing that the powers are empty;
second, knowing that the fearlessnesses are empty;
third, knowing that the unique buddha-qualities are empty.
Fourth, knowing that the aggregate of ethical discipline is empty;
fifth, knowing that the aggregate of meditative concentration is empty;
sixth, knowing that the aggregate of wisdom is empty.
Seventh, knowing that the aggregate of liberation is empty;
eighth, knowing that the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation is empty;
ninth, knowing that emptiness itself is empty.
Tenth, they know ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

Although they know it to be empty, they do not perceive any sign of attainment within that emptiness due to the causal conditions of emptiness; nor do they cling to emptiness, give rise to views of emptiness, or rely upon emptiness. Furthermore, they do not fall into the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) because of the causal conditions of emptiness.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will thoroughly understand the realm of emptiness.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to skillfully cultivate the practice of signlessness (*animitta*).
What are these ten?
First, being free from external signs;
Second, the departure from internal characteristics;
third, the departure from the characteristics of conceptual proliferation;
fourth, the departure from all characteristics of pervasive imagination.
Fifth, to be free from all signs of anything to be attained;
sixth, to be free from all signs of movement and activity;
seventh, to be free from all signs of the false and artificial.
Eighth, it is free from all signs of objective referents;
ninth, it is free from the signs of attaining existence through consciousness;
tenth, it is free from the signs of objects known by consciousness.
“Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to skillfully cultivate the practice of signlessness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Such modes of practice constitute the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the signless practice.
How, furthermore, is the practice cultivated by the Tathāgata perceived?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son, you should know that this is an inconceivable matter.”
Why is this? Because it is beyond the sphere of the mind.
If any sentient being were to claim that the Tathāgata has any thoughts, they would be deranged.
All Tathāgatas—whether matters of this shore or matters of the other shore—even to the point of extreme exhaustion, can never be seen, nor can they be apprehended. Why is this?

The Dharma of the Tathāgata is inconceivable, profoundly deep and difficult to fathom; its limits cannot be reached. It is equal to empty space, transcending all spheres of discursive thought and investigation, and surpassing all marks of attainability. It is beyond the reach of any deliberation, calculation, or measurement.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have a slight doubt that I wish to set forth as a question. If the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha would grant me leave to ask, I pray that you will explain it briefly for me.”
The Buddha said, "Nivāraṇaviṣkambhin!
You should now ask this; it is a matter of constant concern."
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Those who are self-exalting are not true sages. Since the World-Honored One is the Great Dharma King, how is it that you now speak in self-praise? Is this not self-exaltation?”
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good son!
Since your resolve is profound and firm that you are able to pose this question, you should listen attentively and apply your mind with great care; I shall now speak for you."
Then the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: “Good son!

The Tathāgata is free from the mind of *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") and does not exalt himself; he does not give rise to *asmimāna* out of a desire for gain, offerings, or fame, nor does he do so to seek recognition by others, nor does he give rise to *asmimāna* through a mind of flattery or deceit. Rather, he uses the Dharma he has attained solely to extensively bring benefit, welfare, and happiness to all sentient beings.

Why is this? It is because he wishes to cause sentient beings to give rise to a heart of pure joy toward the Tathāgata; for those who are capable vessels of the Dharma, he desires that they obtain all wholesome dharmas, so that they may attain great benefit and happiness throughout the long night.
The Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why is it that sentient beings are unable to know the supreme virtues of the Tathāgata?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son! They truly do not know.”

Why is this? Because the sentient beings within this buddha-field have narrow and inferior faith and understanding, their minds are attached to what is coarse and base, and they possess little wisdom, little faith, and meager roots of virtue; thus, they are unable to know the supreme qualities of the Tathāgata. For this reason, the Tathāgata himself proclaims all his merits, intending to cause these sentient beings to give rise to pure faith and thereby enable them to accomplish the various supreme qualities of a Tathāgata.

“Good son! It is like a man who is a great physician, skilled at curing all manner of ailments, foremost in his country with no equal; yet the people of that land do not recognize that this person is one who clearly understands prescriptions and medicines and possesses the supreme virtues of a healer.”
At that time, seeing one who was oppressed and tormented by the suffering of illness, the physician immediately formed this thought:
"This person’s illness and suffering stem from improper methods and medicine; I should now provide treatment for them."
At that time, the physician went to where the patient was and said to him:
"I am a physician, well-versed in medical arts and skilled in understanding all diseases as well as their causes; I shall effectively treat your ailment."
When that patient heard these words, he immediately conceived a mind of faith and deep respect toward the physician and relied upon him.
The physician then provided medical treatment for him, and his illness was cured.
"Good son, what do you think? Does that physician,
having spoken before the sick person, praise himself by saying, 'I am already able to cure them'?"
The Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying: “No,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! The Tathāgata is likewise thus;

he is a great king of physicians who skillfully cures the diseases of affliction of sentient beings. Knowing the causes of their illnesses, he administers the great medicine of the Dharma. When sentient beings are oppressed by the diseases of affliction such as ignorance, the Tathāgata, having seen them, immediately approaches them and proclaims that the Tathāgata is endowed with supreme merit."

May all sentient beings who are oppressed and afflicted by the suffering of illness, upon hearing the exposition of the Tathāgata’s supreme merits, be able to give rise to a mind of pure faith and reverence, taking the Buddha, the Tathāgata, as their reliance.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, the supreme Great Physician-King, bestows the great medicine of the Dharma upon those who are ill, causing the grave illnesses of affliction of all sentient beings to be completely extinguished.
“Good son! What is the great medicine of the Dharma? It is this:

for sentient beings with excessive greed, one practices the contemplation of impurity; for sentient beings with excessive hatred, one practices the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion; for sentient beings with excessive delusion, one practices the contemplation of dependent origination.”
For this reason, one sees the Tathāgata extolling his own supreme virtues.
"Furthermore, son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, he will attain freedom from attachment regarding all vows."
What are the ten?
First, although one practices giving, one has aspirations and yet does not cling to that giving;
second, although one maintains the precepts, one does not cling to that maintenance of the precepts.
Third, although one practices patience, one does not become attached to patience;
fourth, although one arouses diligence, one does not become attached to diligence;
fifth, although one cultivates meditative concentration, one does not become attached to meditative concentration.
Sixth, although they cultivate wisdom, they do not become attached to wisdom;
seventh, although they rely upon the triple world, they do not become attached to the triple world;
eighth, although they seek bodhi, they do not become attached to bodhi.
Ninth, although they practice the right path, they do not cling to the right path;
tenth, although they enter nirvana, they do not cling to nirvana.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva is free from all attachments; thus, although he engages in all worldly activities, he remains entirely without attachment. Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain freedom from attachment regarding all vows.
Furthermore, son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the perfection of the body of loving-kindness.
What are the ten?
First, compassion that is without spatial limitation;
second, compassion that is without distinction of kind;
Third, the compassion of the Dharma;
fourth, the compassion of meditative concentration;
fifth, the compassion of non-harming;
Sixth, the loving-kindness of benefiting;
seventh, the loving-kindness of an impartial mind toward all sentient beings;
eighth, the loving-kindness of an equanimous mind free from malice.
Ninth is the vast compassion that pervades the ten directions;
tenth is supramundane compassion. Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the perfection of the body of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the perfection of the body of compassion.
What are the ten?
First, when a bodhisattva sees those who are afflicted by suffering, without rescue, without support, and without refuge, they give rise to the bodhicitta upon seeing them;
second, having given rise to the bodhicitta, they seek the Dharma that is to be attained.
Third, having attained the Dharma through enduring hardships and diligent seeking, one universally brings great benefit to sentient beings;
fourth, one causes sentient beings who are stingy and greedy to practice generosity;
fifth, one causes sentient beings who violate the precepts to uphold pure discipline.
Sixth, to cause sentient beings with minds of anger to cultivate the practice of patience;
seventh, to cause sentient beings who are indolent to arouse diligence;
eighth, to cause sentient beings who are distracted to abide in a concentrated mind.
Ninth, to cause sentient beings who lack wisdom to cultivate it;
tenth, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, a bodhisattva does not allow their superior practice of awakening to be ruined, lost, or regressed by hardships.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the perfection of the body of compassion.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will skillfully cultivate the practice of joy.
What are these ten?
First, because the bodhisattva has personally attained liberation from the blazing of the three realms of existence, they give rise to joy.
Second, they give rise to joy because they sever the cords of bondage that bind them to the long-term cycle of saṃsāra’s coming and going;

third, they give rise to joy because the bodhisattva, having distanced themselves from all manner of seeking, has personally crossed over the various evils and multitudes within the ocean of birth and death;
fourth, they give rise to joy because the bodhisattva has personally broken down the banner of arrogance that has stood high for a vast duration.
Fifth, the bodhisattva uses the vajra of wisdom to shatter the high peaks of their own afflictions until they are reduced to fine, dust-like particles; thus, he gives rise to joy.
Sixth, the bodhisattva attains peace and security for himself and likewise causes others to all attain peace and security; thus, he gives rise to joy.

Seventh, within this world, beings are bound by craving and attachment, shrouded by darkness, and lack self-mastery, remaining in a state of long sleep; having himself awakened from this and cleared his vision, he likewise enables others to all awaken; thus, he gives rise to joy.

Eighth, the bodhisattva rejoices because he himself is able to attain liberation and transcend the miserable realms, and likewise enables others to all attain liberation and transcend the miserable realms;

ninth, sentient beings have long dwelt within the wilderness and perilous difficulties of saṃsāra, wandering alone without companions, circling back and forth, ignorant of the path and unaware of their destination; the bodhisattva, being himself able to transcend and distance himself from these, provides guidance and instruction for them all, and thus gives rise to joy;
tenth, the bodhisattva rejoices because he has drawn near to the city of omniscience.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will skillfully cultivate the practice of joy.
Furthermore, good son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will skillfully cultivate the practice of equanimity (*upekṣā*). What are these ten?
First, although the eye perceives forms, one practices equanimity and does not perceive the objects of the eye-consciousness as increasing or decreasing, nor as forming or disintegrating.

Second, although the ear hears sounds; third, although the nose smells odors; fourth, although the tongue discerns flavors; fifth, although the body perceives tangibles; sixth, although the mind cognizes mental objects (*dharma*), it practices the practice of equanimity (*upekṣā*), and furthermore does not perceive any increase or decrease, nor any formation or destruction, regarding the sensory objects of the ear and sound, the nose and odor, the tongue and flavor, the body and tangibility, or the mind and mental objects;

seventh, although it contemplates the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) while practicing the practice of equanimity, it does not perceive the suffering of conditioned existence as increasing or decreasing, nor as forming or decaying;

eighth, although it contemplates the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) while practicing the practice of equanimity, it does not perceive the suffering of suffering as increasing or decreasing, nor as forming or decaying.

Ninth, although he contemplates the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*), he practices the cultivation of equanimity (*upekṣā*) and does not perceive that suffering of change as increasing or decreasing, nor as forming or disintegrating;
tenth, when he observes sentient beings who have already accomplished what was to be done, the Bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of joy and forms this thought:
"I intended to deliver them, yet they have already delivered themselves."
"Therefore, one cultivates the practice of equanimity.
Son of good family!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be well-cultivated in the practice of equanimity."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the play of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-vikrīḍita*).
What are these ten?
First, manifesting the relinquishing of one's lifespan;
second, entering the womb and taking birth;
third, manifesting the appearance of a youth sporting within the palace.
Fourth, renunciation;
fifth, ascetic practice;
sixth, proceeding to the site of enlightenment;
Seventh, attaining equal and perfect enlightenment and subduing the armies of Māra;
eighth, manifesting the aspect of tranquility;
ninth, turning the sublime wheel of Dharma.
"Tenth, they enter great parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what causes and conditions does a bodhisattva manifest the relinquishing of his lifespan in the Tuṣita Heaven, and even manifest entry into great parinirvāṇa?
The Buddha said, "Good son!"

The sentient beings in the Tuṣita Heaven mostly give rise to the notion of permanence; yet when those beings see the Bodhisattva—who is the most supreme and most excellent in all worlds, sublime and radiant, such that beholders never tire of him, and who remains unstained by the realms of the five desires—they are able to conceive the thought of relinquishing their lifespan. Having seen this, those beings turn away from the notion of permanence and give rise to the notion of impermanence; by relying upon this awareness of impermanence, they immediately initiate practices of heedfulness.

"Furthermore, there are sentient beings who give rise to a mind of negligence; although they possess a heart of affection, faith, and respect toward the Bodhisattva, because they develop attachment to various sensory objects, they do not come to approach, honor, or serve the Bodhisattva. Those sentient beings then conceive this thought:
'The Bodhisattva has resided here for a long time, and I too have resided here for a long time.'"
Thus they give rise to a mind of negligence.

The Bodhisattva, desiring to cause those sentient beings to develop revulsion for cyclic existence and attain non-negligence—because by not giving rise to a negligent mind, they will immediately attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—for this reason, the Bodhisattva manifests the relinquishing of his life-span in the Tuṣita Heaven.

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who can be liberated by entering the womb and taking birth, the Bodhisattva immediately manifests the appearance of entering the womb and taking birth, so that upon seeing it, they may give rise to a sense of rare wonder.”

While dwelling in his mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva teaches the Dharma to various sentient beings according to their needs, causing them to attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. For this reason, the Bodhisattva manifests birth.

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who are to be liberated by means of the appearance of sporting within the palace of a youth, or for the sake of maturing and protecting those classes of sentient beings with inferior inclinations and understandings, the Bodhisattva manifests the appearance of sporting within the palace of a youth.”

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who can be liberated by means of the appearance of one who has left the household life, the bodhisattva manifests the appearance of one who has left the household life for the sake of bringing them to maturity.”

“Good son! If there are those whose minds are attached to coarse and inferior gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and so forth, who can be delivered through the appearance of ascetic practice, the bodhisattva manifests the appearance of ascetic practice for the sake of bringing them to maturity and for the sake of subduing various non-Buddhists.”

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who, for a long time, have thought and sought, ‘When will the Bodhisattva go to the site of enlightenment? At that time, I shall perform acts of offering accordingly.’”
Because the Bodhisattva wishes to bring those sentient beings to maturity, he manifests his arrival at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Having reached the site of enlightenment, he causes all sentient beings to make offerings according to their capacity. Once they have made these offerings, those sentient beings immediately attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

“Good son! If there are sentient beings who, relying on their own pride and arrogance, are haughty, the Bodhisattva—desiring to cause them to turn away from such a mind of pride—manifests sitting at the site of enlightenment, attaining equal and perfect awakening, and subduing the armies of Māra.”

Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings who delight in tranquility, [the Bodhisattva] manifests the attainment of supreme realization; thus, the Bodhisattva displays the achievement of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

When the Bodhisattva attains perfect enlightenment, all the various sounds within the trichiliocosm become utterly still. Upon seeing that this trichiliocosm has become entirely tranquil, those sentient beings who delight in tranquility all together make this vow:
"May we also likewise attain the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

"Good son! If there are sentient beings who delight in being teachers and are single-mindedly devoted to seeking that status, yet do not know the Dharma of transcendence, nor understand the causes and effects of future lives."

In order to bring those sentient beings to maturity in their roots of goodness and to render them capable vessels for the Dharma, the Bodhisattva, having attained perfect enlightenment, proceeded to the kingdom of Kāśī to turn the noble and wondrous Wheel of Dharma in its twelve aspects through three revolutions.
“Good son! If there are sentient beings who can be liberated by means of the manifestation of entering nirvana, the bodhisattva then manifests the entry into great parinirvāṇa for them.”
"Good son!
By these causes and conditions, the Bodhisattva manifests the relinquishing of his life-span in the Tuṣita Heaven, up to and including his entry into Great Parinirvāṇa.
Good son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the playful mastery of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-vikrīḍita*).
The *Buddhabhāṣita-nivaraṇaviṣkambhi-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Scroll Eleven.
The *Buddhabhāṣita-nivaraṇaviṣkambhi-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Two Dynasties, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
Great Master of Radiant Dharma, Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Weijing, et al., by Imperial Decree: "Furthermore, good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to leave behind the eight difficulties.
What are these ten?
First, to remain free from unwholesome karma.
Second, not transgressing the precepts established by the Tathāgata;
third, being far removed from stinginess and avarice;
fourth, having planted the roots of various virtues under previous Buddhas.
Fifth, diligently cultivating meritorious conduct;
sixth, being fully endowed with wisdom;
seventh, skillfully understanding expedient means;
Eighth, being fully endowed with superior vows;
ninth, frequently giving rise to a sense of wearying revulsion [toward saṃsāra];
tenth, exerting diligent vigor.

“Good son! Because a bodhisattva does not commit unwholesome karma, he does not fall into the hells. Even if he manifests birth within the hells, he does not undergo the extreme sufferings of those hells; furthermore, he does not remain in the hells for long, nor does he give rise to a mind of anger or affliction toward the sentient beings there.”
Why is this? It is because a bodhisattva inherently cultivates the ten wholesome courses of action; by these causes and conditions, the bodhisattva does not fall into hell.
Furthermore, good son!

Because the bodhisattva does not transgress the prohibitive precepts of the Tathāgata, they do not fall into the realm of animals; even if they manifest birth within that realm, they nevertheless do not undergo the suffering of an animal.
"Furthermore, noble son!

A bodhisattva does not give rise to stinginess; because of the absence of the causes and conditions of stinginess, he does not fall into the realm of hungry ghosts. Even if he should manifest birth within that realm for the sake of demonstration, he nevertheless does not undergo the sufferings of a hungry ghost."
"Furthermore, noble son!
A bodhisattva is not born into a family of wrong views; even if born there, they do not lose their pure faith. Moreover, such a bodhisattva always encounters virtuous spiritual friends."

Why is this? Because the bodhisattva has long cultivated wholesome dharmas and planted the roots of all virtues under previous Buddhas; he is always born into families of right view, and having been born there, he possesses pure faith and further causes that pure faith to grow extensively.
"Furthermore, noble son!
A bodhisattva’s faculties must also be unimpaired; if his faculties were impaired, he would not be capable of serving as a vessel for the Buddha-dharma."

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva extensively accumulates merit and diligently cultivates meritorious practices, constantly honoring and making offerings to the stūpas, temples, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata; and by constantly drawing near to and performing various superior practices, cultivating them extensively within himself through these superior practices, he attains the full perfection of his faculties.
Because they are fully ordained, they are great vessels for the Buddha-dharma.

Furthermore, son of good family, bodhisattvas are not born in borderlands where sentient beings are foolish, deaf, mute, or physically impaired; where they lack capability and do not understand the meaning of well-spoken or ill-spoken words; who are not vessels for the Buddha-dharma and do not recognize their parents, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas.

For this reason, Bodhisattvas are always born in the central lands, where sentient beings possess sharp and keen faculties, where there are many wise ones, and where they are further esteemed by the wise; they are capable and endowed with power and ability, understanding the meaning of both good and evil words, serving as great vessels for the Buddha-dharma, and having deep faith in śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
Why is this? It is because of the power of wisdom previously cultivated.
Furthermore, son of good family!

A bodhisattva is not reborn in the long-lived heavens; for if they were born there, even though countless Buddhas might appear in the world, they would not encounter them, and thus their work for the benefit of sentient beings could not be accomplished.

For this reason, the Bodhisattva is born in the desire realm; herein, sentient beings encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world, and through their joyful affection and close proximity, they may be transformed and delivered. Why is this?
Because Bodhisattvas are well-endowed with skillful means.

Furthermore, son of good family, Bodhisattvas are not born in world-systems where there is no Buddha; even if they were born therein, they would neither see the Buddha, nor hear the Dharma, nor make offerings to the Sangha. Therefore, Bodhisattvas are born within Buddha-fields that are fully endowed with the Three Jewels.
Why is this? It is because he is endowed with the sublime vows cultivated in the past.
Furthermore, son of good family!
If a bodhisattva hears of any matter that is loathsome, there is none for which they do not give rise to a mind of revulsion. Why is this?

As soon as the bodhisattva hears of such matters, they immediately conceive a mind of weariness and aversion; having conceived this weariness and aversion, they arouse diligent vigor to cultivate all wholesome dharmas and sever all unwholesome dharmas.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to remain far removed from the eight unfavorable conditions.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the state of never losing the bodhicitta.
What are these ten?
First, to remain far removed from flattery and deception;
Second, being upright and without crookedness, pure and immaculate, one remains far removed from seeking, hesitation, and discrimination;
third, receiving and upholding the Buddha-dharma;
fourth, not being stingy or secretive regarding the Dharma.
Fifth, to remain far removed from stinginess regarding the Dharma;
sixth, to refrain from creating causes and conditions that obstruct the Dharma;
seventh, to have no false speech.
Eighth, having embraced the teachings of the Mahāyāna, one is able to practice according to what has been taught, and gives rise to a mind of reverence toward those who uphold the Mahāyāna;
ninth, toward those who uphold the Mahāyāna, one conceives the thought of intimacy for the sake of gradually entering the Mahāyāna;
tenth, because of having deeply entered the Mahāyāna, one conceives the thought of the teacher and the venerable one toward those who preach the Dharma.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the non-forgetfulness of the bodhicitta.
Furthermore, good son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). What are these ten?
First, making offerings to all Buddhas;
Second, upholding the true Dharma;
third, practicing and maintaining pure precepts;
fourth, eliminating doubt and departing from hindrances.
Fifth, they frequently give rise to joy;
sixth, they frequently engage in contemplative visualization;
seventh, they constantly abide in a concentrated mind.
Eighth, purity of the place of birth;
ninth, constant rebirth through transformation;
tenth, attainment of clear and sharp consciousness.

“Good son! Because a bodhisattva extensively makes offerings to the Buddhas, he is able to respect the True Dharma. Out of this reverence for the Dharma, he approaches those who uphold the Dharma; through those causes and conditions, he is able to receive, maintain, read, and recite the True Dharma. Having attained the Dharma, he expounds it widely for others. Consequently, he does not begrudge his own body or life as he diligently practices, cultivates, receives, and maintains the True Dharma, and is further able to practice and maintain the pure precepts.”
There are three kinds of precepts, namely those of body, speech, and mind.
Because the precepts of these three types of action are pure, one is able to eliminate doubt and depart from all obstructive defilements. Why is this so?
First, through the purity of ethical conduct (*śīla*), one is able to eliminate doubt and depart from hindrances;
because one is free from doubt and hindrances, great joy arises; because the mind is joyful, one frequently engages in contemplative visualization (*bhāvanā*);
through contemplative visualization, one dwells constantly in a concentrated mind (*samādhi*); and because the mind dwells in concentration, the place of rebirth becomes pure.
Because their dwelling is pure, they are always born through transformation; because they are born through transformation, they attain clear and sharp consciousness.

Because their consciousness is clear and sharp, they are able to know the matters of their past lives—namely, one birth, two births, three, four, five, or ten, twenty, up to hundreds of thousands and countless births—through the supernormal power of recollecting former existences (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives.
Furthermore, noble son!"
