If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will not be separated from spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). What are these ten?
First, not being separated from seeing, hearing, or recollecting the Buddha.
Second, not being separated from hearing the Dharma;
third, not being separated from making offerings to the Saṃgha;
fourth, not being separated from praising, prostrating, joining the palms in reverence, or performing full prostrations to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Fifth, not being separated from hearing and receiving the teachings from those who have heard much;
sixth, not being separated from hearing and receiving the teachings on the *pāramitās*;
seventh, not being separated from hearing and receiving the teachings on the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Eighth, not being apart from listening to and receiving the teachings on the three gates of liberation;
ninth, not being apart from listening to and receiving the teachings on the four Brahma-vihāras;
tenth, not being apart from listening to and receiving the teachings on omniscience.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will not be separated from spiritual friends.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to remain far removed from evil associates.
What are these ten?
First, by remaining far removed from those who violate the precepts, one is thus able to leave behind evil associates.
Second, one should distance oneself from those who have corrupted right view;
third, one should distance oneself from those who have corrupted proper conduct;
fourth, one should distance oneself from those who have corrupted right livelihood.
Fifth, to distance oneself from those who are addicted to sensual indulgence;
sixth, to distance oneself from those who are indolent;
seventh, to distance oneself from those who are submerged in the cycle of birth and death.
Eighth, they distance themselves from those who turn their backs on enlightenment;
ninth, they distance themselves from those who associate with laypeople;
tenth, because they distance themselves from all afflictions, they are able to avoid evil associates.
"Good son!

Although a bodhisattva remains entirely detached from such places as these, he does not give rise toward those people to thoughts of malice, thoughts of harm, or thoughts of contempt. Rather, the bodhisattva gives rise to this thought:

'As the Buddha has taught, all sentient beings are composed of various elements (dhātu) formed through conditions; because their dispositions, desires, and habitual tendencies are mutually defiled and proximate, they undergo destruction. Therefore, I shall now distance myself from these habitual tendencies.'"
“Good son! If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, he will be able to remain far removed from evil associates.
Furthermore, good son!”
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the Dharma-body of a Tathāgata.
What are these ten?
First, attaining the body of equanimity;
Second, attaining a pure body;
third, attaining an inexhaustible body;
fourth, attaining a body accumulated through merit.
Fifth, they attain the Dharma-body;
sixth, they attain a body that is incalculable and difficult to fathom;
seventh, they attain the inconceivable body.
Eighth, they attain a body of tranquility;
ninth, they attain a body equal to space;
tenth, they attain a body of wondrous wisdom.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will immediately attain the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
At what stage does a bodhisattva attain the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! A bodhisattva of the first stage attains the body of equality. Why is this?
Furthermore, this bodhisattva is able to leave behind all perilous and evil bodies and universally knows the dharmas of all bodhisattva stages:
a bodhisattva of the second stage attains a pure body because they are well-endowed with pure precepts;
a bodhisattva of the third stage attains an inexhaustible body because they have already abandoned all anger.
Bodhisattvas of the fourth stage attain a body of accumulated virtue, because they have accumulated all Buddha-dharmas;
Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage attain the Dharma-body, because they thoroughly understand all dharmas;
Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage attain an immeasurable and unfathomable body, because they have accumulated all immeasurable and profoundly deep dharmas.
Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage attain the inconceivable body because they have accumulated skillful means;
Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage attain the tranquil body because they are far removed from all conceptual proliferation and free from all afflictions;
Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage attain the body equal to space because they can manifest immeasurable and vast bodies.
“Because Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage attain the body of wondrous wisdom by having accumulated all knowable phenomena.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Is there any distinction between the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata and the Dharma-body of the Bodhisattva?
The Buddha said,
"Good son!..."
"Their bodies are not distinct, yet the characteristics of their merits each differ.
Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that the body has no distinct marks of special merit?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
The body is truly without difference. Why is this?
Because the body is formed by an accumulation [of parts] and thus shares a single characteristic; however, the characteristics of its qualities each differ.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As for the distinct characteristics of merit, what is their nature?”
The Buddha said: "Good son!
I shall now provide an analogy to clarify this meaning."
For example, as with a mani jewel, whether it has been polished or not, both are reckoned among the mani gems.
Yet that mani jewel which has been polished radiates brilliant light and is so pure and lovely that it cannot be compared to one that has not been polished.
The maṇi-jewel of a bodhisattva’s body and the maṇi-jewel of a Tathāgata’s body are likewise identical in their essential reality;
yet, when compared before the maṇi-jewel of a Tathāgata’s body, the characteristics of the pure radiance of the bodhisattva’s maṇi-jewel cannot be equaled.

Why is this? Because the mani-jewel of the Tathāgata’s body is vast and immeasurable, filling the realm of sentient beings and the realm of empty space, abiding there with its radiance brilliantly manifest and illuminating all.
Why is this? The *maṇi* jewel of the Tathāgata’s body has been polished and purified until it is free from all defilements; it cannot be compared to the *maṇi* jewels of the bodies of bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva still possesses residual defilements.
Furthermore, son of good family!

Just as the moon during the first two nights of the waxing phase and the full moon on the evening of the fifteenth day are far apart in their degree of brilliance and clarity, yet identical in essence—because phenomena possess gradual differences—the bodies of the Tathāgata and the bodies of Bodhisattvas are also like this; both are called "bodies."
However, the radiance of the Bodhisattva’s body, when compared before the Tathāgata, cannot be equaled; it is like the moon on its second day and on the fifteenth day.
Good son!
Therefore, you should know that although the body of the Tathāgata and the body of a bodhisattva are said to share the same characteristics, their merits are different.
"Furthermore, good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain an indestructible body like a vajra.
What are these ten?
First, not being destroyed by greed, hatred, or delusion;
Second, they are not destroyed by anger, affliction, fatigue, pride, or inverted views;
third, they are not destroyed by the eight worldly dharmas;
fourth, they are not destroyed by the sufferings of the evil realms.
Fifth, they are not destroyed by any suffering;
sixth, they are not destroyed by the sufferings of birth, old age, and death;
seventh, they are not destroyed by the heterodox arguments of any outsiders.
Eighth, they cannot be destroyed by the various māras and their retinues;
ninth, they cannot be destroyed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
tenth, they cannot be destroyed by any objects of desire.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain a vajra-like indestructible body.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they become a great guide. What are these ten?
First, gaining the trust and approval of others;
Second, being respected by others;
third, skillfully acting as a guide;
fourth, serving as a refuge for others.
Fifth, they are able to provide for their livelihood;
sixth, they are well-provided with provisions;
seventh, they are rich in wealth and treasures.
Eighth, they have no sense of satiety;
ninth, they act as pioneers;
tenth, they skillfully reach the city of omniscience.
"What is it to gain the trust and approval of others, even unto reaching the city of omniscience? Good son,

just as a maritime guide is trusted and approved by kings and their ministers, so too is the Bodhisattva, the great guide, trusted and approved by all Buddhas and the Śrāvaka disciples of the Buddhas."
"Furthermore, noble son!

Just as a maritime guide receives respectful offerings and veneration from all people, including Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, so too does the Bodhisattva, the Great Guide, receive respectful offerings and veneration from the entire assembly of those in training and those beyond training, as well as from other devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth."
"Furthermore, noble son!

Just as a maritime guide can provide direction within the vast wilderness and perilous difficulties, enabling others to reach safety without becoming weary, so too is the Bodhisattva Great Guide. Within the vast wilderness and perilous difficulties of saṃsāra, he provides guidance for all sentient beings, showing them the locations of the bandits of affliction, so that they may attain peace and security without becoming weary."
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Just as a sea captain serves as a refuge for those who are destitute, distressed, and suffering, enabling them to emerge from the vast wilderness and perilous paths, so too is the Bodhisattva a great guide; he can serve as a refuge for all followers of external paths, enabling them to emerge from the vast wilderness and the great, perilous evil paths of birth and death."
"Furthermore, noble son!

Just as a maritime guide can provide for the livelihood of kings, officials, and other people by supplying their necessities, so too is the Bodhisattva Great Guide; he provides for the livelihood of all sentient beings who are attached to birth and death by employing skillful means."
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a maritime leader who, whether traveling or staying in various regions, accompanies a multitude of merchants across wildernesses and perilous roads, intending to reach a city.
At that time, the guide, having well prepared his provisions, led the entire caravan out of the wilderness and its perilous paths, until they reached the city in safety and security.

The Bodhisattva, the Great Guide, is likewise: desiring to approach and draw near to the presence of the Buddha, wishing to gather and sustain a vast multitude of sentient beings as they traverse the perilous and evil paths of great birth-and-death, and wishing to cause all sentient beings to reach the great city of omniscience, the Bodhisattva thus thoroughly prepares the provisions for practice consisting of merit and wisdom.
"Furthermore, noble son!

Just as a maritime guide who wishes to halt at various regions rich in wealth, treasures, and the necessities of life—namely, jewels such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mani-gems, coral, and musaragalva—so too is the Bodhisattva Great Guide; because he wishes to halt at the great city of omniscience, he extensively gathers all the supreme practices of the Buddha-dharma."
"Furthermore, noble son!

Just as a maritime guide is never satisfied with acquiring even a small amount of wealth and treasures, so too is the Bodhisattva Great Guide never satisfied with accumulating the treasures of the sublime Dharma."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
It is like a maritime guide who serves as an excellent leader for a multitude of merchants. Why is this? "
Because he acts as a sovereign, because he excellently increases [virtue], because his deeds are supreme, and because he is able to gather others through endearing speech,
the Bodhisattva Great Guide is likewise able to act as a pioneer for all sentient beings.
Why is this? Because he has excellently increased his meritorious qualities; because his state is superior; because he is the supreme sovereign; and because he utters words of truth.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Just as a maritime guide reaches a city because he possesses power and capability, so too is the Bodhisattva, the great guide; possessing supreme power, he is able to reach the great city of omniscience."
"Noble son!
These are the ways by which a bodhisattva gains the confidence and trust of others, and even reaches the city of omniscience.
Noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they become a great guide.
Furthermore, son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will skillfully know the right path.
What are the ten?
First, skillfully knowing when the road is level;
second, skillfully knowing when the road is treacherous.
Third, they skillfully know that the road is secure and peaceful;
fourth, they know the excellence of the path;
fifth, they skillfully know whether the road is moist and lush or parched and dry.
Sixth, they are skilled in knowing the locations of the roads;
seventh, they are skilled in knowing the characteristics of the roads;
eighth, they are skilled in knowing whether the roads are straight or crooked.
Ninth, he is skilled in knowing the winding turns of the road;
tenth, he is skilled in knowing the essential exits of the road. Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will skillfully know the right path.
Furthermore, son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be well able to explain and demonstrate the non-perverted path.
What are these ten?
First, for those sentient beings who are to be delivered by means of the Mahāyāna, one should proclaim the teachings of the bodhisattva path and not the teachings of the śrāvaka path;
second, for those sentient beings who are to be delivered by means of the Śrāvakayāna, one should proclaim the teachings of the śrāvaka path and not the teachings of the bodhisattva path.

Third, for those sentient beings who are to be liberated by means of the path of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), one should preach the Dharma of omniscience and not the Dharma of the path of the pratyekabuddhas;
fourth, for those sentient beings who are to be liberated by means of the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, one should preach the Dharma of the pratyekabuddha path and not the path of omniscience;

fifth, for those classes of sentient beings who are attached to the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) and the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), one should, as appropriate, preach the Dharma of emptiness and selflessness, and not the Dharma of the paths of a self, a sentient being (*sattva*), a life-span (*jīva*), a nourisher (*poṣa*), or a person (*pudgala*).
Sixth, for sentient beings who rely on and cling to the two extremes, he teaches the Dharma that transcends the two extremes, rather than teaching the Dharma that clings to the two extremes;
seventh, for sentient beings who are distracted, he teaches the path of śamatha and vipaśyanā, rather than teaching the methods of distraction;

eighth, for sentient beings who are attached to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), he teaches the path of *tathatā*, rather than teaching the methods of conceptual proliferation to which foolish people are attached.
Ninth, for sentient beings who delight in and are attached to birth and death (*saṃsāra*), he teaches the Dharma of the path to *nirvāṇa*, and does not teach the Dharma of birth and death;
tenth, for sentient beings who abide in wrong paths, he teaches the Dharma that removes the thorns of those faults, and does not teach the Dharma of the thorns of affliction (*kleśa*).
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to explain and demonstrate the non-perverted path.
The *Buddhabhāṣita-Pratibhānapratibhāna-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Scroll Twelve, Spoken by the Buddha. Section on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin.
The Scripture on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Thirteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Da Fu, Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
The Great Master of Sanskrit Transmission, the Imperially Ennobled Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Dharmapāla, and others, respectfully translated [this] by imperial decree:
"Furthermore, son of good family, if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the state of abiding eternally in the sublime *samādhi*."
What are the ten?
First, skillfully practicing the application of mindfulness to the body;
second, skillfully practicing the application of mindfulness to feelings;
Third, skillful practice of the foundation of mindfulness of the mind;
fourth, skillful practice of the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena;
fifth, skillful practice of the foundation of mindfulness of objects.
Sixth, skillfully practicing the application of mindfulness regarding forest hermitages;
seventh, skillfully practicing the application of mindfulness regarding royal capitals, kingdoms, cities, and villages;
eighth, skillfully practicing the application of mindfulness regarding matters such as fame and gain.
Ninth, skillfully practicing the foundations of mindfulness as established by the Tathāgata’s gates of training;
tenth, skillfully severing the afflictions and secondary afflictions of defilement through the foundations of mindfulness.
"Good son! What is the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the application of mindfulness to the body?

It means that if a bodhisattva possesses within his body any unwholesome dharmas arising from the notion of 'mine,' he uses his superior wisdom to examine and discern them minutely, and thereby distances himself from them all."

Furthermore, one observes all the defects of the body, from the soles of the feet upward to the crown of the head, seeing it as bound together by sinews and veins. Surveying the entire body, one finds that it is entirely without self; it is a phenomenon subject to decay that cannot endure for even a moment. This body is impure, consisting of immature, foul-smelling, and loathsome things, a mere accumulation of various unwholesome forms and characteristics.

When the bodhisattva contemplates in this manner, if there is within the body any craving for desires, any conception of a self regarding the body, or any attachment to the body—all such phenomena are entirely unapprehendable.
For this reason, all unwholesome dharmas that coexist with the body do not attain mastery, whereas all other wholesome dharmas that coexist with the body do attain mastery.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the foundation of mindfulness of feelings?
It is when a bodhisattva reflects as follows:
"All sensations whatsoever are entirely suffering.
Why do foolish people, in the midst of this, perversely reckon them to be pleasure?

Those who are ignorant do not recognize suffering and pleasure; only the noble ones know them all to be suffering. Having personally and diligently practiced to sever the sensation of suffering, the Bodhisattva further teaches others to practice and train in the same manner as himself."

When the Bodhisattva practices this contemplation, he does not give rise to defiled attachment toward those sensations, nor does he arouse anger; having personally applied himself with diligence, he further causes others to train in the same way. This is called the skillful practice of the mindfulness of sensation.
"What is the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the application of mindfulness to the mind? It is when a bodhisattva reflects thus:

'The mind is truly impermanent, yet it is conceived and clung to as permanent; what is suffering is taken as pleasure; what is non-self is called self; and what is impure is called pure. This mind is restless and cannot rest for even a moment; like the light shifting of the wind, it serves as the primary root of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and also acts as the condition for the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), opening the gates to the evil realms and destroying the happy realms.'"

Furthermore, conditioned by this, greed, hatred, and delusion arise; it acts as the supreme sovereign over all phenomena. Among all phenomena, the mind is the precursor: if the mind has cognition, then all phenomena likewise possess that which is known.

The mind is like a painter who creates all manner of forms; the mind does not see the mind. The mind can accumulate wholesome and unwholesome karma; this mind revolves like a whirling firebrand. This mind turns with such speed as a galloping horse; the mind is like a wild fire burning with fierce flames; the mind is like a great body of water that nourishes and grows all things.

When the Bodhisattva contemplates in this way, although his mind does not yet attain mastery, those who are Bodhisattvas are naturally able to subdue it. If the mind is subdued, then all phenomena are likewise subdued; this is called the skillful practice of the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).
"What is the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*)?

It is when a bodhisattva understands unwholesome phenomena as they truly are—namely, greed, hatred, and delusion, along with their bases—as well as the unwholesome phenomena that serve as the antidotes to greed, and the unwholesome phenomena that serve as the antidotes to hatred and delusion."
When a bodhisattva has diligently severed unwholesome dharmas within these states, they are then able to fully understand all wholesome dharmas.

Regarding wholesome dharmas, they give rise to a mind of affection and joy, abide in the foundations of mindfulness, and seek the accomplishment of those dharmas. Having personally practiced them, they further teach others to train in this way; this is called the foundation of mindfulness of wholesome dharmas.
"What is the bodhisattva’s mindfulness of objects through skillful practice?

It means that when a bodhisattva encounters various objects—whether pleasing or unpleasing forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or tangibles—they do not give rise to greedy attachment nor arouse a mind of anger."
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"I should not now give rise to craving and attachment toward these phenomena that lack intrinsic nature or characteristics. To give rise to craving is to be a fool; it is to possess the nature of delusion, the nature of non-comprehension, and the nature of unwholesomeness."

As the Buddha has taught, if one gives rise to greed, one immediately engenders defiled attachment and the deluded grasping of conceptual constructs; unable to discriminate between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, for this reason one falls into the evil realms.
The Bodhisattva further reflects:

"I should not now give rise to a mind of anger toward these empty dharmas. One who gives rise to a mind of anger is unable to endure the emergence of hatred; such a person is reviled by all noble ones and is collectively shunned by fellow practitioners of the holy life."

When the Bodhisattva performs this contemplation, he is not destroyed by objects nor attached to what is attained. Having himself practiced it, he further teaches others to train in the same way; this is called the "application of mindfulness to the sphere of wholesome conduct."
"What is the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the foundation of mindfulness in the araṇya?
It is when a bodhisattva reflects thus:
'To cultivate the practice of non-contention and the practice of tranquility is precisely what is called dwelling in the araṇya.'"

There are devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others who possess the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, and they are able to know my mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).

Therefore, I should now distance myself from improper attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) and divergent thoughts; in all circumstances, I shall likewise constantly avoid improper attention, and within the teachings that accord with reality (*yoniśo-dharma*), I shall give rise to a mind of affection and joy, increasing and extensively practicing them.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the mindfulness foundation of forest hermitages (araṇya).
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the mindfulness foundation of royal capitals, kingdoms, cities, and villages?

That is to say, when a bodhisattva enters a royal capital, a country, a city, or a village, they should give rise to the conduct practiced by bodhisattvas; they should completely abandon all improper places and likewise completely abandon those places where one who has gone forth should not go.
What are the places that those who have left the household life should not frequent?

These are the residences of kings and officials, assemblies for gambling and games of chance, taverns and banquets, the dwellings of dancers, singers, and performers, and all other such places that are unsuitable for those who have left the household life; one should distance oneself from them and never go there.
This is called the mindfulness of royal capitals, kingdoms, cities, and villages practiced well by the bodhisattva.
What is the bodhisattva’s mindfulness of matters such as fame and gain practiced well?

This means that when a bodhisattva encounters matters such as fame and material gain, they accept them only in accordance with the intention that arises in their mind, solely for the purpose of acting as a field of merit for the donors.

However, regarding what he receives, he does not give rise to craving or attachment, nor does he harbor clinging or conceive the thought that it belongs to himself; he does not give rise to the notion of "mine. Whatever he obtains, he shares immediately with all sentient beings, providing sustenance and relief for those who suffer.
For this reason, one does not give rise to arrogance regarding matters such as fame and gain, nor does one conceive of pride, nor indulge in haughty excess.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"All things such as fame and gain, whether pertaining to oneself or others, arise only for a brief moment and do not endure; because they arise only momentarily, they are entirely unobtainable at all times and in all places."

What wise person, amidst these phenomena that are impermanent, transient, unstable, and lacking in security, would give rise to stained and attached love, or produce haughty pride, arrogance, and self-satisfaction?
This is called the application of mindfulness regarding the proper practice of fame, gain, and offerings.
What is the bodhisattva’s application of mindfulness regarding the gates of training established by the Tathāgata?
That is to say, if a bodhisattva reflects thus:
"All Tathāgatas of the past studied in this way; because they studied in this way, they attained perfect enlightenment and entered great parinirvāṇa.
All Tathāgatas of the future will study in this way; because they study in this way, they shall attain perfect enlightenment and enter great parinirvāṇa."
All Tathāgatas of the present world likewise train in this way; by training in this way, they manifest perfect enlightenment and enter great parinirvāṇa.
For this reason, one should give rise to a pure mind toward this gateway of training, and with reverence and diligent vigor, practice it.
This is called the station of mindfulness established by the Tathāgata as the gateway of training for skillful practice.
What is the bodhisattva’s station of mindfulness for the thorough severance of afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the defilements (*saṃkleśa*)?

This means that by means of right mindfulness, a bodhisattva is well able to thoroughly understand all afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and phenomena of defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
From what cause do they arise? By what condition are they produced?

The Bodhisattva fully understands how these arise through such causes and how they are produced through such conditions; because of this thorough understanding, he completely distances himself from them. This is called the "application of mindfulness that thoroughly severs the afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the defilements (*saṃkleśa*)."
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will always abide in the state of sublime meditative equipoise (samāhita-citta).
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will always wear rag-robes.
What are these ten?
First, firm and resolute vows;
Second, to humble one's mind;
third, to give rise to no weariness;
fourth, to be free from all attachments.
Fifth, not observing faults;
sixth, observing only virtues;
seventh, not praising oneself.
Eighth, not slandering others;
ninth, being fully endowed with ethical conduct;
tenth, associating with noble and holy ones.
“Good son! What is meant by a bodhisattva’s firm resolve, up to their being closely attended by noble sages?

It means that if a bodhisattva possesses pure faith and a fully cultivated intention, they are trusted and approved by all Tathāgatas; even if they encounter circumstances that threaten their very life, they do not break or destroy the vows they have made, and they are able to remain unswerving from those vows.”
Because they are able to make those vows firm, they are able to humble their minds and give rise to no conceit.
Because their minds are humble, they are able to take up all discarded refuse that others despise.
Having taken them up, he washes, cleanses, dyes, and sews them, without giving rise to aversion or weariness.

Because he is not weary, he remains free from all attachments regarding whatever he has done; thus, through the progressive cultivation of superior practice, he succeeds, and is able to perceive no faults in these rag-robes.

Although it is said that these robes are tattered, worn out, and infested with many fleas and lice, and that they produce filth and stains upon the body, the bodhisattva never dwells upon such faults.
Why is it that one contemplates only the merits of this robe?

It is because these rag-robes were worn by the sages (*ṛṣi*), and even the noble ones who have abandoned desire fully conform to them; for they accord with the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), and the Buddha praised them as auspicious and extolled them.
For this reason, one does not praise oneself nor disparage others; by being free from self-praise and the disparagement of others, one attains the perfection of ethical conduct.

Because they are fully endowed with pure precepts, they are approached by all noble ones and praised by all Buddhas; they are protected by all Bodhisattvas and assisted by humans and non-humans alike; Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and all people come to pay them homage, and their fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life all offer them their acclaim.
“Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they shall always wear robes made of discarded rags.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since bodhisattvas possess a vast and great mind, for what reason do they engage in such coarse and inferior practices?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! It is for the sake of protecting the world and acting in accordance with it that the bodhisattva performs these deeds. Good son!”

Among Bodhisattvas, there are those who possess great power and those who do not; for the sake of those who lack such great power, they practice these deeds so as to give rise to remedies against afflictions that have not yet arisen.
"Furthermore, good son!
What do you think?
Do you consider the practice and realization of the Tathāgata to be vast?"
"Is it shallow and inferior?
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
I lack such eloquence as to be able to respond; why is this?

For there is no one who can fathom the conduct and realization of the Tathāgata. Since the Tathāgata has no dharma to be realized and no dharma to be seen, the Tathāgata possesses not even the slightest dharma that could constitute conduct or realization.
The Buddha said:
"Good son, what do you think?"

For what reason do you think the Tathāgata manifests such coarse and inferior conduct among the humans and non-humans of the four great continents, as well as among the assembly of others with inferior inclinations—such as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas—and praises the merits of dhūta practices before them?
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

It is because the Tathāgata desires to transform and deliver all sentient beings, and to cause those bodhisattvas who have newly entered the Great Vehicle to give rise to remedies against afflictions that have not yet arisen, that he performs these deeds.”
The Buddha said:
"Good son! So it is, so it is."

When Bodhisattvas of great power don the robes of refuse-rags (pāṃśukūla) out of a desire to accomplish the transformation and deliverance of sentient beings, this is likewise not an inferior or coarse practice.
For these reasons, the bodhisattva always wears robes made of discarded rags.
Furthermore, son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, he accepts only the three robes.
What are the ten?
First, contentment;
second, fewness of desires.
Third, being free from longing;
fourth, being free from accumulation;
fifth, because one is free from accumulation, there is nothing to be lost or destroyed.
Sixth, because there is no destruction or loss, one is free from all suffering and affliction;
seventh, one is free from that which is disagreeable;
eighth, one is far removed from sorrow and lamentation.
Ninth, there is nothing to be grasped;
tenth, through diligent cultivation, one attains the exhaustion of outflows. "Good son!
What is the Bodhisattva’s contentment, through which, by even diligent cultivation, one attains the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*)? It is this:

if a Bodhisattva gives rise to contentment with whatever robes he obtains, through that contentment he is able to have few desires; because of having few desires, he has no longing and remains free from accumulation; because there is no accumulation, there is no loss or ruin;
because there is no loss or ruin, he is free from the suffering and affliction born of loss or ruin.
Because one is free from suffering and affliction, there is no lack of mental gladness; because one is free from lack of gladness, there is no sorrow or lamentation;

because there is no sorrow or lamentation, there is no further grasping; because there is no grasping, one diligently practices and cultivates, thereby attaining the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they shall accept only the three robes.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they do not follow the conduct of others.
What are these ten?
First, they do not follow the conduct of greed;...
Second, not following the course of hatred;
third, not following the course of delusion;
fourth, not following the course of malice and harm.
Fifth, not following the practice of stinginess and envy;
sixth, not following the practice of prideful arrogance;
seventh, not following the practice of seeking fame and reputation through associating with others.
Eighth, not acting in accordance with the pursuit of gain and offerings;
ninth, not acting in accordance with honoring the celestial Māras;
tenth, not acting in accordance with arrogance and defiled attachment.
This is called not following others.
Son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, he does not follow others.
"Furthermore, noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will always practice alms-gathering (*piṇḍapāta*). What are these ten?
First, one practices begging for alms out of a desire to gather and sustain sentient beings;
second, one practices begging for alms in sequential order;
third, one practices begging for alms without giving rise to weariness.
Fourth, one goes for alms with contentment;
fifth, one goes for alms with the desire to distribute [the food];
sixth, one goes for alms without being attached.
Seventh, one goes on almsround because of knowing the proper measure;
eighth, one goes on almsround for the sake of bringing wholesome qualities into manifestation;
ninth, one goes on almsround for the sake of bringing all roots of goodness to full completion.
Tenth, they practice alms-gathering because they are free from the notion of a self. "Good son!
How does a bodhisattva gather in sentient beings, up to and including practicing alms-gathering because they are free from the notion of a self?

That is to say, when a bodhisattva sees sentient beings undergoing suffering and affliction whose roots of goodness are meager, he goes on almsround for the sake of gathering them in and causing them to become fully endowed with all roots of goodness.

When a bodhisattva enters a city, town, or village to wander for alms, they should abide in right mindfulness with their body upright; their comings and goings should be dignified and their deportment exemplary, with the sense faculties stilled, looking about in accordance with the Dharma, and binding their thoughts to wholesome dharmas.

"In his practice of begging for alms, he follows a regular sequence; he never bypasses the dwellings of the poor to beg from the wealthy. That is to say, he goes from one house to the next—among the dwellings of brahmins, kṣatriyas, elders, householders, and great clans—in successive order. He knows moderation and contentment regarding the food and drink obtained, avoiding only certain specific places and never going to them."

Regarding "other places": these include the homes of those who keep vicious dogs, houses where there are newborn calves, places where one has violated the pure precepts and fallen among the animal realm, locations where those capable of causing disturbance reside, and places shunned by men, women, boys, and girls alike; all such locations are to be completely avoided.

"By means of begging for alms in successive order, one does not give rise to weariness nor incur reproach; toward those sentient beings, one does not give rise to attachment or aversion, nor does one feel revulsion."

Having received the food obtained, he accepts it with contentment as appropriate; having accepted it, he returns to his dwelling, the monastic quarters, where he puts away his robes and bowl, washes his hands and feet, and before an image or a stūpa of the Tathāgata, performs offerings with reverence and respect. Then, entering his own cell, he divides the alms-food into four portions: one portion he gives to his fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*);
one portion he gives as a gift to sentient beings who are poor and suffering; one portion he shall give to those fallen into the miserable realms; and one portion he eats himself.

Although the bodhisattva accepts that food, he does not give rise to stained attachment, nor does he become arrogant or negligent, nor does he grasp at it; he accepts the food solely for the purpose of sustaining the body, ensuring that the body is neither excessively emaciated nor overly heavy.
Why is this? If one is excessively emaciated, it hinders the cultivation of wholesome dharmas; if one is excessively heavy, it increases sleepiness.

Because a bodhisattva desires to bring the category of wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*) into manifestation, having partaken of food accordingly, they arouse diligence and abandon all indolence. Gradually, they shall cultivate and advance the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) until they attain perfection. Because they attain perfection in the cultivation and advancement of the factors of enlightenment, they do not give rise to the grasping of a self (*ātman*). Being without the grasping of a self, they are even able to give their own flesh and body to sentient beings.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they shall constantly practice begging for food.
Thus ends the thirteenth fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll 14.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Da Fu, Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Imperial Preceptor for Transmitting the Sanskrit, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Fahu, and others, by imperial decree:
"Furthermore, son of good family, if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, he attains the dharma of a single sitting."
What are the ten?
First, while sitting alone at the site of enlightenment, all demons are struck with terror yet he remains forever unmoved;
second, having realized supramundane concentration, he remains forever unmoved.
Third, possessing supramundane wisdom while remaining forever immovable;
fourth, attaining supramundane knowledge while remaining forever immovable;
fifth, realizing emptiness while remaining forever immovable.
Sixth, they realize all phenomena as they truly are and remain forever immovable;
seventh, they attain the dharmas of the noble path and remain forever immovable;
eighth, they abide in the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and remain forever immovable.
Ninth, they realize the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) and remain forever unmoving;
tenth, they perfect the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) and remain forever unmoving. Good son!

This single sitting is called the seat of omniscience, and it is also named the Dharma-seat; therefore, once a Bodhisattva ascends this seat, they never move again—this is precisely what is meant by the "Dharma of a single sitting."
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they attain the practice of 'sitting once.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they shall always practice eating a single meal a day.
What are these ten?
First, not giving rise to greed or indulgence;

Second, not giving rise to defiled attachment: that is to say, once one has received a single meal, one should no longer accept any other food for sustaining the body—whether at the proper time or otherwise—that ought not to be accepted; this includes ghee, oil, rock honey, roots, stalks, flowers, fruits, and all manner of delicious flavors, none of which one accepts.
Third, if one sees others receiving ghee, oil, and other such delicacies, one does not give rise to thoughts of malice or harm.
Fourth, one does not give rise to a mind of jealousy.
Fifth, if a bodhisattva is afflicted by a severe illness at an improper time, he should accept whatever food is necessary for the sake of treatment;
sixth, if a bodhisattva’s life is in danger, he should accept whatever food is necessary;
seventh, if there are obstacles to wholesome dharmas, he should accept whatever food is necessary.
Eighth, after having accepted them, the bodhisattva does not regret it;
ninth, after having accepted them, the bodhisattva does not doubt them;
tenth, at the time of accepting them, the bodhisattva should regard them as medicine.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they shall always observe the practice of eating only one meal a day.
Furthermore, good son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will dwell well in an araṇya hermitage. What are these ten?
First, having long cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya).
Second, being well-versed in the codes of discipline;
third, having all faculties complete;
fourth, possessing extensive learning.
Fifth, possessing great power and capability;
sixth, being free from the grasping of self;
seventh, being like a wild animal;
Eighth, the body attains dwelling in seclusion;
ninth, tranquility manifests before one;
tenth, there is neither aversion nor attachment.
“Good son! What is meant by a bodhisattva who has long cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*), yet remains free from weariness or aversion, as well as free from attachment?

It means that when a bodhisattva, within the supreme Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha, leaves home for homelessness with the three spheres purified (*trimaṇḍalapariśuddha*), is fully endowed with ethical conduct (*śīla*), possesses skill in its essential nature, and has a profound understanding of the rules of discipline (*vinaya*) and the protocols for movement and conduct; and regarding all the teachings of the Buddha—whether superior, middling, or inferior—that they have studied, they achieve excellent self-comprehension without relying on external conditions, namely the meaning of the teachings and the methods of transcendence.”
Furthermore, he knows all transgressions and the methods for their deliverance; he fully understands which matters should be avoided and which matters should be honored.
Furthermore, regarding those offenses that are subject to censure or reproach, he extensively performs repentance and does not conceal them.

Moreover, he knows which matters constitute offenses and which do not, and he is fully capable of discerning whether they are light or heavy, and whether they are superior, middling, or inferior offenses.

Furthermore, because he knows and understands with perfect accuracy how the causes of karma created in the world bring about their respective ripened fruits (*vipākaphala*), the bodhisattva’s faculties are not deficient and his physical form is complete. Because his body is complete, he is able to dwell in forest hermitages (*āraṇya*).

Because one dwells in reliance upon it, this place is tranquil and free from all disturbances; it is neither too near nor too far, so that alms-food is easily obtained. There is sweet, pure water to be taken without toil, making the place delightful. The groves are verdant and the flowers and fruits are lush and abundant; it is free from insects and beasts, with secure caves and crags. Though high, it is level; it is blissful and harmonious, utterly silent and without companion.

"Once the bodhisattva has taken up residence in such a tranquil aranya and established himself therein, he recites day and night throughout the six periods without interruption the various scriptures he has studied and previously heard. His intonation is harmonious, neither too high nor too low; his deportment is serene and his mind does not wander toward external objects. Thus, all things are purified, the various sensory realms are stilled, and as he contemplates the meaning of the teachings, he remains free from drowsiness."
"When he dwells in that forest hermitage, there may come to the Bodhisattva's presence kings and their ministers, as well as other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and all manner of people."
Immediately, one should rise with reverence to meet him, saying:
"Welcome, Great King!
Please be seated."
He then prepared a seat according to the king's requirements.
If the king sat, he would sit; if the king did not sit, he would remain standing as was appropriate.
Furthermore, he observed the king, and if he saw that the king’s faculties were agitated or disturbed, he would immediately offer words of praise:
"How wonderful, Great King!

You have gained excellent benefit in governing this great realm. Within your borders dwell many who uphold the precepts and possess great virtue, as well as many learned śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who reside together in harmony; furthermore, there is no disturbance from thieves, royal officials, or similar troubles."

Furthermore, observing that the king’s faculties were well-pacified and his deportment composed, such that he was capable of receiving the teachings, [the teacher] immediately expounded various dharmas for him.
When the king no longer took pleasure in those various dharmas, [the teacher] then taught him the dharmas conducive to revulsion and renunciation.

Furthermore, when they take no pleasure in the teachings on disenchantment and renunciation, one should then preach to them the Tathāgata’s vast, majestic, and sublime Dharma; or for any other Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, or members of the general public who may come, one should speak to each according to what is appropriate for them in that same way.

Because the bodhisattva possesses extensive learning by virtue of this, they have great power and are able to skillfully expound the Dharma, causing those who hear it to give rise to great joy and to develop a pure heart of affection and delight.

"Because the Bodhisattva possesses such power, he is able to initiate the remedies for the afflictions of all sentient beings, thereby attaining great learning and vast power. Consequently, he is able to abandon the grasping at a self; because he has abandoned the grasping at a self, he dwells in an araṇya, free and fearless, without giving rise to alarm or terror. Thus, in that place, he manifests tranquility before him, remaining free from clamor like a wild beast."
However, these bodhisattvas are not like wild beasts, who are constantly filled with fear and possess faults. Why is this?
Because wild beasts keep their distance from humans and human dwellings, fleeing far away to protect their own lives.

“A bodhisattva dwells far removed from places of clamor and bustle solely to remain unmixed with all worldly beings—whether men, women, boys, or girls—and because they consider such clamorous matters to be causes of distraction that would create obstacles and difficulties for their mind of aspirational resolve.”
For this reason, having cultivated the practice of cessation and attained manifest tranquility, one is able, by virtue of that tranquility, to perceive the superior merits of dwelling in an araṇya.
Because one dwells in tranquility through seeing these merits, there is neither revulsion nor attachment.

Thus, one is able to accomplish the dharma of being without revulsion and without attachment; this constitutes a bodhisattva’s long cultivation of the holy life, culminating in being without revulsion and without attachment.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain firm abiding in the araṇya.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they shall always sit beneath a tree. What are these ten?
First, one must not sit beneath a tree that is too close to a village settlement.
Second, one must not sit beneath a tree that is too far from a village;
third, one must not sit beneath a tree in a thicket of thorns;
fourth, one must not sit beneath a tree entwined with creeping vines.
Fifth, one should not sit under a tree with withered leaves;
sixth, one should not sit under a tree where there are monkeys;
seventh, one should not sit under a tree where there are birds.
Eighth, one should not sit under a tree where vicious dogs dwell;
ninth, one should not sit under a tree near a road;
tenth, one should not sit under a tree where wicked people dwell.
Why is this? If a bodhisattva can leave such places and sit beneath a tree, their body will attain lightness and their mind will give rise to serenity and joy. Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they shall always sit beneath trees.
Furthermore, son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they shall always sit in the open air.
What are the ten?
First, not to sit against walls during spring, summer, autumn, or winter;
second, not to sit beneath forest trees;
Third, one should not sit upon a heap of straw;
fourth, one should not sit in the hollows between mountain slopes;
fifth, one should not sit on the banks of a river or beside a ditch.
Sixth, not providing means for warding off the cold;
seventh, not providing means for blocking the wind;
eighth, not providing means for repelling the rain.
Ninth, one does not set out implements for warding off heat;
tenth, one does not set out implements for receiving dew. "Good son!
Although a bodhisattva usually sits in the open air, if at times they are afflicted by a serious illness and their limbs and body have become weak, they should reside within that monastic dwelling.
At that time, the Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"As the Buddha has taught, the merits of *dhūta* (ascetic practices) are praised by the Buddha in order to counteract the arising of afflictions and to bring about detachment from grasping.

I am likewise; although I dwell in a monastery, it is solely for the purpose of severing afflictions and abandoning attachment, and furthermore, for the sake of receiving the offerings of donors. Thus, even while dwelling in a monastery, I shall constantly maintain the perception of being in the open air."
“Good son! If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they shall always sit in the open air.
Furthermore, good son!”
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to dwell in cemeteries. What are these ten?
First, wherever a bodhisattva finds a favorable place to stay, they give rise to a sense of weary detachment toward it.
Second, constantly giving rise to the perception of death at all times;
third, constantly giving rise to the perception of what remains;
fourth, the perception of observing everything as crimson in color.
Fifth, the perception of universal observation of the livid corpse;
sixth, the perception of universal observation of the festering corpse;
seventh, the perception of universal observation of the bloated corpse.
Eighth, the contemplation on the withered and parched;
ninth, the contemplation on the disintegrating;
tenth, the constant contemplation on the skeleton.

“Good son! Those who dwell in cemeteries—namely, the bodhisattvas—constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of vast benefit, and a mind of compassion for all sentient beings; they maintain pure ethical conduct and perfect cultivation, and thus do not eat meat.”

Why is this? Because there are many non-human spirits and ghosts dwelling all around the cemeteries; when they see a Bodhisattva eating meat, they do not give rise to a pure or affectionate mind, but instead produce affliction and distress.
"Furthermore, noble son!

When a *śmāśānika* bodhisattva enters a monastic dwelling (*saṃghārāma*), he should first go before a stūpa of the Tathāgata to pay respectful homage; next, he should pay his respects to the senior venerable ones; thereafter, he should inquire after the health of the junior bhikṣus; and he must not sit upon the beds, mats, or seats belonging to the community of monks."
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva acts to protect the characteristics of the world.
Furthermore, by dwelling among burial mounds, the bodhisattva accords with the noble ones and opposes the various foolish worldly people.
If there is a bhikṣu who dwells alone, he should bring his own seat and offer it to that bodhisattva in the cemetery, inviting him to take the seat.

At that time, the bodhisattva should firmly decline and not sit; however, if he further examines the bhikṣu’s intention and finds no subsequent regret, and even observes that the rest of the bhikṣu saṃgha will not harbor slander, then he may sit upon it.
At that time, one should likewise humble one’s mind, being no different from a *caṇḍāla* youth.
Son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to dwell in cemeteries.
"Furthermore, noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to practice constant sitting (*prahāṇa*). What are these ten?
First, one sits constantly not for the sake of afflicting the body;
second, one sits constantly not for the sake of afflicting the mind;
third, one sits constantly not for the sake of abandoning sleep.
Fourth, one sits constantly not out of bodily fatigue;
fifth, the bodhisattva sits constantly because he desires to fulfill the practices for awakening;
sixth, one sits constantly in order to abide in one-pointedness of mind.
Seventh, one sits constantly in order to bring the noble path into manifestation;
eighth, one sits constantly in order to ascend to the site of enlightenment;
ninth, one sits constantly for the benefit of all sentient beings.
Tenth, one sits constantly for the sake of severing all afflictions.
Son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, he is able to sit constantly.
"Furthermore, noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, he will arrange seats according to what is appropriate.
What are these ten?
First, not being attached to beds or seats;
second, not personally arranging beds or seats;
third, not causing others to arrange beds or seats.
Fourth, one should arrange seats and couches so as not to create a fixed appearance;
fifth, in other locations, one should sit wherever one happens to find grass or leaves;
sixth, regarding various places where there are holes and burrows inhabited by venomous insects, mosquitoes, gadflies, and the like, one should avoid them from afar and must not arrange a seat there.

Seventh, when the bodhisattva lies down to sleep, he rests on his right side with one foot upon the other, covers his body with a robe, and remains with right mindfulness and right awareness, maintaining a clear perception and a focused intention to rise;
eighth, he does not become attached to the pleasurable taste of sleep;
ninth, when fatigued from lying on his right side, he does not turn over to his left to seek further pleasure in sleep, but does so only for the purpose of nourishing the great elements.
Tenth, by constantly recollecting all dharmas of the wholesome categories, they become manifest before them. Noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, he may then arrange his seat as appropriate.
"Furthermore, noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will accomplish the practice of yoga. What are these ten?
First, frequently practicing the contemplation of impurity;
second, frequently practicing the contemplation of loving-kindness;
third, frequently practicing the contemplation of dependent origination.
Fourth, they are well able to eliminate and sever all faults and afflictions;
fifth, they frequently cultivate the contemplation of emptiness;
sixth, they frequently cultivate the practice of the contemplation of signlessness.
Seventh, they extensively cultivate yogic contemplative practices;
eighth, they are always able to apply themselves with diligent cultivation;
ninth, their minds do not waver or regret.
Tenth, the perfection of ethical conduct.
"Good son, how does a bodhisattva cultivate the practice of the contemplation of impurity?"

That is to say, when a bodhisattva dwells alone in a secluded place, remaining physically tranquil and composed with a clear and attentive mind, sitting cross-legged and abiding in right mindfulness without directing the mind toward external objects, he reflects thus:

"Whatever food and drink exists among humans—whether of pure flavor or supreme flavor, endowed with exquisite fragrance or coarse and unrefined—the moment these foods and drinks are touched by the body-fire, they all become impure, foul-smelling, and loathsome."
The foolish people of the world hold views that are contrary [to reality] and become intoxicated by, stained with, and attached to their flavors;

we, however, as noble ones who rely on the True Dharma and Vinaya, ought to investigate these things as they truly are with right wisdom, and should not give rise to attachment or craving for such bodies.
For this reason, one should always give rise to a mind of weary detachment; this is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the contemplation of impurity.
What is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the contemplation of loving-kindness?

That is to say, when a bodhisattva dwells alone in a secluded place, straightening the body and maintaining a composed and deliberate posture, he sits cross-legged with a clear and alert mind, abiding in right mindfulness so that the mind does not wander toward external objects, and reflects thus:
"If sentient beings, having frequently given rise to anger and malice, commit unwholesome deeds and unjustly harbor resentment and harm toward me."

Whether in the past, the future, or the present—among all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time—I shall cause every instance of malice and harm they direct toward me to be utterly extinguished, and I shall cause them all to sit at the site of enlightenment.

"This is the profound intention of a bodhisattva that is constantly contemplated; it is not merely a matter of verbal expression, for all things are exactly as they truly are. This is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of the contemplation of a compassionate mind."
"What is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the contemplation of dependent origination?
It is when a bodhisattva, regarding those states already arisen—namely, greed, hatred, and harmful intent—reflects thus:

'If any phenomenon that arises does so from conditions, then these very conditioning phenomena also arise from conditions. Since the conditions that produce them belong to the category of conditioned phenomena, how could a wise person conceive of a notion of "self" within these empty phenomena that arise dependently? "
This is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the contemplation of dependent origination.
From the *Buddhabhāṣita-sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, scroll fourteen [or scroll ten].
Furthermore, son of good family, the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial,
Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, and Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Fahu, and others, translated [this] by imperial decree: "Furthermore, son of good family!"
How does a bodhisattva skillfully eliminate all faults and afflictions?

It means that if a bodhisattva diligently practices the elimination of all faults and afflictions within his own person, and instructs others to sever and extinguish all faults and afflictions within their persons—while abandoning those who are incapable of doing so.

What are these faults? They are as follows: failing to give rise to respect for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; and likewise failing to give rise to respect toward the training in ethical discipline, the noble ones, and fellow practitioners of the holy life—whether they be of superior, middling, or inferior status. In such matters, one gives rise to self-conceit (*māna*) and treats others with contempt; one accords with objects of attachment and turns one's back on *nirvāṇa*; one gives rise to the view of a self (*ātman*), as well as views of a sentient being (*sattva*), a living soul (*jīva*), a person (*pudgala*), a nourisher (*poṣa*), and an individual (*puruṣa*); and one clings to the views of nihilism or eternalism, and to the views of permanence or impermanence.

They take no pleasure in associating with the noble ones but instead attach themselves to foolish people; they distance themselves from those who are pure and uphold the precepts, yet honor and make offerings to those who violate them; they follow after evil friends while abandoning virtuous friends, and they slander the profound sūtras of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, they give rise to fear and dread toward the profound sūtras; they are indolent, lazy, and neglectful, holding themselves in contempt; their disposition is base and inferior, lacking majesty and splendor, and they possess no eloquence. They commit evil in inappropriate places and harbor doubts regarding matters that should not be doubted, while failing to doubt where they ought to do so. They are shrouded by hindrances and fetters, pursued by flattery and deception, and obscured by dullness and torpor.

“Delighting in and clinging to gain and offerings, craving their own lineage, kin, and homeland, they give rise to various views of attachment and crave assemblies. Furthermore, they constantly study and rely upon the scriptures of non-Buddhists; they feel aversion toward the True Dharma and destroy their vows.”

They habitually practice unwholesome dharmas and do not habitually practice wholesome dharmas; they associate intimately with those who are not renunciants, and furthermore, they associate intimately with men, women, boys, girls, and various non-Buddhists.

They take no delight in forest hermitages, do not know moderation in eating, do not attend upon their teachers, elders, or seniors, and are likewise ignorant of the proper time for study and recitation.

Furthermore, they do not know the direction or place in which they should proceed; they do not respect even the subtle training in the precepts; they perceive no fear in minor transgressions; they consider those of a deluded and dark disposition to be tranquil; and toward those of superior faculties and great benefit, they act with arrogance, giving rise to various false attachments and constantly uttering evil words.

They follow along with and cling to all pleasant and unpleasant forms; seeing those who are angry, they do not give rise to a mind of loving-kindness; seeing those who are suffering, they do not produce compassion; seeing those who are ill, they do not feel revulsion; and seeing those who are dying, they harbor no fear.
Within this burning house, they do not seek liberation; they are unable to carefully examine their own bodies, nor do they observe their moral conduct.
They do not consider what has already been done, nor what ought to be done.
What is meant by "manifest activity"?
It refers to being entirely unable to examine or investigate with precision;

to engage in reflection where there should be no reflection, to engage in deliberation where there should be no deliberation, and to engage in pursuit where there should be no pursuit; to conceive the notion of renunciation where there is no renunciation, to conceive the notion of the true path where there is no path, and to conceive the notion that one has attained what has not been attained.

They focus their minds exclusively on worldly activities and do not apply diligent effort toward what should be done; they constantly distance themselves from vast wholesome dharmas, slander the Mahāyāna teachings, praise the Śrāvaka vehicle, revile those who have deep faith in the Mahāyāna, and extol practitioners of the Śrāvaka path; they are constantly engaged in verbal disputes with others, frequently inciting strife, and using harsh and coarse speech.

By nature they are haughty and arrogant, relying on their own subjective opinions; they are cruel, poisonous, and violent, giving rein to their greed. Their speech lacks sincerity and truth, as they disparage others; they speak what should not be said, their words being full of falsehoods, and they delight in and cling to all manner of worldly conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
These are the various faults and afflictions.

Once the bodhisattva has thoroughly severed such faults and afflictions, he abandons all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and diligently cultivates the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
Although the bodhisattva extensively cultivates the contemplation of emptiness, his mind may still scatter toward various objects and find pleasure in dwelling upon them.
The Bodhisattva immediately seeks the intrinsic nature within all objective spheres and finds that they are entirely empty and ultimately unobtainable.

Because the objects are empty, he observes that the mind is likewise entirely empty; because both mind and object are empty, the wisdom capable of observation is also empty and ultimately unobtainable.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva diligently practices the contemplation that all marks are empty. Although the bodhisattva contemplates the signless (*animitta*), various marks still appear before him as obstacles; therefore, he contemplates that there are no internal marks. Because there are no internal marks, the body cannot be apprehended, and the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) likewise cannot be apprehended. He does not bind his mind to the body, nor can any external marks be apprehended, nor can the application of mindfulness to external marks be apprehended. Since the mind is not attached and external marks are absent, the marks of the body are also absent.

"Once internal signs have been brought to cessation, one diligently applies oneself with the intention of cultivation; through the frequent practice of various contemplative exercises, one is able to constantly and diligently cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā, without interruption in the practice being cultivated."
That which is called one-pointedness of mind is *śamatha*; the thorough investigation of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena as they truly are is *vipaśyanā*.
Because one abides in *śamatha* through one-pointedness of mind, one experiences joy and freedom from regret within the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*).
Why is this? If one’s precepts are pure and one’s precepts are complete, this is precisely the bodhisattva’s practice of yoga.
Because the precepts are complete, yoga increases; because the precepts are complete, one cultivates yoga. This is what is called practicing the yoga-way.
“Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will skillfully cultivate the practice of yoga.
Furthermore, good son!”
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to uphold the sūtra teachings of the Tathāgata.
What are these ten?
First, they listen to and receive and uphold [the teachings] for the sake of protecting the true Dharma, not for the sake of material wealth.
Second, they listen to and uphold [the teachings] for the sake of guarding the doctrine, not for the sake of gain and offerings;
third, they listen to and uphold them so that the lineage of the Three Jewels may remain unbroken, not for the sake of seeking the respect of others;
fourth, they listen to and uphold them out of a desire to gather in and sustain those sentient beings who abide in the Mahāyāna, not for the sake of fame.
Fifth, one listens to and upholds [the teaching] for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings who are without support or refuge;
sixth, one listens to and upholds it for the sake of enabling suffering sentient beings to attain peace and happiness;
seventh, one listens to and upholds it for the sake of enabling those without the eye of wisdom to obtain the eye of wisdom.
Eighth, they listen to and uphold [the teachings] in order to explain and demonstrate the path of the śrāvakas to those who abide in the Śrāvaka Vehicle;
ninth, they listen to and uphold [the teachings] in order to explain and demonstrate the Mahāyāna Dharma to those who abide in the Mahāyāna;
tenth, they listen to and uphold [the teachings] for the sake of personally realizing unsurpassed wisdom, and not for the sake of seeking the inferior vehicles.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to uphold the sūtra teachings of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to uphold the teachings of the Vinaya.
What are these ten?
First, being well-versed in the Vinaya;
Second, being well-versed in the protocols and models of the Vinaya;
third, being well-versed in the profound meaning of the Vinaya;
fourth, being well-versed in the subtle characteristics of the Vinaya.
Fifth, being skilled in knowing what should and should not be done;
sixth, being skilled in knowing natural transgressions;
seventh, being skilled in knowing proscribed transgressions.
Eighth, they skillfully know the causes and conditions for the origin of the Prātimokṣa;
ninth, they skillfully know the Vinaya rules of the Śrāvakas;
tenth, they skillfully know the Vinaya rules of the Bodhisattvas.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will properly uphold the teachings of the Vinaya.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be well-versed in rules, their sphere of activity, and will be fully endowed with dignified deportment.
What are these ten?
First, they skillfully study the training precepts (śikṣāpada) of the śrāvakas.
Second, being well-trained in the training rules of the pratyekabuddhas;
third, being well-trained in the training rules of the bodhisattvas;
fourth, fully cultivating and perfecting all those training rules.
Fifth, having attained perfection in the rules of conduct, he is able to remain far removed from non-śramaṇa behavior;
sixth, for this reason, the bodhisattva does not engage in conduct at improper places, in improper directions, or at improper times;
seventh, having attained perfection in the conduct of the śramaṇa rules, he is not unjustly reviled by other śramaṇas or brahmins.
Eighth, causing others to likewise train in this way;
ninth, because the rules of conduct are fully perfected, one’s appearance is dignified and majestic, and one’s deportment is tranquil;
tenth, being endowed with such decorum, one is free from artifice or pretension.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be well-versed in rules and regulations, their sphere of activity, and will be fully endowed with dignified deportment.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to remain free from stinginess and envy. What are these ten?
First, acting as a donor oneself;
Second, teaching others to practice giving;
third, praising the act of giving;
fourth, feeling sympathetic joy when seeing others give.
Fifth, it causes other donors to feel joy, satisfaction, benefit, and delight;
sixth, when seeing someone else being given a gift, one should not harbor the thought:
"This should be given to me and not to another; my own family should receive it, while another family should not."
"Seventh, the Bodhisattva generates such a mind as to cause all sentient beings to obtain the necessities for sustaining life and to attain complete peace and happiness;
eighth, to cause all sentient beings to be able to achieve the supreme, transcendent, and most excellent peace and happiness;
ninth, the Bodhisattva forms this thought:"
"I shall constantly and diligently cultivate deeds that benefit sentient beings.
Tenth, the bodhisattva forms this thought:
"I shall never give rise to a mind of stinginess or envy."
“Good son! If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to remain free from stinginess and envy.
Furthermore, good son!”
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to abide in a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
What are these ten?
First, they give rise to impartial skillful means toward all sentient beings;...
Second, to give rise to a mind free from obstruction toward all sentient beings;
third, to give rise to a mind free from malice and affliction toward all sentient beings;
fourth, to practice extensive giving for the sake of all sentient beings.
Fifth, guarding the practice of ethical discipline;
sixth, cultivating patience;
seventh, exerting diligent effort;
Eighth, abiding securely in meditative concentration;
ninth, cultivating transcendent wisdom;
tenth, accumulating that omniscience—thus does the bodhisattva accumulate by relying on the non-dual mind.

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva accumulates [merit and wisdom] with equanimity toward all sentient beings, and because they accumulate it by taking all sentient beings as their object of focus, they are thus able to cause all beings everywhere to swiftly realize the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Having themselves escaped the great burning house, the bodhisattva further causes others to escape as well; for, abiding in a mind of equanimity, their mind is free from high or low.

“Good son! It is like a householder who has six sons, each of whom is pleasing to his father’s mind; he loves and cherishes them all equally. These sons are young, lacking knowledge and understanding; their father therefore trains and nurtures them all together through skillful means.”
At one time, a fire suddenly broke out in the father’s house, and his sons were each in different places.
"Good son, what do you think?"
At that time, the elder thought to himself:
"Should I cause all these sons to go out together,
or should they go out one after another?"
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying: “No,
World-Honored One!”

Why is this? Because that elder, with a mind of equanimity, cherished them all without distinction; thus, although the sons were each in different places, he caused them all to come out at the same time through his equal love.
The Buddha said,
"Good son, it is the same for a bodhisattva:
all sentient beings are merely foolish worldlings and not noble ones."
Having long dwelt within the great burning house of birth and death, they are ignorant, lacking discernment, and further lack clarity, each scattered among the various realms of existence.

For the sake of their deliverance, the Bodhisattva employs skillful means to cause them all to emerge from that great burning house simultaneously; once they have emerged from the burning house, he causes them all to dwell securely within the realm of tranquility.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to abide in a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be well able to serve and make offerings to the Tathāgata.
What are these ten?
First, making offerings through the Dharma is what constitutes serving and making offerings to the Tathāgata, rather than making offerings with material wealth.
Second, practicing according to what has been taught is an offering;
third, performing deeds that bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings is an offering;
fourth, gathering in and sustaining sentient beings is an offering.
Fifth, to act in accordance with the conduct of all sentient beings is an offering;
