sixth, not abandoning one's vows is an offering;
seventh, not abandoning the bodhisattva activities is an offering.
Eighth, to practice according to what one has taught is an offering;
ninth, to never give rise to weariness or indolence in whatever one does is an offering;
tenth, not abandoning the bodhicitta is serving and making offerings to the Tathāgata—an offering of non-material things.
Why is this? Good son!
The Dharma-body is itself the Tathāgata; therefore, to make offerings to the Dharma is to make offerings to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, to accumulate that which has been taught by the Tathāgata is itself to practice according to the teaching;
to initiate various matters of benefit and happiness is itself to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings;
and to perform activities for the sake of sentient beings is itself to gather and sustain sentient beings.

“Good son! If one is unable to perform deeds that benefit sentient beings, and if one’s vow is weak and inferior such that one abandons the bodhisattva activities, then one will be unable to act in accordance with the conduct of sentient beings, increase one’s vows, or make firm the bodhisattva activities.”
Furthermore, if one gives rise to false speech and the resolve becomes deficient, one will be unable to act according to what has been said.
Moreover, if one gives rise to weariness, one will be unable to remain free from weariness regarding all that is to be done.
Furthermore, if one has experienced a regression from the bodhicitta and has not yet attained realization, one cannot help but abandon the bodhicitta. Why is this?
O son of good family!

Regarding Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, a bodhisattva fundamentally has nothing to be attained and nothing to be realized; therefore, you should now understand it thus: to make an offering of the Dharma is to serve and make offerings to the Tathāgata, rather than making offerings of material wealth.
“Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, he is well able to serve and make offerings to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, good son!”
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they can subdue and overcome pride.
What are these ten?
First, when a bodhisattva leaves home to renounce the world, they depart from all relatives, friends, kinsmen, and acquaintances as if they were dead; thus they subdue and overcome pride.
Second, by disfiguring one's physical appearance and wearing dyed robes, one subdues pride because of conforming to the True Dharma;
third, by shaving off beard and hair and carrying the alms-bowl to wander from house to house begging for food, one subdues pride;
fourth, by humbling one’s mind for the sake of begging for food, being no different from a *caṇḍāla* youth, one subdues pride.
Fifth, they constantly maintain this thought:
"I beg from others; my body and life are dependent upon others.
Thus, they subdue their pride.
Sixth, because the food I receive is pure and is permitted by all Buddhas, I subdue my pride;
seventh, because I wish to draw near to ācāryas, preceptors, and the noble assembly, I subdue my pride;
eighth, because I am endowed with dignified conduct and perform my actions according to the Dharma, wishing to cause my fellow practitioners of the holy life to see me and rejoice, I subdue my pride.
Ninth, because one aspires to attain the full completion of all Buddha-dharmas that have not yet been completed, one subdues the conceit of "I";
tenth, because one intends to constantly practice the conduct of patience toward those sentient beings who are angry, resentful, or harmful, one subdues the conceit of "I."
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, he is able to destroy the pride of 'I'.
Furthermore, good son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to give rise to pure faith.
What are these ten?
First, the accomplishment of meritorious deeds.
Second, because they possess the correct cause, they attain the perfection of roots of goodness from past lives;
third, because they do not give rise to false faith, they possess right view;
fourth, because they do not rely on false teachers, they achieve the fulfillment of aspiration.
Fifth, because they are free from flattery and deception, they attain upright conduct without crookedness;
sixth, because their faculties and natures are sharp, they attain superior wisdom;
seventh, because their continuity is pure, they attain freedom from all hindrances.
Eighth, because they distance themselves from evil associates, they constantly gain the opportunity to draw near to all virtuous spiritual friends;
ninth, because they constantly seek out all well-spoken teachings, they are able to eliminate the mind of overweening pride;
tenth, because they possess great faith in the Dharma taught by the Buddha, they are able to abandon all false attachments and clearly understand the vast majesty and virtue of the Tathāgata.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to give rise to pure faith.
Thus ends the fifteenth fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-apanītaparyutthāna-guhyaprabha-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-sūtra*.
The Sūtra on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Sixteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu, Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.

Translated by the Imperial Preceptor for Transmitting the Sanskrit, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Dharmapāla, and others, by imperial decree. At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will explain even a small portion of the vast majesty and virtue possessed by all Tathāgatas.
The Buddha said, “Good son!
"You should listen attentively!
I shall now briefly describe for you the vast majesty and virtue of the Tathāgata.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent,
World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.”
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: “Good son!
The Tathāgata has accomplished great compassion that is immeasurable and impartial, extending universally to all sentient beings.

Just as the Tathāgata practices this compassion toward a single sentient being, he likewise practices it universally toward all others throughout the entire realm of sentient beings; even extending to the limits of the realm of empty space, its practice remains the same, yet in truth, one cannot know the ultimate limit of the Tathāgata’s great compassion.
"Furthermore, noble son!
The Tathāgata has accomplished the merit of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which is not equal to that of any śrāvaka or bodhisattva.

Once the Tathāgata has exercised great compassion toward a single sentient being, he does the same for all others throughout the entire realm of sentient beings, extensively bringing benefit to those beings."
"Furthermore, noble son!
The Tathāgata has accomplished inexhaustible preaching of the Dharma.

According to what he has accomplished, whether for one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, or even for immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, for as many sentient beings as there may be—of various types, with diverse names and terminology and differing principles—the Tathāgata is simultaneously able to preach the Dharma for them; yet, in truth, it is impossible to know the limit of the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma."
"Furthermore, noble son!
The Tathāgata has accomplished immeasurable questions and answers.

Should all sentient beings—even those merely included within the category of 'sentient beings'—simultaneously each pose various distinct questions to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, regarding names, phrases, and meanings, the Tathāgata is able to answer them all within a single kṣaṇa, a lava, or a muhūrta."
Yet, in truth, one cannot know the ultimate characteristics of the Tathāgata’s eloquence in responding.
"Furthermore, noble son,
the Tathāgata has attained the unimpeded realm of meditative concentration."

Even if all sentient beings were to abide on the tenth bhūmi and simultaneously enter countless hundreds of thousands of samādhi-doors, and even if they remained in such entry for countless billions of hundreds of thousands of kalpas—with each entering a distinct and different samādhi—they would still be unable to know any of the Tathāgata’s samādhi-doors or the realms of his samādhis.
"Furthermore, noble son!
The Tathāgata has accomplished immeasurable gateways for the transformation of the form-body (*rūpakāya*).

If there are sentient beings who should be liberated by means of the Tathāgata’s physical marks, the Tathāgata is able to manifest the body of a Tathāgata before each and every one of them, within a single kṣaṇa, a single lava, or a single muhūrta."
If there are sentient beings who are to be liberated by means of various distinct physical forms, the Tathāgata, within a single kṣaṇa, manifests all manner of diverse bodies.
"Furthermore, noble son!
The Tathāgata has accomplished the sphere of immeasurable divine sight (*divyacakṣus*).

If there were sentient beings throughout the entire realm of sentient beings who possessed the radiance of divine sight rather than that of the fleshly eye—beings such as these being beyond all calculation, thought, and estimation."
In all these worlds, the Tathāgata is able to perceive each and every one of them clearly, as if looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of his hand.
Furthermore, son of good family!
The Tathāgata has attained the realm of the immeasurable divine ear.

Even if boundless worlds were filled with all sentient beings as previously described, should all such classes of sentient beings simultaneously produce sounds at a single moment—each with distinct and complex vocal modulations—the Tathāgata is able to hear every single one of those sounds at once and understand each one individually.
"Furthermore, noble son!
The Tathāgata has accomplished immeasurable, supreme wisdom.
Even if all sentient beings throughout the infinite and boundless realm of sentient beings—equal in extent to the realm of empty space—were each to reflect and each to deliberate upon it;
According to their various modes of conceptualization and deliberation, they each create distinct and differing karmas.
Within a single kṣaṇa, a lava, or a muhūrta, the Tathāgata is able to fully comprehend that these types of sentient beings think in such a way:
"These types of sentient beings deliberate in this manner; these types of sentient beings create such karma and obtain such fruit."
The Tathāgata, by means of his unimpeded and pure power of knowledge regarding the three periods of time, is able to know all of this.
"O son of good family!
The Tathāgata constantly abides in samādhi and never departs from samādhi."

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata is free from loss of mindfulness, his faculties are not distracted, he has no divergent thoughts, he has already severed all afflictions, and the Tathāgata is tranquil and utterly serene.
“Good son! If there are afflictions, the mind is immediately distracted; because the mind is distracted, one cannot accumulate all wholesome dharmas.

Therefore, the Tathāgata has already severed the afflictions, is free from all defilements, has attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), and has obtained equal mastery over all dharmas, thereby accomplishing the sublime practices of the realms of *samādhi* and *samāpatti*.

"Good son! The Tathāgata constantly practices each and every mode of conduct and each and every samādhi; even at the time of entering nirvāṇa, his conduct remains without fail—how much more so during a single moment of meditative equipoise (samāhita)?"
"Good son!
Thus has the Tathāgata accumulated merit over countless kalpas; therefore, all the merits of the Tathāgata are immeasurable, incomparable, inconceivable, and incalculable."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is it not the case that the Tathāgata accumulated merit over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas?”
The Buddha said:
"No, son of good family!"
Because the realm of the Tathāgata is inconceivable, it can only be accumulated by a bodhisattva who abides in the inconceivable; it cannot be accumulated within three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

Why is this? Only when a bodhisattva has attained entry into the equality of all phenomena can they enter the calculation of kalpas; this is not something that those who have merely first resolved their minds upon awakening are able to enter.
The Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are those who, having heard this vast majesty and virtue of the Tathāgata as it has been described, are able to give rise to pure faith, joy, and gladness, one should know that such persons possess great merit, perform all manner of wholesome deeds, have severed all karmic obstructions, and possess extensive faith and understanding. Such people shall draw near to Bodhi; how much more so for those who, having heard this Dharma, are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and master it, and further proclaim it extensively for others? One must know that such people will before long be able to give rise to such vast majesty and virtue of the Tathāgata.”
The Buddha said, “So it is,
so it is. Good son!”
As you have said, that person shall receive the protection of all Buddhas and deeply plant roots of goodness, honoring and revering many Buddhas.
Therefore, if a son or daughter of good family hears this discourse on the Tathāgata’s great majestic virtue, they must not give rise to doubt or hesitation.
If those sons or daughters of good family can, for seven days and nights, focus their attention with undistracted minds and contemplate the vast majesty and virtue of the Tathāgata.

Following whatever one contemplates, with profound and firm attention and profound faith and understanding, and in accordance with that realization after seven days and nights have passed, one should prepare and arrange various offerings with meticulous purity; donning fresh, clean robes and giving rise to a pure mind, one should contemplate with clear presence before the image, and on that very night, one shall behold the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, even if one cannot follow the ritual procedures or there is some deficiency, provided that one can focus the mind with single-minded concentration, at the time of death, this person will likewise have the Tathāgata appear before them.
The Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
when some people hear the proclamation of the Tathāgata’s great majestic power, do they give rise to lack of faith?”
The Buddha said:
"Good son, there are also sentient beings who,
upon hearing of the Tathāgata’s great majestic power, give rise to coarse and malicious thoughts and an extremely harmful mind, conceiving the notion of an evil friend toward that Dharma-preacher."
For this reason, when their body perishes and their life ends, they fall into hell. "Good son!

If there is another person who, upon hearing the description of the Tathāgata’s great majestic virtue, gives rise to pure faith and conceives of that Dharma-preacher as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and as a teacher and master."

Such persons must have, in previous lives, heard this Dharma of the Tathāgata’s vast majesty and virtue; from lifetime to lifetime until the present life, they have likewise been able to hear of the Tathāgata’s merits within this assembly.
“Good son!
As the Buddha has said, if a person hears this True Dharma, it is because they have already heard it in previous lives.

At that time, the World-Honored One extended his pure tongue-mark so that it completely covered the circle of his face; having covered the circle of his face, it next covered the circle of his crown; having covered the circle of his crown, it turned to cover the circle of his body; and having covered the circle of his body, it completely covered the lion throne all around.
In succession, it covered the assembly of bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas, extending even to the great assemblies such as Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protecting Devas (Lokapālas).
Having thus successively extended and covered everything in its entirety, he withdrew his tongue-organ back to its original state and addressed the assembled multitude, saying:
"O sons of good family!

Observe this tongue-mark of the Tathāgata, which signifies that the words of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, are free from falsehood. You all should each give rise to a superior and pure faith, so that you may obtain great benefit and happiness throughout the long night [of saṃsāra].

When this Dharma was being taught, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas within the assembly attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Furthermore, there were countless sentient beings who had never before resolved their minds toward enlightenment; they all now resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, saying:
"Good son!..."
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will skillfully understand conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). What are these ten?

First, although the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is provisionally designated, in the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) the aggregate of form cannot be apprehended and there is no attachment to it; likewise, although the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are provisionally designated, in the ultimate truth the aggregate of consciousness cannot be apprehended and there is no attachment to it.

Second, although the earth element is conventionally designated, in the ultimate sense the earth element is unapprehendable and there is no attachment to it; likewise, although the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are conventionally designated, in the ultimate sense the consciousness element is unapprehendable and there is no attachment to it.
Third, although the eye-base is conventionally designated, in the ultimate sense the eye-base is unapprehendable and there is no attachment to it.

1. Although the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are provisionally designated, within the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), the mind base is unattainable and there is no grasping toward it;
2. although the self is provisionally designated, within the ultimate truth, the self is unattainable and there is no grasping toward it;
3. although sentient beings are provisionally designated, within the ultimate truth, sentient beings are unattainable and there is no grasping toward them.

Sixth, although one may provisionally designate a life-spanner (*jīva*), a nourisher (*poṣa*), a person (*puruṣa*), an individual (*pudgala*), or a human being (*manuṣyaka*), in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) none of these can be found, nor is there any attachment to them;
seventh, although one may provisionally designate the world (*loka*), in the ultimate truth the world cannot be found, nor is there any attachment to it;
eighth, although one may provisionally designate worldly phenomena (*lokadharma*), in the ultimate truth worldly phenomena cannot be found, nor is there any attachment to them.
Ninth, although one provisionally designates the Buddha-dharma, within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) the Buddha-dharma cannot be apprehended and there is no attachment to it;
tenth, although one provisionally designates bodhi, within the ultimate truth bodhi cannot be apprehended and there is no attachment to it, nor is there anyone who attains bodhi.
“Good son! The designation of names and signs is called a conventional phenomenon, yet the ultimate truth does not exist apart from conventional phenomena.”
If there were no conventional phenomena, one could not attain that ultimate truth.
If a bodhisattva understands the conventional in such a manner, this is called being skilled in understanding conventional phenomena.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be well-versed in the conventional truth.
Thus spoke the Buddha in the *Sūtra of the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin*, Volume Sixteen.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll Seventeen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Da Fu, Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Imperial Preceptor for Transmitting the Sanskrit, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Dharmapāla, and others, by imperial decree:
"Furthermore, noble son, if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will thoroughly understand the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya)."
What are the ten?
First, the accomplishment of the dharma of non-arising;
second, the accomplishment of the dharma of non-ceasing.
Third, because they have accomplished the indestructible dharma;
fourth, because they have accomplished the dharma that neither emerges nor enters;
fifth, because they have accomplished the transcendence of the realm of speech.
Sixth, because they have accomplished the dharma that transcends verbal expression;
seventh, because they have accomplished the dharma that is free from conceptual proliferation;
eighth, because they have accomplished the dharma that is ineffable.
Ninth, because they have accomplished the dharma of tranquility;
tenth, because they have accomplished the dharma of the noble ones. Why is this so?
Good son! Because the principle of ultimate truth is fundamentally indestructible, whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, it has always been thus:
unborn and unceasing, neither emerging nor entering, beyond what can be expressed by words, beyond what can be signified by words, and to be realized by departing from all conceptual proliferation.
"Noble son!
This ultimate truth is profoundly tranquil and beyond verbal expression; it is realized only within by the noble ones themselves.
Furthermore, noble son!"
This ultimate truth, whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, is fundamentally indestructible.
For this reason, there are sons of good family who give rise to right faith, leave the household life in purity, shave off their hair and beards, and don the saffron robes;

having left the household life, they exert diligent effort and cultivate various wholesome deeds, just as one whose head is wrapped in silk would strive to extinguish a fire that has broken out—such is the pursuit of the Dharma.

“Good son! If the dharma of ultimate truth were not attained, then the brahma-faring one practices would be fruitless and devoid of benefit, and the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world would likewise be without fruit or benefit.”
Therefore, son of good family!
If there were any ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) that could be expressed, it would be called a bodhisattva’s thorough knowledge of the ultimate.
Son of good family!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will thoroughly understand the ultimate truth.
Furthermore, noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will thoroughly understand dependent origination.
What are the ten?
First, knowing that all phenomena are empty;
second, knowing that phenomena have no inherent existence.
Third, knowing that phenomena are not real;
fourth, knowing that phenomena are like images;
fifth, knowing that phenomena are like shadows.
Sixth, knowing that phenomena are like echoes;
seventh, knowing that phenomena are like illusions;
eighth, knowing that phenomena do not abide for long.
Ninth, knowing that phenomena are unstable;
tenth, knowing that all phenomena arise from conditions.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"This dharma is thus empty, thus non-existent, thus unreal; it is thus like a reflection, like a shadow, like an echo, like a magical illusion; it is thus impermanent, thus fluctuating, and thus dependently arisen."

Although they thoroughly understand that all phenomena of birth are definitively non-abiding and swiftly proceed toward destruction, they nevertheless establish the phenomena of birth, the phenomena of cessation, and those of abiding.
Again, he reflected:
"From what conditions do these phenomena arise?
From what conditions do they cease?"

Having reflected thus, he came to know that these phenomena arise from ignorance; they exist because of ignorance, with ignorance as their precursor and support. Relying upon ignorance, volitional formations arise; relying upon volitional formations, consciousness comes to be.

Because consciousness exists, name-and-form is established; because name-and-form is established, the six sense bases arise; because the six sense bases exist, contact arises accordingly; because contact exists, sensation arises; from the cause of sensation, the fool gives rise to craving; because he is oppressed by craving, grasping arises; because grasping exists, he is bound to existence; from existence comes birth; from birth comes old age; and because there is the nature of old age, the person (pudgala) and the individual (puruṣa) both die. Relying on the nature of death, there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering is accumulated.

"Therefore, the wise should diligently strive to sever ignorance, destroy ignorance, uproot the root of ignorance, and extinguish the phenomena of ignorance; for by the extinction of ignorance, one is able to eliminate the phenomena upon which those lacking wisdom rely."
Just as when the life-faculty ceases, all other faculties cease, so too it is with the cessation of ignorance: all phenomena that serve as the basis for non-wisdom cease as well.

Why is this? Because there is no lack of wisdom, there is no accumulation; all afflictions do not cause one to transmigrate through the various realms of existence. Since there are no afflictions to drive transmigration through the realms, one is able to sever the causes of birth and death and draw near to nirvana.
“Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will thoroughly understand dependent origination.
Furthermore, noble son!”
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to understand them for themselves.
What are these ten?
First, the bodhisattva skillfully observes themselves:
"Now, from which lineage was this body of mine born?
Is it from the Brahmin caste,
or is it from the Kṣatriya caste?"
Is he of the merchant class?
Or perhaps of a noble and wealthy lineage?
Or is he of a lowly and humble birth?
"If I am born into a noble or wealthy family, I shall not rely on this condition to give rise to arrogance; even if I am born into a lowly or humble family," he should form this thought:
"It is because of the mixed karma I created in past lives that I have been born into such a family."
"By means of this very condition, he becomes weary of and detached from the world; because he has become weary and detached, he seeks to go forth.
'Second, once the Bodhisattva has gone forth, he should immediately observe:
"For what purpose have I now sought to go forth?"'"""
He then reflected to himself:

"Now that I have left the household life, having attained deliverance for myself, I shall cause others to be delivered as well; having attained liberation for myself, I shall likewise cause all others to attain liberation."
For this reason, one shall never give rise to indolence or laziness.
"Third, the bodhisattva observes in this way:
'Now that I have gone forth, I must sever all sinful and unwholesome dharmas, extinguishing them completely without remainder.'"
If I have already severed all unwholesome states, I shall experience great joy, satisfaction, and exhilaration;
if I have not yet severed all unwholesome states, I should exert myself with diligence to quickly eliminate and sever them.
"Fourth, the Bodhisattva observes thus:
'Now that I have left the household life, I ought to extensively increase and cultivate all wholesome dharmas.'"
If I have already been able to extensively increase all wholesome dharmas, my mind shall give rise to joy, satisfaction, and gladness;
if I have not yet increased or cultivated wholesome dharmas, I should exert diligence to cause them to grow swiftly.
"5. Fifth, the bodhisattva observes thus:
'If I rely upon the venerable teacher, I shall be able to increase all wholesome dharmas and destroy all unwholesome dharmas.'"

For this reason, toward one's preceptor, one should regard them as the Great Teacher, the Buddha, regardless of whether they have heard little or much, whether they possess wisdom or lack it, or whether they uphold the precepts or violate them.

Toward that venerable teacher, he feels affection, faith, respect, and serves him with reverence; likewise, toward his preceptor, he shows the same respect and veneration as he does toward his own instructing teacher.
"Sixth, the bodhisattva observes in this way:

'If I rely upon a preceptor, I shall be able to fulfill those factors conducive to enlightenment that are not yet fulfilled, and I shall be able to sever all afflictions that have not yet been severed.'"
Therefore, toward that preceptor, one should serve him with reverence as if he were one's own teacher, with a mind of great joy.
That venerable master is able to sustain me through all wholesome dharmas of the right path, rather than sustaining me through unwholesome dharmas of a deviant path.
"Seventh, the bodhisattva observes in this way:
'Who is my teacher?
and then reflects with careful deliberation:"

"The Omniscient One is my Great Teacher; he, who clearly understands all things and has compassion for the world, has given rise to great compassion, acts as a supreme field of merit, and is able to serve as the teacher of gods, humans, asuras, and the world."
For this reason, he gave rise to great joy, delight, and a sense of exultation.
Furthermore, he reflected:
"If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is my Great Teacher, I have truly attained a great and wholesome benefit."

"Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has established the path of training, I shall practice and study it throughout my entire life in accordance with his instructions; following what I have heard, I shall never transgress it."
"8. Furthermore, the Bodhisattva reflects thus:
'From whom should I seek alms?
Having investigated thoroughly:"

"I should go on alms-round among the families of those brahmins, kṣatriyas, and householders, so that by giving food they may obtain a great reward, achieve great benefit and purpose, and possess great majesty."
"It is for this reason that I beg for alms, so as to enable them to attain the fruit [of their merit].
Ninth, the Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"What kind of perception do those Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others have when they give me food?"
Thus he reflected:

"Those brahmins, kṣatriyas, and others must surely have conceived the notion that I am a śramaṇa, the notion that I am a bhikṣu, and the notion that I am a field of merit; therefore, they give me food."
"I should now accumulate and practice the virtues of a śramaṇa, the virtues of a bhikṣu, and the virtues of a field of merit.
Tenth, the bodhisattva reflects:
"How can I bring about liberation from this beginningless cycle of birth and death?"
Thus he examines:
"First, that I have attained the appearance of a bhikṣu is the first way of departing from birth and death;
second, that I have accomplished all the virtues of a bhikṣu is the second way of departing from birth and death."
Third, I am able to initiate diligence to abandon indolence, cultivating all wholesome practices to realize the nature of phenomena; this is the third way of escaping birth and death.
Fourth, universally cultivating all practices until attaining Buddhahood to transform and deliver sentient beings; this is the fourth way of escaping birth and death.
“If a bodhisattva can thus examine and constantly observe with such discernment, this is called being well-versed in self-understanding. Good son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be well-versed in self-understanding.”
"Furthermore, noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will have thorough knowledge of the world.
What are these ten?
First, seeing those who are haughty and arrogant, one is able to humble oneself;
second, seeing those who are conceited, one is able to abandon pride;
third, seeing those who are deceitful and crooked, one is able to establish uprightness.
Fourth, seeing those who speak falsely, one speaks words of truth for them;
fifth, seeing those who speak harsh words, one speaks words of affection for them;
sixth, seeing those who are coarse and violent, one manifests a gentle and supple demeanor.
Seventh, seeing those who are wrathful and malicious, one is able to practice great patience;
eighth, seeing those who harm others with poison, one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness;
ninth, seeing those who are afflicted by suffering and distress, one gives rise to compassion.
Tenth, seeing those who are stingy and miserly, one practices giving.
Son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will have a thorough knowledge of the world.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be born in the pure buddha-fields.
What are these ten?
First, they possess pure ethical discipline that is uninterrupted and unadulterated, further achieving a course of conduct free from defilement;
second, they practice an impartial mind, establishing impartial skillful means for the sake of all sentient beings;
third, they have accomplished vast roots of goodness, rather than meager ones.
Fourth, they remain far removed from worldly fame, gain, and offerings, and are further unstained by attachment to them;
fifth, they possess pure faith and a mind free from doubt;
sixth, they exert diligent effort and abandon indolence.
Seventh, they fully cultivate meditative concentration with a mind free from distraction;
eighth, they practice extensive learning without possessing malicious wisdom;
ninth, they possess sharp faculties and keen wisdom, devoid of dullness or obtuseness.
Tenth, extensively practicing acts of loving-kindness with a mind free from malice.
Son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be born in the pure buddha-fields.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, must one fully cultivate all ten dharmas in order to attain rebirth there?
Or can one attain rebirth by cultivating even a single dharma without deficiency or impairment?"
The Buddha said: "Good son!

If one cultivates even a single dharma according to this principle—such that it is uninterrupted and indestructible, unmixed and unstained, pure and immaculate—one will be able to accomplish the practices of all other dharmas."
“Good son! The meaning herein is this:
if one can fully cultivate all dharmas without deficiency, one will be born in a pure buddha-field, of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, good son!”
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be born unstained by the impurities of the womb.
What are these ten?
The first is to repair and maintain images of the Tathāgata.
Second, to adorn and restore ruined stūpas and temples;
third, to anoint and repair the Tathāgata’s precious stūpas with exquisite incense;
fourth, to bathe the Buddha images with exquisite scented water.
Fifth, to plaster, repair, sweep, and sprinkle water upon the grounds of the Tathāgata’s stūpa;
sixth, to serve one’s parents with reverence;
seventh, to serve one’s preceptors, teachers, and fellow practitioners of the holy life with reverence.
Eighth, although it is thus, they have no expectations;
ninth, they dedicate all such roots of goodness, vowing that by means of this merit, may all sentient beings everywhere be born without being defiled by the impurities of the womb;
tenth, their profound resolve is firm and steadfast.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be born without being defiled by the impurities of the womb.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to dwell both as a householder and as one who has gone forth.
What are these ten?
First, attaining that which is without grasping.
Second, dwelling without confusion;
third, turning one's back on all sensory objects;
fourth, remaining far removed from all attachment to sensory objects.
Fifth, they are untainted by any faults inherent in sensory objects;
sixth, they are able to reverently practice the trainings established by the Tathāgata, applying themselves with diligence and without weariness;
seventh, even if they obtain only a small amount of food, drink, clothing, bedding, or medicinal requisites for illness, their minds are always content.
Eighth, to accept whatever bowl and robes one obtains while remaining free from all grasping and attachment;
ninth, to feel weary of and detached from all sensory objects, constantly giving rise to a sense of dread toward them;
tenth, to always diligently cultivate the tranquility that manifests before one.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to both dwell as a householder and leave the household life.
*The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin*, Scroll Seventeen.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll Eighteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
The Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, the Imperially Ennobled Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Dharmarakṣa, and others, translated this by imperial decree:
"Furthermore, noble son, if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, he will attain pure livelihood."
What are the ten?
First, to remain far removed from seeking gain through flattery;
second, to remain far removed from "feigning appearances for the sake of gain."
Third, to remain far removed from using empty words to entice and seduce for the sake of gain and offerings;
fourth, to remain far removed from seeking gain and offerings through improper means;
fifth, to remain far removed from unrighteous gain and offerings.
Sixth, to remain far removed from impure gains;
seventh, not to be addicted to gains;
eighth, not to be defiled by craving for gains.
Ninth, one does not allow the mind to become distressed for the sake of gain and offerings;
tenth, one gives rise to contentment upon obtaining gain and offerings that are in accordance with the Dharma. "Good son!
What is meant by a bodhisattva being skillfully able to remain far removed from deceitful seeking of gain and offerings?
It means that a bodhisattva, for the sake of gain and offerings, does not engage in deceit and crookedness through the actions of body, speech, or mind.

Regarding "not practicing deceit with the body": if a bodhisattva, upon seeing a donor or an assistant to the donor, does not intentionally "arouse a display of dignified deportment"—such as lifting the feet and stepping forward slowly and calmly, looking straight ahead with focused composure;
nor does he look with an expression of aversion;
nor does he remain in a state of silent stillness with a gaze devoid of alertness—this is called not practicing deceit with the body.

Regarding "not practicing deceit in speech": because of the causes and conditions of gain and honor, a bodhisattva does not employ slow or hesitant speech, nor gentle speech, nor affectionate speech, nor compliant speech; this is what is called "not practicing deceit in speech."

Regarding "the mind does not practice flattery": when a bodhisattva sees a donor or an assistant to the donor summoning him with offerings and gains, he does not speak of having few desires while his mind gives rise to craving and he harbors inner distress; this is what is meant by "the mind does not practice flattery."
These and others like them are called the bodhisattva’s skillful distancing from seeking gain through flattery.
What is meant by "skillfully distancing oneself from feigning appearances for the sake of gain"?

This means that even if a bodhisattva is pressed by the need for robes, alms bowls, medicinal requisites for illness, or other such necessities, because they are free from hypocrisy, they never speak to solicit those donors or their supporters; this is what is meant by a bodhisattva being well-able to remain far removed from "hypocritically manifesting signs for the sake of gain."
"What is meant by being well-able to distance oneself from 'using empty words to entice for the sake of gain'?
It means that if a bodhisattva sees a donor or an assistant to the donor, they do not utter such words as:

'A certain donor has bestowed such-and-such items upon me; because he perceives me as one who upholds the precepts, is learned, and is of few desires and contented, he has specifically bestowed these various things upon me. Rather, it is when [the bodhisattva] gives rise to a mind of compassion, performs acts of benefit, and accepts them only after having gathered the donor under their care."
This is what it means for a bodhisattva to be well able to remain far removed from "using empty words to entice and seduce for the sake of gain and offerings.
What is meant by being well able to remain far removed from seeking gain and offerings through improper means?
This means that if a bodhisattva does not engage in evil conduct of body or mind for the sake of seeking gain and offerings.
Regarding "evil conduct of the body":
it refers to coming and going, rushing about, competing, enduring various hardships, and violating the pure precepts.
Regarding those who act with malice in their hearts:

for the sake of gain and offerings, upon seeing fellow practitioners of the holy life receive such gain and offerings, they give rise to a mind of harm toward them—this is what it means for a bodhisattva to be well able to distance themselves from the evil pursuit of gain and offerings.
“What is meant by being well able to distance oneself from unrighteous gain?

It means that if a bodhisattva does not practice deception with measures or scales, does not misappropriate what others entrust to them, and further does not engage in wicked accumulation of wealth and profit, this is called a bodhisattva being well able to distance himself from unrighteous gain.”
“What is meant by being well able to distance oneself from impure gains?

It means that if, among the gains a bodhisattva receives, there are items belonging to a stūpa, or items belonging to the Dharma or the Saṃgha, which have not been given or permitted, the bodhisattva, having recognized this, does not accept them at all; this is what is meant by a bodhisattva being well able to distance himself from impure gains.”
"What is meant by not being attached to gain and offerings?

It means that even when a bodhisattva obtains gain and offerings, they do not regard them as their own possession, nor do they consider themselves wealthy, and furthermore, they do not accumulate them."

When one is able to give universally to other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, as well as to parents, relatives, friends, and acquaintances, or when one uses [wealth] for one's own enjoyment at the proper time, this is what it means for a bodhisattva not to be attached to gain and offerings.
"What is meant by 'being unstained by attachment to gain and offerings'?

It means that although a bodhisattva makes use of such things, they do not give rise to various forms of stained and attached thoughts; this is what is meant by a bodhisattva being unstained by attachment to gain and offerings."
“What is meant by not giving rise to mental distress for the sake of gain and support?

It means that when a bodhisattva does not receive gain and support, their mind does not give rise to suffering, nor do they experience distress; furthermore, they do not harbor feelings of aversion or rejection toward the donor or those who assist the donor. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva not giving rise to mental distress for the sake of gain and support.”
"What is it to be content with gains obtained in accordance with the Dharma?

It means that when a bodhisattva receives gains in accordance with the Dharma according to the order of the monastic assembly—gains permitted by the Tathāgata, not censured by the community of bodhisattvas, praised by the noble ones, and not disparaged by fellow practitioners of the holy life—having accepted them in this way, they give rise to a mind of contentment. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva being content with gains obtained in accordance with the Dharma."
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, he attains pure livelihood.
Furthermore, good son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, their mind will be free from weariness. What are these ten?
First, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, they dwell for a long time within saṃsāra without weariness.
Second, undergoing the suffering of birth and death for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings without weariness;
third, acting for the benefit of all sentient beings without weariness;
fourth, performing various virtuous deeds for the sake of sentient beings without weariness.
Fifth, to be free from weariness in performing all activities for the sake of sentient beings;
sixth, to be free from weariness in teaching the path and its dharmas to those seeking the Śrāvaka vehicle;
seventh, not to speak with disbelief regarding the Dharma before those of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Eighth, accomplishing the factors of enlightenment without weariness;
ninth, perfecting the provisions for enlightenment without weariness;
tenth, not realizing nirvana and not giving rise to the aspiration to proceed toward nirvana.
By virtue of these conditions, the bodhisattva is able to advance toward enlightenment, gradually drawing near to it and realizing it.
Son of good family!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, their mind will be free from weariness and fatigue.
"Furthermore, noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to carry out all the instructions of the Tathāgatas.
What are these ten?
First, diligently cultivating the practice of heedfulness by remaining free from all negligence;
second, possessing virtuous discipline by not committing evil through the body;
third, possessing virtuous discipline by not committing evil through speech.
Fourth, they possess excellent discipline, because their minds do not engage in evil;
fifth, they fear future worlds, because they completely sever all evils;
sixth, they speak according to reason, because they avoid irrational speech.
Seventh, proclaiming the words of the True Dharma because they are free from unrighteous speech;
eighth, abandoning unwholesome karma because one cultivates wholesome karma;
ninth, never speaking of faults or evils within the teachings of the Tathāgata because one is free from the defilements, impurities, and poisons of all afflictions.
Tenth, they accord with and protect the True Dharma of the Tathāgata in order to ward off all unwholesome dharmas.
Son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to carry out all the instructions of the Tathāgatas.
"Furthermore, noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain a countenance that is serene and free from all frowning.
What are these ten?
First, the faculties are excellent and sublime;
second, the faculties are pure;
third, the faculties are without deficiency.
Fourth, the faculties are free from defilement;
fifth, the faculties are pure and bright;
sixth, they are far removed from anger and hatred.
Seventh, they are far removed from latent tendencies;
eighth, they are far removed from fetters;
ninth, they are far removed from knots and resentments.
Tenth is to remain far removed from anger.
Son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain a countenance that is serene and joyful, free from all frowning.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, because the sense faculties are pure, the Bodhisattva attains a countenance that is serene and joyful; because all afflictions have been severed, he is free from frowning.”
The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is.
O son of good family!”
Because his faculties are pure, the Bodhisattva attains a face with a serene and joyful expression; because he has severed all afflictions, he is free from frowning.
"Furthermore, good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain great learning.
What are these ten?
First, knowing as it truly is that within saṃsāra the fire of craving blazes fiercely;
Second, knowing as it truly is the intensification of the fire of hatred;
third, knowing as it truly is the confusion of the fire of delusion;
fourth, knowing as it truly is that all conditioned phenomena are entirely impermanent.
Fifth, knowing as it truly is that all conditioned phenomena are suffering;
sixth, knowing as it truly is that the world is entirely empty;
seventh, knowing as it truly is that all dharmas are without self.
Eighth, they are able to remain free from worldly conceptual proliferation;
ninth, they understand as it truly is that all those phenomena arise from conditions;
tenth, they understand as it truly is the tranquility of nirvana.

These various dharmas can only be realized through the wisdoms produced by hearing, reflection, and cultivation; they cannot be understood or entered into merely by means of sounds and verbal expressions.
Having understood this, the bodhisattva immediately gives rise to a firm mind of compassion and exerts diligent effort to perform deeds for the benefit of all sentient beings. Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain great learning.
Furthermore, son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to uphold the true Dharma.
What are these ten?

First, in a later time, a later period, during the final five hundred years when the True Dharma declines and vanishes, and as the era shifts, sentient beings will establish false paths within the Buddha’s teaching, and the lamp of wisdom will fade and be extinguished.

At such a time, there may be those who can proclaim and expound the vast sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, which bring great benefit and possess great majesty and virtue; those who, like the mothers of all dharmas, are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, revere, and serve them, will be able to sustain the True Dharma.
Second, they shall expound them for others, causing them to hear, accept, and understand their meaning.
Third, toward those who practice the True Dharma, they shall feel affection, faith, respect, joy, and delight, thereby embracing and supporting them.
Fourth, to proclaim the true Dharma for others without harboring any expectations;
fifth, to conceive of the Dharma teacher as a venerable master;
sixth, to regard that true Dharma as nectar.
Seventh, regarding them as a sacred medicine;
eighth, regarding them as an excellent medicine;
ninth, not sparing one's body or life in the pursuit of the True Dharma.
Tenth, having attained the Dharma, one brings its practice to perfection.
Son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to embrace the true Dharma.
"Furthermore, noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, he becomes a prince of the Dharma. What are these ten?
First, being fully endowed with the adornment of the primary marks;
second, the body attaining the secondary signs;
third, being complete in all marks and having the sense faculties perfected.
Fourth, to approach and attend upon the Buddha, the Tathāgata, in accordance with those who have approached him;
fifth, to practice the right path traversed by the Buddha, the Tathāgata, in accordance with it;
sixth, to awaken to the Dharma realized by the Buddha, the Tathāgata, in accordance with that awakening.
Seventh, to rescue and deliver the world from all suffering and affliction;
eighth, to be skillfully able to study and practice all noble conducts;
ninth, to be skillfully able to cultivate and perfect all pure practices (*brahmacarya*).
Tenth, they dwell well within the city of omniscience where the Tathāgatas abide.
Son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they become a prince of the Dharma.
"Furthermore, noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to surpass Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protecting Devas, and others."
What are the ten?
First, attaining non-retrogression from the Buddha’s bodhi;
second, not being moved by any māras; [and so forth].
Third, not being separated from all Buddha-dharmas;
fourth, being able to penetrate and enter the correct principle of all dharmas according to one's capacity;
fifth, thoroughly comprehending the equality of all dharmas.
Sixth, not relying on the faith of others;
seventh, attaining the wisdom of excellent awakening within the Buddha-dharma;
eighth, not being equal to any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Ninth, they transcend all worlds;
tenth, they realize the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to surpass Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protecting Devas, and others.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to know the inclinations and latent tendencies of sentient beings.
What are these ten?
First, they understand, as it truly is, the inclination toward desire in all sentient beings.
Second, understanding the disposition of hatred;
third, understanding the disposition of delusion;
fourth, understanding the superior disposition.
Fifth, he thoroughly understands middling dispositions;
sixth, he thoroughly understands inferior dispositions;
seventh, he thoroughly understands all virtuous dispositions.
Eighth, understanding the firm resolve;
ninth, understanding the ever-arising latent tendencies;
tenth, understanding the violent and malicious latent tendencies.
Having understood such dharmas as these as they truly are with respect to a single sentient being, it is likewise for all that is to be known throughout the entire realm of sentient beings. Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to know the inclinations and latent tendencies of sentient beings.
Furthermore, son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will skillfully know the methods for maturing sentient beings.
What are these ten?
First, for those who are to be disciplined by the physical form of a Buddha, he manifests the form of a Buddha;
second, for those who are to be disciplined by the physical form of a Bodhisattva, he manifests the form of a Bodhisattva.
Third, for those who are to be tamed by the physical form of a pratyekabuddha, he manifests the form of a pratyekabuddha;
fourth, for those who are to be tamed by the physical form of a śrāvaka, he manifests the form of a śrāvaka;
fifth, for those who are to be tamed by the physical form of Śakra, he manifests the form of Śakra.
Sixth, for those who should be tamed by the appearance of a Māra king, he manifests the appearance of a Māra king;
seventh, for those who should be tamed by the appearance of a Brahmā king, he manifests the appearance of a Brahmā king;
eighth, for those who should be tamed by the appearance of a Brāhmaṇa, he manifests the appearance of a Brāhmaṇa.
Ninth, for those who should be tamed by the appearance of a kṣatriya, he manifests the appearance of a kṣatriya;
tenth, for those who should be tamed by the appearance of a householder, he manifests the appearance of a householder.
"Good son!
For those sentient beings who are to be tamed by various such forms and appearances, the bodhisattva is able to manifest distinct appearances according to what is appropriate for each."
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be well-versed in the methods for maturing sentient beings.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain a state of supreme and blissful dwelling.
What are these ten? First, uprightness.
Second, gentleness;
third, a mind free from flattery and crookedness;
fourth, a mind free from anger and resentment.
Fifth, having a mind free from defilement;
sixth, possessing a pure mind;
seventh, being free from harsh speech;
Eighth, to abandon foul and evil speech;
ninth, to constantly practice patience;
tenth, to possess wholesome affection and joy.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain a state of supreme and blissful dwelling.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain dwelling in peace and happiness.
What are these ten?
First, being fully endowed with right view;
Second, possessing pure vision and perfecting the practice of ethical discipline;
third, purity of conduct and demeanor;
fourth, acting in accordance with the sphere of one's practice.
Fifth, dwelling without being mixed with various afflictions;
sixth, attaining freedom from faults;
seventh, fully cultivating the holy life (brahmacarya).
Eighth, they find their own kind;
ninth, they abide in the path of the One Vehicle;
tenth, they do not serve other teachers.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain dwelling in peace and happiness.
The Sūtra on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll 18.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll Nineteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu, Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial.
Translated by the Imperial Preceptor for Transmitting Sanskrit, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Dharmapāla and others, by imperial decree:
"Furthermore, noble son, if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, he will be able to skillfully understand the practice of the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu)."
What are the ten?
First, practicing the giving of benefit to gather and transform sentient beings;
second, practicing the giving of happiness;
Third, practicing inexhaustible giving;
fourth, beneficial speech;
fifth, speech that accords with the truth.
Sixth, speaking in accordance with the Dharma;
seventh, speaking in accordance with reason;
eighth, acting for the benefit of others.
Ninth, they act for the benefit of others by sharing their wealth;
tenth, they act for the benefit of others and gather in sentient beings by sharing with them matters such as the necessities of life and resources.
“Good son! That which is the gift of benefit is called the gift of Dharma;
that which is the gift of peace and happiness is called the gift of material wealth.”
Inexhaustible giving refers to proclaiming the right path to others.
Beneficial speech refers to the proclamation of all dharmas of the virtuous category.
Meaningful speech refers to the proclamation of the principle of reality.
Speaking according to the Dharma means proclaiming all phenomena in accordance with the Tathāgata’s true teaching.
Speaking according to principle means not subverting the meaning of reality.
Benefiting through practice means causing unwholesome states not to arise in sentient beings and establishing them in wholesome dharmas.
Benefiting through shared resources means equally enjoying food, drink, wealth, and other such necessities for sustaining life and livelihood together.

Regarding the practice of benefiting others: this refers to utilizing gold, silver, mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth, sharing these resources with others to bring them benefit.
“Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, he will be able to skillfully understand the practice of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Furthermore, good son!”
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the perfection of the excellent marks. What are these ten?
First, constantly cultivating tranquil deportment;
Second, constantly cultivating a demeanor free from hypocrisy;
third, constantly cultivating a pure demeanor;
fourth, causing all who see one to give rise to love and joy.
Fifth, all who see him give rise to auspicious signs;
sixth, those who see him never tire of doing so;
seventh, those who see him find delight in their minds.
Eighth, all sentient beings who see him encounter no obstruction;
ninth, all sentient beings who see him give rise to a heart of joy;
tenth, all sentient beings who see him give rise to a pure heart.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the perfection of the wondrous marks.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they become a refuge for others. What are these ten?
First, for those sentient beings who have long dwelt in the terrors of saṃsāra, they act as their protectors.
Second, for sentient beings who have long dwelt in the wilderness and perilous difficulties of saṃsāra, he acts as a virtuous guide;
third, for sentient beings submerged in the great ocean of saṃsāra, he provides a means of rescue and crossing;
fourth, for sentient beings who lack kinsmen, he acts as their sovereign protector.
Fifth, for those sentient beings who have long been afflicted by the severe suffering of the illness of afflictions, he acts as their physician;
sixth, for those sentient beings who lack protection, he acts as their protector;
seventh, for those sentient beings who lack a place of refuge, he acts as their dwelling.
Eighth, for sentient beings who have no refuge, one acts as their refuge;
ninth, for sentient beings who have no place of rest, one acts as their island;
tenth, for sentient beings who have no direction, one acts as their destination.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they are able to serve as a refuge for others.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they are like a great medicinal tree.
Son of good family!
For example, in the world there is a great medicinal tree named Sudarśana; if any sentient beings afflicted by all manner of painful illnesses take and use it, their diseases are entirely healed.
What are the ten?
First, the enjoyment of its roots;
second, the enjoyment of its stems.
Third, they enjoy its branches;
fourth, they enjoy its leaves;
fifth, they enjoy its flowers.
Sixth, the enjoyment of its fruit;
seventh, the enjoyment of its color when seen;
eighth, the enjoyment of its fragrance when smelled.
Ninth, one experiences its flavor when tasting it;
tenth, one experiences its touch through movement. "Good son!

The Bodhisattva is likewise in this regard: from the moment he first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], he has been well able to treat the diseases of the afflictions of all sentient beings, and as those sentient beings practice according to his instructions, their illnesses are entirely cured.
First, the enjoyment of the bodhisattva’s perfection of generosity;
second, the enjoyment of the bodhisattva’s perfection of ethical discipline;
third, the enjoyment of the bodhisattva’s perfection of patience.
Fourth, the enjoyment of the bodhisattva’s perfection of diligence;
fifth, the enjoyment of the bodhisattva’s perfection of meditative concentration;
sixth, the enjoyment of the bodhisattva’s perfection of wisdom.
Seventh, seeing the physical form of the Bodhisattva’s body and enjoying its appearance;
eighth, hearing the name of the Bodhisattva and enjoying its sound;
ninth, tasting the flavor of the Dharma of the Bodhisattva’s pure merits.
Tenth, to draw near to bodhisattvas and to honor and make offerings to them.
Son of good family!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will become like a great medicinal tree.
"Furthermore, noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to diligently practice meritorious deeds.
What are these ten?
First, to make offerings to the Triple Gem according to one's ability;
second, to bestow excellent medicines upon sentient beings suffering from illness;
third, to provide food and drink to sentient beings afflicted by hunger and thirst.
Fourth, if any sentient beings are oppressed by cold or heat, one should provide them with protection;
fifth, one should always respect and revere one’s preceptors and teachers;
sixth, upon seeing fellow practitioners of the holy life, one should rise to welcome them, join one’s palms in reverence, pay homage, and inquire after their well-being.
Seventh, he maintains and repairs gardens, groves, and monasteries;
eighth, from time to time, he brings forth goods such as wealth and grain from his treasuries to practice giving and charity;
ninth, he nurtures and protects all his slaves and laborers with impartiality.
Tenth, from time to time, they constantly practice making offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who uphold the precepts.
Son of good family,
if a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to diligently cultivate meritorious conduct.
"Furthermore, noble son,
if a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be well able to perform various transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa*). What are these ten?
First, without moving from his physical form within a single buddha-field, he is able to inquire about profound meanings before all Tathāgatas in countless buddha-fields;
second, without moving from his physical form within a single buddha-field, he is able to listen to and receive the profound Dharma from all Tathāgatas in countless buddha-fields;
third, without moving from his physical form within a single buddha-field, he is able to serve and make offerings to all Tathāgatas in countless buddha-fields.
Fourth, while remaining unmoved from their physical form within a single buddha-field, they are able to fully perfect the provisions for enlightenment within countless buddha-fields;

fifth, while remaining unmoved from their physical form within a single buddha-field, they are able to show respect and perform acts of offering whenever various bodhisattvas attain perfect enlightenment within countless buddha-fields;
sixth, while remaining unmoved from their physical form within a single buddha-field, they are able to manifest their own attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment within countless buddha-fields.
Seventh, while remaining unmoving in physical form within a single buddha-field, they are able to manifest their arrival at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) within countless buddha-fields;
eighth, while remaining unmoving in physical form within a single buddha-field, they are able to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma within countless buddha-fields;
ninth, while remaining unmoving in physical form within a single buddha-field, they are able to manifest parinirvāṇa within countless buddha-fields.

Tenth, while remaining unmoving from his physical form within a single buddha-field, he is able to perform all manner of transformative manifestations throughout countless buddha-fields, according to the needs of those sentient beings who are to be converted. Although the bodhisattva performs these various transformations, he does not discriminate between the one who transforms and those who are transformed.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that a bodhisattva performs various transformative acts without discriminating between the transformer and the transformed?”
The Buddha said, “Good son!
I shall now speak by way of a parable; you should listen attentively.”

For example, just as the sun and moon illuminate the four great continents, universally shining upon and encompassing all sentient beings in the world, yet those suns and moons do not make such distinctions as "I am the illuminator" and "all sentient beings are the illuminated."
Why is this? Those suns and moons are all able to illuminate because of the karmic retribution from what was practiced in the past. "Good son!

The Bodhisattva is also like this: although they perform various transformative acts, they do not discriminate between the transformer and the transformed; there is no awakening whatsoever, nor is there any deliberate creation.

Why is this? It is because it is accomplished through the retribution of the Bodhisattva’s past superior wholesome karma; for when the Bodhisattva formerly practiced the bodhisattva path, according to his power of aspiration and his various deeds, he is now able to perform all transformative activities without any conceptual discrimination.
"Noble son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be well able to perform various transformative manifestations.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva cultivates ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to swiftly realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are these ten?
First, being able to perfectly fulfill and skillfully accumulate the practice of giving;

Second, they are fully endowed with the precepts, having well accumulated the precepts, possessing precepts without flaw or leakage, and precepts untainted by defilement; they possess the aggregate of precepts that is pure, stainless, and surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Third, they are fully endowed with patience.
Fourth, they are fully endowed with diligence.
Fifth, being well-endowed with meditative concentration;
sixth, being well-endowed with supreme wisdom;
seventh, being well-endowed with skillful means;
Eighth, they are well-endowed with all vows;
ninth, they are well-endowed with all powers;

tenth, they are well-endowed with correct wisdom and have skillfully accumulated wisdom, such that because the Bodhisattva has accomplished the non-common wisdom, they are able to surpass the wisdom of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and transcend the wisdom from the first Bodhisattva stage up to the ninth Bodhisattva stage.
"Good son!
If a bodhisattva cultivates these ten kinds of dharmas, they will be able to swiftly realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
When the Blessed One proclaimed these sublime teachings, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways.

Furthermore, all the Sumeru Kings, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, as well as other jewel mountains, Black Mountains, and various small hills within this trichiliocosm—along with their peaks and crags—naturally bent low toward Elephant Head Mountain, extending their homage to the Buddha and the sublime Dharma.
Furthermore, in this trichiliocosm, all flowering trees and all fruit-bearing trees bowed low toward Mount Gajaśīrṣa, making offerings to the World-Honored One and his True Dharma.

At that time, there were again countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas who manifested various kinds of clothing and ornaments; their accumulated volume was like that of Sumeru, the king of mountains, as they made offerings to the World-Honored One and his True Dharma.

Furthermore, there were countless hundreds of thousands of Śakras, Brahmās, and World-Protecting Devas, all of whom joined their palms and prostrated to the World-Honored One, raining down celestial māndārava flowers and mahāmāndārava flowers, scattering them over the Buddha.

Furthermore, there were countless hundreds of thousands of devaputras, each holding celestial robes, who remained in mid-air, whirling their entire bodies in circles, producing hundreds of thousands of kinds of pure and wondrous sounds as they extended their offerings.
They further scattered heavenly flowers over the Buddha and all spoke these words:
"Today we behold the Buddha, the World-Honored One, appearing in the world for a second time, turning the wheel of the true Dharma for a second time."
World-Honored One!

If there are sentient beings who possess great merit and cultivate various wholesome deeds, having planted the roots of virtue under previous Buddhas, only such persons as these are able to hear this True Dharma; how much more so those who, having heard it, are able to give rise to a pure mind?
Furthermore, there were countless hundreds of thousands of mahoragas, all of whom simultaneously thundered with the great sound of clouds and lightning.

They further manifested various kinds of great clouds that completely covered this trichiliocosm and Mount Elephant Head, raining down various fragrant waters until they were entirely filled; yet the sentient beings therein were not disturbed or distressed. Thus they performed these deeds as an act of offering.
Furthermore, there were countless hundreds of thousands of nāga maidens who, before the World-Honored One, produced the sounds of song and chant as an offering.

Additionally, there were countless hundreds of thousands of gandharva hosts and kinnara hosts who circumambulated this trichiliocosm and Mount Elephant Head, producing exquisite sounds of song and chant as an offering.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll Nineteen.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Questions of Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Scroll Twenty.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Appointed Court Disperser and Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of Fan Translation, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject, by Imperial Decree.

At that time, there were again countless hundreds of thousands of hosts of yakṣas who rained down various lotus flowers as an offering; furthermore, they blew and struck gentle breezes that brought peace and happiness to all who were touched by them.

Furthermore, from each of those various Tathāgatas within countless Buddha-fields, a great radiance was emitted from between their eyebrows in order to make offerings to the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Buddha and his True Dharma.

That light possessed various colors—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and crystal—as well as various hues such as that of emerald, and various marks. With these diverse radiances, it circled clockwise around this trichiliocosm, illuminating it everywhere and completely dispelling all darkness. The light then returned, circling Mount Elephant Head, before finally entering through the crown of the World-Honored One’s head.

Furthermore, there were countless hundreds of thousands of brahmins, kṣatriyas, and commoners who each held incense, flowers, scented ointments, powdered incense, various exquisite flower garlands, robes, banners, streamers, and precious parasols, placing them before the Buddha as an offering.

When the Buddha proclaimed this True Dharma and the devas, nāgas, and spirits presented their offerings, seventy-two nayutas of bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings, who had never before resolved upon awakening, all gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta.
At that time, there was a goddess named Dīrghāyuṣī who had long resided on this Elephant Head Mountain; she and her own retinue were already present at the Buddha’s assembly.

He immediately rose from his seat and, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha, went to his own palace, took various articles of worship, and returned to where the Buddha was. Having arrived at the Buddha’s presence, he paid him honor and respect with single-minded devotion, presenting all the offerings.
Having thus performed the offering with utmost sincerity,
he came before the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One!"
I know that throughout my long succession of past births, there were seventy-two thousand Buddhas, Tathāgatas,
all of whom once preached this True Dharma here on Mount Gajaśīrṣa.
"It is also of this same meaning, this same principle, and this same phrasing.
The Buddha said,
"Long-lived Goddess!"
"You have gained a most excellent benefit, having encountered such a jewel of the Dharma appearing in the world and hearing it personally, point by point.
At that time, there were among those in the assembly various devaputras who all had this thought:
"This goddess has long since heard such true Dharma and has previously drawn near to many Buddhas and Tathāgatas; for what reason is she unable to transform this female body?"
Then, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, having understood the thoughts in the minds of the devaputras, addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!

For what cause and for what reason does this long-lived goddess possess such great majesty and virtue? Having already heard such True Dharma in the past and having personally attended upon many Tathāgatas, why has she not yet transformed this female body?"
The Buddha said, “Good son!
One does not transform the female body for the sake of the great causal conditions that extensively bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.”
Why is this so? Good son!
This goddess has already established herself in the rank of a bodhisattva who dwells in the inconceivable liberation.
I know that this long-lived goddess of heaven, in the presence of countless Tathāgatas beyond calculation, exhorted them to resolve upon bodhicitta, up until their entry into great parinirvāṇa.
For this reason, this goddess has attained such vast supernatural powers and majestic virtue. Good son!

This goddess of Long Life, having made offerings to all the Buddhas within this Bhadrakalpa, shall attain Buddhahood within this Buddha-field, known by the name Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Long Life.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the goddess Dīrghāyuṣā, saying:
"You should now manifest the adornments of your own buddha-field.
Thereupon, the goddess Dīrghāyuṣā entered the samādhi called Manifesting All Forms and Appearances.

Within this samādhi, he manifested this trichiliocosm with its earth as level as the palm of a hand, removing the Black Mountains, the mountains of earth and stone, and all other pre-existing trees; it was pure, lovely, and composed of lapis lazuli.
